Hydrogen storage mechanisms are based on chemical adsorption and endohedral storage, where hydrogen mol-
ecules can bond to the carbon structure and hydrogen can be trapped inside the hollow fullerene cages. Advantages 
of 0D materials are unique properties due to curvature effects and quantum confinement and potential for chemical 
modifications to enhance hydrogen uptake. However, their practical application is hindered by complications such as 
a controlled mechanism to fill the fullerene nanocages with hydrogen and then release it when required and a proper 
synthesis route at moderate conditions. According to the analysis performed, most studies are based on fullerene using 
DFT calculations. Based on calculations, it might be said that these structures have a high content of hydrogen, which 
can be released in a controllable way, suggesting their potential to be excellent hydrogen storage media. While DFT is a 
powerful tool for understanding the fundamental properties of carbon materials for hydrogen storage, its limitations in 
handling dispersion interactions, finite temperature effects, large system sizes, and realistic environmental conditions 
might make it less suitable for providing precise predictions for practical applications.

1D NMs have received exceptional consideration as potential storage materials given their low cost, easy accessibility, 
good recycling characteristics, low densities, vast diversities of bulk and pore structures, and reasonably good chemi-
cal stability. For example, carbon nanotubes (CNTs) are one-dimensional materials with a hollow geometry that exhibit 
a significant specific surface area, superior electrical conductivity, and outstanding mechanical strength and thermal 
conductivity. Multi-wall carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) are metallic, whereas single-wall carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) are 
semiconducting, dependent on their helicity and diameter, and can significantly influence charge transfer processes. 
As appealing supports for heterogeneous catalysts, CNTs are considered ideal and unique templates for immobilizing/
depositing metallic nanoparticles (NPs) to build nanostructures.

Hydrogen might be stored in a bunch of carbon nanotubes, with  H2 molecules physisorbed on the outer surfaces of 
the CNTs or interstitial areas among the CNTs, which separate the distances between the tubes in a pressurized envi-
ronment. Previous studies of hydrogen storage in carbon nanotubes contended high storage capacities and were the 
impetus for extensive research worldwide. Further investigation revealed that the hydrogen adsorptive capacity was 
primarily a function of the specific surface area of the carbonaceous material [90–93]. Various studies have shown that 
physisorbed and chemisorbed hydrogen species can be stored in CNTs at gravimetric densities of 0.1–6.3 wt% and pres-
sures of 0.01–20 MPa [94–96]. Although CNTs appear to be more efficient at storing hydrogen than metal hydrides, the 
storage pressure in CNTs is approximately 5–10 times higher, resulting in increased storage costs.

In the paper of [97], NiFe decorated bamboo-like CNTs (NiFe@CNT) were applied as catalyst to improve hydrogen 
storage properties of Mg/MgH2. Following the surfactant model, the “magnesophilic end” of the NiFe combines with 
the Mg/MgH2 to form  Mg2Ni/Mg2NiH4 and α-Fe, while the “magnesiphobic end” of the CNT is broken down into a 
dispersion medium upon mechanical ball milling and hydrogen combustion. In Fig. 13(a–f ), NiFe@CNT’s SEM and TEM 
microstructures were shown depending on the calcination temperature. At 973 K, the length of the CNTs is short and 
the growth of the NiFe alloy particles is not very homogeneous (Fig. 13 (a–b)), but as the temperature increases to

absorbing 6.67wt% of  H2 within 60 s and 7.16wt% within 30 min after the addition of 5%wt% NiFe@CNT. Based on 
these findings, CNTs with a special structure supported by transition metal catalysts are essential in heterogeneous 
catalysis in Mg-based hydrogen storage. NiFe particles are warped by the carbon at the top, and the wall thickness 
of synthesized CNT is much lower.

Another study [16] examines how multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) acid functionalization affects their phys-
isorptive hydrogen storage mechanism at room temperature. In this respect, an array of functionalized CNTs is fabricated 
and exposed to extensive material characterization techniques and hydrogen storage measurements. Increased rough-
ness and apparent defects at the side walls increased after treating MWCNTs in the mixture of  H2SO4:HNO3. The highest 
interlayer spacing, oxygen/carbon ratio (26.09 at%), defect content, and specific surface area (215.3  m2/g) were found 
for the  H2SO4:HNO3 functionalized sample at 100 °C. The modifications mentioned above were crucial in increasing the 
hydrogen storage capacity of CNTs by ~ 150% at 298 K and 50 bar, with 51% hydrogen reversibility. The study showed that 
hydrogen molecules with a kinetic diameter of 2.89 Å could enter the increased interlayer spacing and move or diffuse 
between the layers. In summary, the presence of oxygen functional groups and defects is responsible for the additional 
hydrogen storage density since the enhancement in hydrogen absorption was more significant than the expansion in 
the surface area of the specimen.

From polyacrylonitrile-based nascent fibers (PAN-NF) with skin–core structure, nitrogen–oxygen co-doped activated 
carbon hollow fibers (N/O-ACHF) are fabricated [17]. The different activation difficulties between the skin and core parts 
provide a better structural condition for producing activated carbon hollow fibers. The resulting specimen has a relatively 
smooth outer-walled structure. The inner walled structure is dispersed with micron-sized macropores (0.31–2.18 μm). 
The benefits of the obtained compound rely on abundant micro-/mesoporous structure (0–6 nm) and oxygen-/nitrogen- 
functional groups. The surface oxygen functionalities are predominantly C–O, C = O, O = C–O, and P = O, and the surface 
nitrogen functionalities are predominantly pyridine, N–H,  NH4+, and  NO2. Its multi-stage pore structure and abundant 
surface functional groups provide excellent physical and structural conditions for hydrogen storage. At atmospheric pres-
sure, the hydrogen uptake of N/O-ACHF is equal to 1.35 wt%. Various transition metal-based nanocatalysts adsorbed on 
the CNT surface are considered to improve the properties of CNTs [18, 99–101]. The chemical dissociation of hydrogen 
molecules by adsorbed nanocatalysts enhances the storage of hydrogen atoms on the CNT surface [18, 99]. CNTs doped 
with transition metals can store hydrogen with a gravimetric density of 3.0 to 7.0 wt% at a pressure of approximately 
0.1 MPa [99]. For example, the concentration of chemisorbed H atoms increases (from 1.61 to 5.25 wt%) when the con-
centration of Ni nanoparticles on the surface of SWNT (0 to 8 wt% Ni) is increased. However, the hydrogen capacity of 
SWNT (2.99 wt%) is dramatically reduced when the nickel concentration is further increased (12 wt% Ni), attributed to 
the blocking effect due to the association of Ni nanoparticles on the surface of SWNT [100]. Alternatively, this is due to 
confinement-induced SWNT surface physical properties alteration by nanocluster binding patterns [101].

In the paper of U.Khalilov et al. [102], the effect of endohedral transition metal, particularly nickel, on the hydrogena-
tion properties of the single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) has been discovered. The study on this subject was 
achieved via MD simulations. The confinement effect is the interior of the SWNTs’ interaction with Ni metals/clusters. Due 
to the presence of endohedral atoms, the changes in the partial charges were observed, positively affecting the hydro-
genation properties. According to simulations, the gravimetric density of hydrogenated SWNTs is 1.86%, while endohedral 
Ni-doped SWNTs show a gravimetric density of 2.32–2.92% under ambient conditions depending on Ni concentration.
Additionally, Liang et al. [103] proposed a new method of CNT modification that regulates their hydrogen sorption 
active sites. To achieve this, the friction between hydrogen molecules and CNTs should be reduced, which enhances 
the hydrogenation reaction in the CNTs. Compared to conventional functional doping of composite, authors suggested 
function group grafted CNTS with nitrogen,  La2O3, and nickel and PLLA composite (N-CNT-  La2O3, fg-N-CNT-PLLA, and 
fg-Ni-CNT-PLLA). In addition, the TEM and XPS directly prove that  La2O3 or Ni, due to the adjustment of the grafted OH 
and  CONH2, the electron-donor effect of the doped metal, affects the peak position of the C-single bond and improves 
the polarity of the C-single bond, which is beneficial for the PLLA-Ni CNTs interaction. According to data, fg-Ni-CNT-
PLLA and N-CNT-  La2O3 possess outstanding hydrogen storage characteristics. The hydrogen sorption capacity of CNTs 
would be defined through the active sites in the porous CNTs. N-CNT-  La2O3 exhibits the maximum  H2 storage potential 
of 7.4 wt% and demonstrates a more than 20-fold steady hydrogen absorption/desorption cycle at 100 °C and 18 bar. At 
100 °C and 18 bar, fg- Ni-CNT-PLLA offers  H2 uptake of 6.2 wt%. Since the aggregation of the CNTs is due to the molecular

Salehabadi et al. have studied  Dy3Fe5O12 (DFO) nanoparticles by incorporating them into MWCNTs in acidic propyl-
ene glycol [104]. The results show a homogenous structure and spherically distributed particles with a size in the range 
between 10 and 35 nm. It was found that incorporating DFO reduces MWCNTs tube stacking and enhances the practical 
surface areas. Moreover, it was evident that DFO particles with a size between 10 and 14 nm could enter the tube, and 
other DFO particles either formed aggregates or absorbed onto the wall surface. As a result, compared to the initial state, 
the electrochemical hydrogen storage capacity of the device was increased up to 1000 mAh/g (~ 3.54%) at 15 cycles 
through the incorporation of DFO on the surfaces of MWCNTs.With the help of the reviewed articles, it can be concluded 
that using one-dimensional materials, including nanotubes, is problematic in ambient room conditions. However, with 
modifications involving chemical activation and doping, it is possible to significantly improve the sorption properties 
up to almost 3% under ambient conditions.

All in all, 1D nanostructures maintain great solid-state storage of hydrogen and alter hydrogen adsorption capacity by 
enhancing adsorption/desorption cycles. Hydrogen storage mechanisms of these materials is based on physisorption 
and spillover effect, where high surface area and curvature enable moderate hydrogen adsorption and they can act as 
a bridge for hydrogen spillover from a catalyst. The drawbacks of 1D nanomaterials hinder their practical application, 
notably inadequate sorption and desorption at high temperatures and the expense of their manufacture. Decorating 
CNTs with metals or metal oxides creates additional active sites and enhances hydrogen binding energy through chem-
isorption or physisorption. In the Table 3, hydrogenation properties of 1D materials with storage capacities reaching 
1.35–5.14 wt% at 77 K in the ambient-higher pressure, respectively are shown. Introducing elements such as nickel, 
nitrogen and  La2O3 into 1D carbon materials has been shown to significantly enhance their hydrogen storage capacity. 
Yet, high-pressure and low-temperature conditions are required to achieve appreciable hydrogen storage capacities for 
most of the works in Table 3. Pristine CNTs have a tendency to aggregate due to van der Waals forces. Decorating CNTs 
with nanoparticles or functional groups introduces steric hindrance, preventing aggregation and ensuring uniform dis-
persion, which improves overall stability. Recent advances in using different one-dimensional nanomaterials and their 
compounds in hydrogen storage, which were discussed in detail in this review, illustrate the progress made over the 
recent years in fabrication methods.

3.3   Two‑dimensional nanostructured carbon materials

2D material has become a hot topic recently due to its promising physical, electrical, chemical, and optical properties. 
2D nanomaterials are composed of thin layers that may be at least atom thick. Unlike bulk materials, 2D nanomaterials 
feature a high aspect ratio (surface-to-volume ratio), offering many atoms on their surface. These atoms render 2D materi-
als with different functions than internal atoms, making their surface area more excellent, thus changing the behavior of 
two-dimensional nanomaterials. Graphene has emerged as one of the most regarded and pivotal 2D materials, manifest-
ing several desirable features. Graphene’s unique characteristics encompass large surface area (2630  m2/g), lightness, 
conductivity (~ 5 × 103 W/(m K)), mechanical and chemical endurance, oxygen-containing functional groups, making it 
a good matrix material suitable to be used as support and substrate for oxide nanotechnology.

Due to its hydrophilicity, chemical structure, and atomic pore size, graphene oxide (GO) has found applications in 
water purification and gas separation [107, 108]. For instance, GO has recently been investigated as a material for key gas 
separation challenges. Interestingly, this research has shown that  H2 is highly permeable to other atmospheric gases like 
 O2 and  N2 for atom-thin, selective barriers for sensitive hydrogen storage devices. Related research has also shown that 
reducing GO to reduced GO (rGO) further reduces water permeability, with the retention of desirable gas permeability 
properties. In the present work, Mg nanocrystal-filled 2D rGO composites have been prepared for hydrogen storage.

This paper [109] introduces mixed dimensional reduced graphene oxide (GO)/Mg nanocrystals. In this compound, 
rGOs are the atomic boundary for barrier materials in functional compounds to ensure the highest level of environ-
mental protection for the lowest possible amount of inactive mass. rGO is an ideal encapsulant for the nano-laminate 
system described here, offering an atom-thin structure with minimal additional mass, inhibiting the degradation of Mg 
nanocrystals and enhancing rate-limiting hydrogen absorption/desorption processes. According to XANES measure-
ments, carbon K-edge intensities of 288.4 and 290.3 eV were achieved, showing the formation of carbon–oxygen or other 
oxygen-containing groups. Authors ascribe these measurements to the stabilization of multilaminate and Mg–O–C bond 
formation. In addition, the decrease in the average domain size of the  sp2 hybridized regions might be referred to as

According to a study by Patchkovskii et al. [110], by increasing the interlayer spacing of graphene from 6 to 8 Å, it 
is possible to enhance the storage capacity from 2–3%, achieving a range of 5.0–6.5 wt% of hydrogen at an operating 
pressure of 5 MPa. An early study by Carrete et al. [111] was reported that replacing graphene nanosheets with Al atoms 
could enhance hydrogen storage capacity. Graphene nanoribbons (GNRs) can be defined as strips of graphene. In GNRs 
featuring hydrogen-passivated edges, the spins are aligned in a zigzag pattern along each edge, exhibiting metallic or 
semiconducting behavior contingent on the alignment of spins at the edge pairs. However, their results did not satisfy 
DOE targets.

The present work [19] studies the effect of Al doping on the electronic states of graphene using DFT calculations. 
A chemical bond is formed between the  Al3+ ion and the hexagonal site of the benzene ring of graphene nanoflakes 
(GR). Diffusion of the Al species from one hexagonal site to the next occurs via the C–C bond center of benzene rings. 
The  Al3+ ion height was found to be 2.406 Å from the GR surface, with an observed increase in height corresponding to 
an incremental rise in Al charge (from + 1 to + 3). This phenomenon can be attributed to the observation that the posi-
tive charge of GR increases in tandem with the charge of Al. Consequently, the repulsive interaction between Al + and 
GR + intensifies with the growth of the valence charge. Figure 14 illustrates the structures of  H2 adsorbed on GR-Al 
(GR19-Al3 + -(H2)n, n = 1–4). When n = 1,  H2 is bonded to Al with a side-by-side arrangement, where the two hydrogen 
atoms of  H2 are bonded to Al with near-equal distances (R1 = 2.445 Å, R10 = 2.415 Å). The second  H2 molecule,  (H2)2, is 
bonded to Al with a similar side-by-side configuration with n = 2. The hydrogen binding energy to GR-Al3 + was equal to 
0.7 kcal/mol, which is considered low. The doping of GR with Al ions results in the formation of new electronic bands in 
the low-energy regions, suggesting the possibility of electronic applications.

In the work of Luhadiya et al. [56], the authors investigated the hydrogen adsorption behavior of functionalized Ti 
and N-doped graphene sheets containing a variety of defects (D–G) using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. In 
particular, graphene sheets with monovacancy, Stone–Wales, and multiple double vacancies. The research showed that 
the hydrogen adsorption capacity of the graphene sheets improved significantly as the concentration of Ti atoms on 
the D-G sheets increased. Due to DV(III)-G sheets having a small number of large pores that bind hydrogen with high 
binding energy, the adsorption capacity of DV(III)-G sheets is maximal at 300 K. The N doping on the D–G sheets initially 
reduced their hydrogen adsorptive capacity, but the N–D–G sheets increased their hydrogen adsorptive capacity with 
increasing Ti atom concentrations. The Ti-N-DV(III)-G sheet with a Ti concentration of 10.5% showed a hydrogen uptake 
of 5.5 wt% compared to all other defect types at 300 K and 100 bar pressure.

in this paper [112]. Heteroatom (B, N, S, P, etc.) doping is frequent and efficient in research to enhance the hydrogen 
storage performance of porous graphene. The empty p-orbitals of the B atom increase the adsorption energy of the 
modified atom. B-doping can significantly improve the binding energy of Be when graphene is modified with Be 
atoms. Calculations show that for these four B doping methods, B transfers electrons to C by calculating the charge

the storage of hydrogen [21]. Boron doping of PG enhances hydrogen storage efficiency from 4.79 wt% to 7.30–7.40 
wt%. In the case of V2-B16-PG, each vanadium atom can adsorb up to five hydrogen atoms with a mean adsorption 
energy of—0.34 eV/H2. The hydrogen storage capacity of the structure reaches 8.07% by weight, well above the 
original V-modified PGs. This investigation highlights that boron doping can be efficient in upgrading the hydrogen 
storage capacity of the structure, and it is anticipated that boron-doped PG modified with beryllium or vanadium 
will also be able to achieve hydrogen storage.

Currently, the properties of cobalt alloys are not suitable for use in this area, and their ability to preserve hydrogen 
will need to be subsequently strengthened. As a substitute for noble metal doping, graphene was doped with two 
non-metallic elements (nitrogen and sulfur) by hydrothermal technique [113]. The experimental findings reveal that, in 
contrast with the single-element doping, the electrode co-doped with sulfur and nitrogen acquires greater values in the 
electrochemical storage of hydrogen. Since nitrogen atoms can provide more active centers in graphene, the discharge 
capacity cycle stability of NSG-doped alloys is better than that of GO-doped and NG-doped alloys that are appropriate 
for hydrogen storage. Its large specific surface area provides more reaction sites for hydrogen to diffuse, and its excellent 
conductivity enhances interfacial charge transfer. The sulfur in graphene contains a larger atomic size than the nitrogen, 
raises the polarization, and prompts an increased density of electrons in the graphene network.

The one-step hydrothermal synthesis of  CeVO4/rGO nanocomposites is expected to enhance hydrogen storage effi-
ciency owing to their unique features, such as appropriate electrochemical behavior, high specific surface area, and 
good porosity [22]. As well as controlling  CeVO4 nanoparticle growth, hydrazine is responsible for reducing graphitic 
oxides (GO) to reduced graphite oxides (rGO), allowing a single-step synthesis. Storage results indicated that adding 
graphene enhanced interlayer synergy, increasing hydrogen storage capacity. Compared to other nanostructures, the 
highest electrochemical hydrogen storage was achieved in the fabricated nanocomposite with the largest surface area 
and volume of pores. Research has shown that pore size is a very effective determinant of hydrogen storage capacity. 
The amount of hydrogen uptake is substantially raised due to the stronger hydrogen bonds formed in the smaller pores. 
Fine-grained and mesoporous materials have been reported to be promising for hydrogen storage. The application of 
porous fine-grained materials is limited due to the slow mass transfer rate, whereas mesoporous materials overcome 
this limitation. The smaller the pore diameter, the larger the surface area needed to absorb hydrogen, which is evident.
Using a straightforward and innovative hydrothermal route, the ternary solid phase of  UO3⋅NH3H2O has been efficiently 
manufactured in an ammoniated environment [114]. Uranium may serve as a powerful chemical store for hydrogen, 
which contains nearly twice the weight of gas by volume of liquefied hydrogen. In addition, the strong interactions 
between the graphene matrix and the metal oxide nanoparticles are exciting. Hydrogen adsorption on uranium-doped 
graphene nanosheets was the area of interest of Vanik Ghoulipoura et al. [115] and he found that, in addition to ura-
nium’s significant propensity for interaction with graphene, the obtained U-decorated graphene nanoparticles perform 
hydrogen adsorption storage surfaces. The hydrogen storage capacity for graphene oxide was only 2.30 wt%, whereas 
by adding  UO3⋅NH3H2O nanoparticles in GO, it was 61.46% by weight. As the number of cycles and repetitions rise, the 
amount and power of hydrogen storage escalates in all samples, likely due to the formation of new empty sites that 
foster hydrogen adsorption.

J. Ikot et al. proposed a study [116] about metals (Al, Ca, Mg, Ni, and Zn) and phosphorus-doped graphene by apply-
ing the DFT computational method. By replacing the carbon atom in the graphene structure, the nonmetallic phosphor 
(P) dopant increases the activation region on the surface as it acts as a free charge carrier, improving its conductivity, 
surface chemical activity, and structural features of the graphene surface. The effect of some transition metals on car-
bon materials’ surfaces is known to be influenced by the Kubas interaction, which produces strong bonds due to the 
hybridization of hydrogen sigma (s) and anti-sigma (s*) orbitals with transition metal d-orbitals [117]. To reduce the 
possibility of clustering of the transition metal on the surface—the main drawback of the Kubas interaction [118], the 
surface has to be doped with phosphorus. The original bond distance from H54 to H55 within the  H2 molecule is 0.752 A. 
The hydrogen atoms are bonded to either side of the metal atoms for each structure. On the metals used to decorate the 
graphene surface, the hydrogen  (H2) molecule interacted directly. The adsorption energies of hydrogen at  H2@Ni-G and 
 H2@Al-G were the highest, which is appropriate for their low adsorption distance. In addition to this, those two samples

For developing novel energy materials, efficient engineering strategies to synthesize hydrides with high capacity 
and favorable reversibility are essential. In this work [119], by confinement on graphene via a solution self-confinement 
method, a nano-sized Mg-based borohydride, Mg(BH4)2, having a stable structure, has been fabricated. With a layer of 
8.8 nm (Fig. 14c), graphene-bonded Mg(BH4)2 displays a crumpled 2D nanosheet pattern according to Fig. 15a, b. The 
wrinkly morphology of 2D Mg(BH4)2@GR is less clear than that of GR. This observation suggests that the successful 
confinement of Mg(BH4)2 is the reason for this phenomenon, which was previously studied by Han et al. [120]. With a 
superior capacity of 12.0 wt.%, such 2D nano-Mg(BH4)2 can start dehydrogenation at 67.9 °C and 100 bars of hydrogen 
pressure, which is 190.5 °C lower than pure Mg(BH4)2. According to isothermal dehydrogenation tests and kinetic fitting 
results, the 2D composite has significantly upgraded dehydrogenation kinetics, with an activation energy of 31.3 kJ/
mol. Theoretical calculations of Mg(BH4)2 and the graphene-bound intermediate  MgB12H12, the charge transfer state 
of both samples is modified to facilitate de/rehydrogenation, resulting in substantial thermodynamic improvements in 
reversible hydrogen storage performance for graphene composite.

Graphene-supported nickel catalysts were discovered to ameliorate alloy particle size and grain size uniformity, declin-
ing the hydrogen-releasing temperature of the composite by approximately 90 °C. For the synthesis of the  CeMg12/Ni 
alloy, the mechanical ball milling method was employed [121]. The broadening of the diffraction peaks of the alloy with 
increasing graphene content can be seen from the diffraction peak analysis. The gradual widening of the diffractometric 
peak suggests that the addition of graphene in the process of ball milling of the alloy helps to refine the alloy particles, 
thus increasing the alloys’ internal specific surface area and hydrogen diffusion channel and strengthen the dissolution 
of Ni in the primary state of the alloy. By lowering the thermal stability of the alloy hydride, the addition of graphene 
reinforces its dehydrogenation performance. Adding graphene is advantageous in building folded or granular features 
on the surface of the particles and enhancing surface activity. It has been shown that the ratio of ID to IG directly reflects 
the change in the surface defects of the treated specimen, increasing the pore density and the surface activity of the alloy 
by bonding to the surface of the alloy grains. Based on the lowest activation energy for dehydrogenation of 85.23 kJ/
mol and a special dehydrogenation time of 1090 s, superior dehydrogenation kinetic performances were obtained for 
the alloy with 6 wt% graphene.

In summary, various modified graphene structures, such as decorated graphene, doped graphene, vacancy-doped 
graphene, vacancy-doped, and decorated-doped graphene, have been investigated to modify the reactivity of pristine 
graphene. Hydrogen storage of these mechanisms based on physisorption and chemisorption, where large specific area 
follows for efficient hydrogen adsorption and hydrogen atoms can chemisorb to the graphene surface or edges. Advan-
tages of 2D materials comprise high surface area (~ 2630  m2/g for single-layer graphene) and tunable interlayer spacing 
as well as easy chemical modifies (e.g. doping with metals or heteroatoms). Table 4 reviews the hydrogenation properties 
of 2D materials reaching about 5.16–14.13 wt% from ambient temperature to 300 °C, respectively. When combined with 
other storage materials (e.g., metal hydrides), decorated graphene enhances overall hydrogen storage performance.

3.4   Three‑dimensional nanostructured carbon materials

Alternatively to CNT and graphene, 3D-based carbon composites can extend the dimensions along all three directions. 
In addition to well-studied 3D nanomaterials, containing mesoporous carbon and activated carbon (AC) [126], there are 
novel types of carbonaceous materials which can assemble CNTs and graphene. Plenty of 3D nanocarbon structures, 
such as vertically aligned CNTs [127], sponges [128], foams [129], graphene arrays [130], graphene foams [131], etc., can 
be synthesized in an attempt to create novel materials for hydrogen storage. The merits of 3D carbon nanostructured 
materials for hydrogen storage comprise characteristics of 1D and 2D nanomaterials, such as outstanding conductivity, 
high charge transport, excellent surface area, and durability. Besides, these materials offer new hierarchical structures 
and minimize transition resistance.

Ongoing research is being undertaken to develop and characterize multifunctional materials for energy and environ-
mental applications. A recent study by N. Kostoglou et al. [23] is concluded that a nanoporous polymeric/polyaniline-
derived activated carbon (PDAC) with a large surface area (~ 2200  m2/g) and pore volume (~ 1  m3/g) has been exten-
sively investigated for its potential use in  H2 storage and supercapacitor energy storage. Coral-like fibers with diameters 
between 100 and 200 nm and a foam-like porous structure for the former were observed for the freeze-dried polymer 
and commercial activated carbon (YP80F). According to the signal-to-noise ratio, the high-frequency region showed a 
comprehensive feature consisting of two components—the 2D band at ~ 2700 cm-1, due to second-order scattering 
processes, and the combination D + D’ defect-activated mode at ~ 2900  cm-1. A turbostratic structure with significant 
distortions in the stacking of the graphene sheets is suggested by the absence of a pronounced 2D band. The average 
porosity is significantly smaller in PDAC than in the YP80F reference, indicating significantly smaller pores in PDAC [132]. 
PDAC exhibited a completely reversible type I(a) isotherm, as classified by IUPAC [133], with a distinct saturation plateau, 
indicating a purely microporous material (< 2 nm pore size). The shape of the YP80F isotherm is more characteristic of 
the I(b) type, which is the IUPAC classification for microporous materials with a broader distribution. The PDAC achieved 
a high and completely reversible gravimetric excess  H2 uptake of ~ 5.5 wt.% at 77 K and ~ 60 bar, together with the heat 
of adsorption of ~ 8.3 kJ/mol at zero coverage, indicating excellent  H2 adsorption efficiency at low temperatures.

A novel process for the preparation of porous carbon materials from the vapors of biomass pyrolysis using a calcium 
citrate template has been proposed [134]. The effects of pyrolytic temperature, pyrolytic heating rate, and carbonaceous 
precursor preparation temperature on biomass pyrolytic product yield, composition of light biofuel, and porous carbon 
structure have been studied. As the heating rate increases, the specific surface area and volume of the porosity of the 
carbon increases and decreases, peaking around 10 K/min. Simultaneously, the microporosity exhibits a rising trend 
and remains almost unchanged after 10 K/min. Porosity in carbon materials prepared by CaO template process can be 
attributed to removing nano-CaO and internal activation by  CO2 and  H2O. Slow heating rates, e.g., 2 K/min, produce low 
pyrolysis steam and excess calcium citrate in the carbonaceous feedstock. This leads to overdevelopment of the pore 
structure of BG-2, with macro- and mesopores dominating. This allows the complete mixing of pyrolysis fumes and cal-
cium citrate, promoting the formation of a mesoporous and microporous pore structure in the subsequent carbonation. 
If the heating speed is too fast, too much steam is produced, and the quality of the pores is reduced. Optimal pyrolytic 
temperature (823 K), heating rate (10 K/min), and carbonaceous precursor preparation temperature (473 K), the manu-
factured porous carbon material has the largest specific surface area of 1703  m2/g, a relatively high microvoid volume 
of 0.51  cm3/g and a microporosity of 24.17%. At 77 K at atmospheric pressure, the  H2 adsorptive capacity of the carbon 
material can be as high as 170.12  cm3/g (1.53 wt%).

This study [24] conveys the use of a novel three-dimensional graphene structure that can overcome the limitations of 
the two-dimensional nature of graphene and its application in hydrogen absorption. These findings evidence hydrogen 
bonding on single-layer graphene conformally grown by the epitaxial growth method on the (0001) face of a porous 
4H-SiC wafer. Due to its two-dimensional nature, hydrogen storage devices based on pristine flat graphene would require 
prohibitively large surfaces. Graphene can be folded into 3D compact structures that retain its outstanding properties. 
These atoms rearrange themselves into graphene’s characteristic hexagonal geometry. The first layer formed is the so-
called buffer layer, where 30% of the C atoms are covalently bonded to Si atoms. Subsequent sublimation of Si results 
in the growth of the second buffer layer, separating the first layer and transforming the latter into a single layer of free-
standing graphene. Van der Waals interactions are the only way the resulting layer is bonded to the substrate. The mor-
phology of the 3D substrate is closely followed by the graphene layers grown by this method. They form a meandering

three-dimensional structure by covering the pores of the SiC structure. Three-dimensional graphene forms a chemical 
bond with deuterium atoms when exposed to  D2. This suggests a catalytic cleavage mechanism and is the first report 
of such a phenomenon in unfunctionalized graphene-based materials. It also shows that the porous material’s three-
dimensional dendritic structure temporarily retains desorbed molecules, inducing delayed emission. Their ability to 
chemisorb atoms after catalytic hydrogen decomposition and large surface area/volume ratios make them promising 
substrates for hydrogen storage devices.

Of all the transition metal catalysts, Fe effectually modulates the de/rehydrogenation features of  MgH2 [25]. The usage 
of an appropriate support for the scaffolding/nanoconfinement of nanoparticles can assist to alleviate the agglomeration 
of Fe particles [135]. A proper support for metallic catalysts has been discovered to be hollow carbon spheres (HCS) due 
to their mesoporous nature. One-pot methods can manufacture a highly porous carbon network [136, 137]. Depending 
on their shape and size, HCS structure significantly affects hydrogen sorption properties (a high BET value, voids, hol-
low spaces, doping). To enhance these features, the defects and thin walls can be created to increase the amount of  H2 
in HCS. This work found HCS in sizes between 200 and 500 nm with an interconnecting tubular network with pore size 
between 10 and 25 nm. The high-pressure hysteresis loop shows that HCS contains large pores ranging from mesopores 
to macropores. The TEM image shows that the  MgH2 particles are trapped inside the HCS together with the tiny Fe parti-
cles. A clear indication of the interaction between the Fe nanoparticles and the carbon atoms of the HCS is the formation 
of the Fe3C phase. This interaction is expected to prevent the accumulation of Fe particles during de/rehydrogenation 
by keeping the Fe particles intact with the HCS. This is a favorable environment for the synergistic enhancement of the 
sorption properties of  MgH2. The initial desorption temperature for  MgH2 catalyzed by hollow carbon spheres and Fe 
nanoparticles  (MgH2-Fe-HCS) was observed to be 225.9 °C with a hydrogen storage capacity of 5.60 wt%.

Enriching hydrogen storage in 3D graphene remains to be explored, with metal atoms being added to functionalize the 
material, such as Pd, Pt, or Ti, which have already been proven to improve hydrogen storage in flat graphene [138–140]. 
Decorated Pt–Co bimetallic nanoparticles on N-doped mesoporous carbon (Pt–Co@NMC) were developed to improve 
performance [141], whereas Co was added to increase capacity and Pt to enhance kinetic performance. The specimens 
showed a standard IV isotherm and a type  H2 hysteresis loop, reflecting a mesoporous nature and cage-like pores (3 mm) 
with small entries. 2% Pt–Co@NMC composite contains many defect sites, which may positively affect hydrogen storage. 
This was reported according to the integrated intensity ratio of D and G bands of 1.27, which value was high enough. The 
neighboring N doping, which can introduce more defects, provide more active sites, and increase the insertion of H atoms 
into the carbon composites, will also affect the carbon atoms’ spin density and charge distribution. All the samples were 
similarly spherical, and those with platinum inlays were rough, and the particles were agglomerated. The carbon matrix 
encapsulates the metal particles, as the high-magnification SEM images show. This carbon-covered metal structure offers 
excellent advantages regarding hydrogen storage capacity and may delay or even prevent metal particle aggregation 
during charging and discharging to some degree. Significant elements in enhancing the electrochemical performance 
of hydrogen storage are the synergistic effect of metallic cobalt and platinum and the highly dispersed metallic Co and 
Pt nanoparticles in the carbon composite material.

Hydride-graphite composites have obtained considerable focus due to their elevated thermal conductivities [142]. 
Milling the alloy with nano graphite (NG) powder, nanocomposite materials with unique microstructures of nano-sized 
graphite flakes and graphene-embedded and supported nanocrystalline-amorphous alloys can be fabricated [143, 144]. 
 Sm5Mg41 + x wt% nano-graphite (NG) (x = 0, 2, 4, 8, 12) components are synthesized via ball-milling [145]. As a result of 
grinding and NG doping, the intensity of the hydrogen absorber/desorber peak decreases, and the peak width increases, 
resulting in a significantly smaller powder size and storage of strain energy, contributing to hydrogen desorption. Mg 
produced by ball milling is easily precipitated on the surface of nano graphite due to its good thermal conductivity 
and large specific surface area. Furthermore, many microstructural defects, such as nanocrystalline grain boundaries, 
dislocations, sub-grain boundaries, and micro-twins, are seen, resulting from crushing and cold welding during milling. 
As the nano graphite content rises, an increasing number of nanocrystalline Mg phases appear on the surface of the NG 
sheets as shown in Fig. 16a–c. NG has been found on the surface of hydrogen storage alloys, forming an extremely stable 
composite. Many NG nanosheets are embedded in the alloy, introducing more nanosurfaces into the composites. It is 
found that nano-interfaces of NG exert a structural constraint on  MgH2 nanocrystal growth during hydrogen absorption 
and that nanocrystals dominate composite microstructure after hydrogen absorption. This helps attain a substantial 
outcome on the Mg-based alloy’s hydrogen hydriding and dehydriding reaction.

Carbon aerogels are highly encouraging for hydrogen storage due to their lightweight, porous structure and tunable 
properties. Pure carbon aerogels rely on physisorption, which is less efficient at room temperature Enhancements via 
doping or functionalization are requmeired to enhance surface properties and resolve temperature-dependent limita-
tions. In the work of Cheng et al. [148], incorporating nitrogen and nickel nanoparticles enhances binding energy and 
storage performance, exhibiting hydrogen storage capacity of 7.4 wt% at 77 K. The morphological study showed that the 
material is primarily composed of micro- and mesopores. Due to weak hydrogen-surface interactions at 298 K, storage 
experiments are conducted at 77 K to meet the DOE’s 5.5 wt% target. However, at this low temperature, hydrogen dis-
sociation from metal ions becomes challenging, leading to reduced storage capacity with increased Ni particle loading. 
The CAs quantity was kept constant while varying the Ni dopant mass percentages, producing samples labeled NixN2-
CAs (x = 1, 2, 5, 10). The Ni1N2 sample achieved a hydrogen storage capacity of 7.4 wt%, 25% higher than the original 5.9 
wt%. This improvement is attributed to nitrogen doping, which altered the charge distribution around nitrogen atoms, 
enhancing hydrogen interactions.

Table 5 outlines the hydrogen absorption properties of carbon nanomaterials within the 3D morphologies for vari-
ous hydrogen storage systems. The collected data analysis demonstrates that carbon nanomaterials can be applied as 
catalysts, coating layers, substrates, etc. The different dimensionality of carbon materials, their synthesis routes, hydrogen 
uptake, wt.% (in some cases electrochemical performance based on discharge capacity), conditions of absorption/des-
orption cycles, and required time are illustrated. According to Table 5, maximum hydrogen storage capacity of 10.2 wt%. 
is reached at 77 K and 55 bars, while at 25–340 °C hydrogen sorption capacities vary from 3,15 to 3,75 wt% in the pres-
sure range of 0–75 bars. At room temperature, the weak hydrogen-carbon interaction is insufficient to retain hydrogen 
molecules effectively. However, at 77 K, the reduced kinetic energy of hydrogen molecules enables efficient physisorp-
tion, leveraging the large surface area and microporous structure of 3D materials [149]. At cryogenic temperatures, the 
high surface area of 2D materials may not fully compensate for their lack of a 3D interconnected structure, limiting gas 
diffusion and storage. However, at room temperature, their functionalized surfaces enable stronger hydrogen binding, 
making them more effective for ambient storage applications [150, 151].

In summary, 3D carbon-based materials for hydrogen storage maintain characteristics of 1D and 2D nanomateri-
als. The material offers significant advantages, including high volumetric and gravimetric hydrogen storage capacities, 
extensive tunability of pore size and distribution, and scalable, cost-efficient production techniques, such as those utiliz-
ing biomass. The drawbacks associated with 3D materials encompass lower electronic conductivity compared to their 
2D counterparts, and the critical need for pore size optimization to enrich adsorption performance. Carbon aerogels 
provide hierarchical porosity and outstanding cryogenic storage potential, whereas porous carbon materials are both 
cost-effective and easily scalable. Future research will likely focus on optimizing their properties through functionaliza-
tion and hybridization with other materials to achieve practical hydrogen storage systems.

4   Summary and outlook

This review summarizes the various routes for the design and synthesis of carbon nanomaterials that have been devel-
oped and studied extensively for their application in the field of hydrogen storage. Research on carbon nanomaterials 
has continually attracted significant attention and has resulted in pivotal advances. They are highly sought-after in a 
variety of fields, including lithium-ion battery materials, optoelectronic materials, catalyst carriers, chemical and biological 
sensors, hydrogen storage materials, supercapacitor materials, and other significant applications due to their distinctive 
structure and exceptional physical and chemical properties. Generally, carbon materials ranging from 0D to 3D are con-
sidered promising hydrogen storage materials owing to their chemical stability, low molar mass, high surface area, and 
variations of different forms and structures. The surface area of carbonaceous materials is regarded as one of the pivotal 
aspects of hydrogen sorption properties since hydrogen storage capacity is proportional to a given area. Taking this into 
consideration, efficient hydrogen storage via carbon-based materials is established on porous spatial structures along 
with high surface area. Thus, structural and spatial alterations or catalytic enhancements of carbon-based materials are 
necessary for building safe, reliable, and high-surface-area hydrogen storage systems working at moderate conditions.
The activity of carbon materials for hydrogen storage varies significantly depending on their dimensional structure. 
These discrepancies arise due to variations in surface area, pore structure, electronic properties, and interaction mecha-
nisms with hydrogen. For most practical hydrogen storage applications, 3D carbon materials are the best option due to 
their balance of high storage capacity, scalability, and cost-effectiveness. They are particularly effective for physisorption-

and microporous structure of 3D materials. For cutting-edge, high-efficiency designs that incorporate room-temperature 
storage, 2D carbon materials offer a promising path forward, provided the challenges of aggregation and cost can be 
addressed. For room-temperature storage, 2D carbon materials are promising due to their functionalized surfaces, which 
enable stronger hydrogen binding, despite hindrances like aggregation and cost. However, at cryogenic temperatures, 
their lack of a 3D interconnected structure limits gas diffusion and storage efficiency.

Currently, the best hydrogen storage capacity range for carbon-based materials lies between 4.65 and 6.5 wt% 
obtained experimentally at ambient conditions. However, studies using DFT and Monte Carlo calculations show higher 
values up to 8 wt%.

Creating affordable materials and techniques that possess the necessary kinetics and thermodynamics is a primary 

obstacle in the field of hydrogen storage technologies. The review highlights some main points:

1.  The most prevalently used methods to improve hydrogen storage characteristics are incorporation of different ele-
ments/catalysts, nanostructuring and nanoconfinement, and chemical and physical activation of biomass and coal-
based carbons.

2.  Several studies based on carbon structures, entailing graphene, graphite, nanotube, and fullerene, have been inves-

tigated for hydrogen storage, involving DFT studies, and promising results have been acquired.

3.  As a result, various approaches, such as defect engineering and surface functionalization, have been applied to 
enforce the hydrogen storage properties of these structures. These strategies allow us to improve hydrogen storage 
in carbon structures such as graphene, carbon nanotubes, and fullerenes.

4.  Nanostructuring has improved the surface area of carbonaceous materials. It also affects better hydrogen storage 

capacities due to the formation of nanosized pores.

The ultimate objective is to craft carbon-based materials capable of achieving a hydrogen storage capacity of around 
6.5 wt% while maintaining the essential adsorption/desorption rate under standard room temperature and pressure con-
ditions. Although some materials have potential storage capacities, difficulties still exist in properly integrating carbon-
based materials with hydrogen storage technologies. Therefore, addressing upcoming issues should be a primary focus.

We now discuss the several noteworthy attributes of our AM Cu-
ANP composite. First of all, the complete elimination of printing
defects (such as microvoids) due to inadequate fusion, is difﬁcult for
L-PBF copper-based materials because of their low laser absorptivity in
the infrared laser range13,17,18. We measured the laser absorptivity of our
initial Cu-B4C powder mixtures with different microparticle fractions,
revealing a surprisingly high laser absorptivity of more than 70% for
composite powders (8 and 12 vol.%) at a wavelength of 1064 nm
(Supplementary Fig. 7a). This represents a nearly fourfold improve-
ment in absorptivity compared to pure copper. The mechanisms of
microparticles in mediating the laser-powder interaction can be
revealed by using computational full laser ray tracing (Methods). The

reﬂections, are found to be eventually absorbed by the microparticles
as a result of their signiﬁcantly higher absorptivity compared to cop-
per powders (Supplementary Fig. 7b–d). This prevents powder spat-
tering and localized laser heating in the composite powder bed,
promoting a uniform energy absorption process19. Moreover, previous
reports indicate that the particle-induced increase in melt viscosity can
stabilize vapor depression ﬂuctuations and control liquid droplet
coalescence20,21, enabling a dramatic reduction of defects. Due to these
effects, the relative density of all our as-built samples is as high as
>99.8%. Such an improvement of microstructural consistency and the
elimination of printing porosities would help the nanocomposites to
fully display their intrinsic mechanical properties.

Strengthening and stress delocalization behaviour
The high yield strength of our as-built copper nanocomposites can be
explained by the Orowan strengthening mechanism due to densely
distributed nanoparticles, aided also by the high densities of disloca-
tions and grain reﬁnement introduced during L-PBF, as revealed by our
strengthening mechanism analyses in Methods subsection ‘Estimating
the yield strength of the as-built nanocomposites’. Traditionally, dis-
locations bypassing obstacles could accumulate in the form of Orowan
loops22. The microstructural heterogeneity adds long-range back
stresses on the ensuing dislocations to promote hardening. However,
the dislocations stored would normally cause interface stress con-
centrations and crack nucleation, leading to reduced ductility. Our
Cu–ANP does not face this traditional dilemma, such that the ductility

is much improved. This is evidenced by the ﬁndings via fracture sur-
face analyses. Notably, Cu-12%–ANP shows no evidence of nano-
particles in the dimples, in contrast to the corresponding Cu-12%-CNPs,
which contain many nanoparticles at the bottoms of their dimples
(Supplementary Fig. 8a, b). This observation indicates that the CNPs
led to stress concentrations at interphase interfaces and tend to
nucleate cracks/decohesion upon deformation, similar to the failure
behaviours of precipitate-strengthened alloys22. In stark contrast,
amorphous nanoparticles do not suffer from this drawback. The
absence of premature failure in Cu-ANP nanocomposites is consistent
with the presence of necking, as predicted by the Considère criterion
(see Supplementary Fig. 6d); however, the Cu-12%-CNP nanocompo-
site fractures before necking occurs, indicating signiﬁcant stress con-
centration. As shown in Fig. 4a, a group of grains after 3% strain is
examined using high-resolution EBSD, which enables a quantitative
cross-correlation-based analysis of strain and stress (Methods). As
observed, the residual elastic strain ﬁeld relative to the reference
region (i.e., the lowest kernel average misorientation value within a
grain) in the Cu–ANP sample exhibits much lower magnitudes and
more uniform distributions across all selected grains, compared with
its crystallized counterpart. For a further precise evaluation of the
deformation compatibility in Cu–ANP, we conducted precession
electron diffraction (PED)-based automated crystal orientation map-
ping (ACOM) via TEM for the 3%-deformed sample, with a mapping
spatial resolution of 1 nm (Fig. 4b). Speciﬁcally, the two-beam bright-
ﬁeld TEM images show random distributions of dislocations inside the
copper grains, and no discernible dislocation pile-ups are observed at
the matrix-nanoparticle interface. The overall dislocation density, as
estimated from the TEM images of the deformed Cu–ANP, is higher
(~1.1 × 1015 m−2) than that in the as-printed state (~2.3 × 1014 m−2), sug-
gesting dislocation multiplication and therefore strain hardening. Note
that the point-to-point misorientation proﬁle reveals a very low local
misorientation across the interface (less than 0.5°, Fig. 4b), indicating a
more uniform spread of the stored dislocations. It appears that the
geometrically necessary dislocations that would otherwise pile-up
near the interfaces have been accommodated via shear transforma-
tions at the surface of the ANPs (to be discussed below). On the con-
trary, in the CNP case dislocations piled up as expected, to accumulate
at the Cu-CNP interface, as evidenced by both the post-deformation
TEM and electron channelling contrast imaging analyses (Supple-
mentary Fig. 9). This ANP-induced stress delocalization at the interface
is the primary mechanism driving stable deformation without pre-
mature failure in the L-PBF nanocomposites.

In situ synchrotron XRD and atomic scale modelling
We also employed in situ synchrotron XRD experiments with crystal
plasticity ﬁnite element (CPFE) modelling (Methods)9. This approach
allows us to dissect the mechanical behaviour of each sample com-
ponent despite the amorphous nature of the nanoparticles. Figure 4c
shows the lattice strain εhkl along the loading direction against the
applied true stress (σ) for several representative {hkl} reﬂections of
copper in different nanocomposites (hollow symbols, 8 vol.% of
nanoparticles). Initially, all reﬂections exhibit elastic deformation, with
slopes differing due to the elastic anisotropy of diffraction planes.
Upon straining, the lattice strain of the {220} reﬂection in both samples
ﬁrst shows a nonlinear trend, turning upwards, and the lattice strain of
the {200} reﬂection deviates from a linear trend in a downward
direction due to the occurrence of load transfer from the soft {220} to
hard {200} reﬂections, revealing the early onset of microplastic yield-
ing. As deformation proceeds, progressive yielding occurs sequentially
from the {111}, {311} to {200} reﬂections. Notably, compared with those
of Cu–CNPs, the crystallographic families of Cu–ANPs are more resis-
tant to softening due to the greater uniform elongation values of the
composites. We calibrate our CPFE model in terms of simulated lattice
strain responses based on in situ diffraction data (solid lines in Fig. 4c).

The stress‒strain curves derived from the CPFE model closely match
the experimental data (Supplementary Fig. 10a). Then, we inversely
determine the constitutive relationships between copper and nano-
particles as a function of applied strain during deformation, the results
of which are displayed in Fig. 4d. Copper in Cu–ANP has a lower initial
yield strength due to the lower initial dislocation density (Supple-
mentary Fig. 10b; a higher dislocation density in Cu–CNP may be
attributed to thermal misﬁt upon sample cooling after heat
treatment23); however, its dislocation accumulation and strain hard-
ening rates are slightly greater. Importantly, the ANPs demonstrate
remarkably improved strain hardening, contributing to most (61%) of
the strain hardening magnitude of Cu–ANP (the true strain ranges
from 1% to 7%). This signiﬁcantly improved hardening is primarily
attributed to the self-hardening (and stiffening) of the ANPs as well as
the associated hardening of the interface-affected zone24. Here, the
ANPs have been rapidly melt-quenched at cooling rates around 108 K/s,
such that many dangling bonds and much excess volume would be
available for bond switching to accomplish shear transformations25.
This latter process accommodates the dislocations running into the
nanoparticles, and relieves the strain incompatibility across the metal-
nanoparticle interface. Hence, ANPs can play a dual role in the tensile
properties of the L-PBF nanocomposites. They themselves dynamically
work harden while simultaneously eliminating excessive dislocation
loops and stress concentrations at the interfaces. In addition, the dis-
location segments that interact locally with ANP at the interface
undergo a thermally activated process with small activation volumes.
This behaviour is reﬂected in multiple stress relaxation tests, which
revealed a physical activation volume (V*) of ~20 b3 for the repre-
sentative Cu-8%-ANP nanocomposite (Supplementary Fig. 11). This
value is comparable to, or even smaller than, those reported in nano-
grained metals (on the order of tens of b3), highlighting the unique
dislocation manipulation behaviour induced by ANPs.

Atomic scale information lends support to the above mechanisms
in our Cu–ANPs. Recent studies have shown that the nanosized
amorphous phases
can act as
high–capacity sinks for dislocations26–28, enabling the absorption of
excess energy transported by the dislocations. In our molecular
dynamics (MD) simulations, we do not observe any dislocation loops
storing at the ANPs after the dislocation bypassing (Fig. 4e), suggesting
their absorption by the ANPs along with straining. This is a key dif-
ference from the stress concentration at the usual crystalline disloca-
tion obstacles. Moreover, the elastic strain ﬁeld induced by incoming
dislocations and the residual interfacial stress after the previous dis-
location bypass is also relieved by the emission of dislocations on a
different slip plane from the ANP interface (Supplementary Movie S1).
As a result, the local nonhomogeneous deformation at the interfaces
and the loops after dislocation bypassing can be effectively accom-
modated in the Cu–ANP nanocomposites, leaving minimal stress
concentrations at the interfaces (Fig. 4e, right panel). The accom-
modating ability of the rapidly quenched amorphous nanoparticles is
noteworthy: the pre-existing excess volume within the particles would
enhance the atomic shufﬂing events (collective atomic rearrange-
ments are known as shear transformations via bond switching) to
accommodate the incoming dislocations and local strain7,27. In other
words, the local structural conﬁgurations inside the ANPs evolve dur-
ing straining, and the associated bond breaking and reforming (with
other neighbours) help to relieve stress concentrations at metal–ANP
interfaces. This is consistent with the dynamic evolution of local strains
in the ANP (Supplementary Movie S2) and the nonuniform distribution
of the von Mises equivalent strain at the moment of dislocation
bypassing (Fig. 4f). The high cooling rate of up to 108 K/s during L-PBF
endows the formed ANPs a highly rejuvenated state with a high
potential energy. Such a rejuvenated state contains many fertile sites
for bond-switching shear transformations under loading, and also for
subsequent structural relaxation to relatively low energy states. The

Exceptional fatigue resistance and other properties
Our reduced propensity for damage initiation/accumulation at inter-
faces may also render exceptional fatigue resistance. This is found to
be true, as demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. 12a. Both the
ascending and descending branches of the hysteresis loops of Cu–ANP
(4% B4C as a representative) overlap completely throughout the cyclic
loading process, even after 107 cycles at a maximum stress of 70% of its
tensile strength. This stable cyclic deformation is distinct from the
strain localization and cyclic hardening characteristics of alloys or
conventional metal composites32,33. The fatigue strength limit is
greater than 70% of the tensile strength, surpassing that of state-of-the-
art copper materials, including nanograined, gradient and nanot-
winned copper (Fig. 3d), see Supplementary Note 4. Other properties
of interest, which have also been much improved, include the electrical
conductivity and thermal stability. Precipitates in alloys at high num-
ber densities (1020–1024/m3)34 usually scatter electrons and reduce
electrical conductivity. Also, these precipitates suffer from diffusion-
controlled coarsening (i.e., Ostwald ripening) and are micro-
structurally unstable at high temperatures35. As indicated in Fig. 3e, the
L-PBF copper nanocomposites retain 90% of the initial strength to
temperatures as high as 1173 K (or 0.87Tm, where Tm is the melting
point of copper), which is better than the immiscible copper–niobium
alloy (one of the most thermally stable copper alloys). The combina-
tion of high strength and high conductivity (Supplementary Fig. 12b)
rivals Cu-Ag alloys, which are believed to have the best combination of
strength and conductivity among all copper alloys but usually have low
thermal stability. This synergy of excellent mechanical and functional
properties in one material has prospective applications. For example,
as-built strong yet ductile copper nanocomposites with high fatigue
and thermal resistance properties are highly sought after for com-
bustion chambers in rocket engines36–38.

explained by the Orowan strengthening mechanism due to densely

Exceptional fatigue resistance and other properties
Our reduced propensity for damage initiation/accumulation at inter-
faces may also render exceptional fatigue resistance. This is found to
be true, as demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. 12a. Both the
ascending and descending branches of the hysteresis loops of Cu–ANP
(4% B4C as a representative) overlap completely throughout the cyclic
loading process, even after 107 cycles at a maximum stress of 70% of its
tensile strength. This stable cyclic deformation is distinct from the
strain localization and cyclic hardening characteristics of alloys or
conventional metal composites32,33. The fatigue strength limit is
greater than 70% of the tensile strength, surpassing that of state-of-the-
art copper materials, including nanograined, gradient and nanot-
winned copper (Fig. 3d), see Supplementary Note 4. Other properties
of interest, which have also been much improved, include the electrical
conductivity and thermal stability. Precipitates in alloys at high num-
ber densities (1020–1024/m3)34 usually scatter electrons and reduce
electrical conductivity. Also, these precipitates suffer from diffusion-
controlled coarsening (i.e., Ostwald ripening) and are micro-
structurally unstable at high temperatures35. As indicated in Fig. 3e, the
L-PBF copper nanocomposites retain 90% of the initial strength to
temperatures as high as 1173 K (or 0.87Tm, where Tm is the melting
point of copper), which is better than the immiscible copper–niobium
alloy (one of the most thermally stable copper alloys). The combina-
tion of high strength and high conductivity (Supplementary Fig. 12b)
rivals Cu-Ag alloys, which are believed to have the best combination of
strength and conductivity among all copper alloys but usually have low
thermal stability. This synergy of excellent mechanical and functional
properties in one material has prospective applications. For example,
as-built strong yet ductile copper nanocomposites with high fatigue
and thermal resistance properties are highly sought after for com-
bustion chambers in rocket engines36–38.

Nanoparticles or precipitates are long used to block dislocations to strengthen
metals. However, this strengthening mechanism unavoidably adds stress
concentrations at the obstacles, instigating crack initiation that hampers
ductility. Here, we demonstrate a strategy that replaces the traditional crys-
talline dispersions with dense amorphous nanoparticles, which is made pos-
sible via laser powder bed fusion. Porosity-free copper-based nanocomposites
are demonstrated as a prototype, consisting of densely and uniformly dis-
tributed amorphous boron–carbide nanoparticles (~47 nm in average dia-
meter, up to 12% volume fraction) via an in situ nanofragmentation and melt-
quench process. The amorphous nanoparticles act as dislocation sinks,
thereby alleviating local stress concentration. They also self-harden along with
tensile deformation, promoting strain hardening and therefore homogeneous
plastic ﬂow. The as-built composite achieves a tensile strength of more than
one gigapascal and a total elongation of approximately 10%, more than twice
that of its crystalline dispersion counterpart. Defect accumulation is also
suppressed upon cyclic deformation of the as-built bulk nanocomposites,
delivering a fatigue strength limit (at > 107 cycles) of more than 70% of the
tensile strength. Our results demonstrate an effective strategy for additive
manufacturing of metallic materials with superior properties.

In metallic materials, dispersing obstacles (such as hard particles and
precipitates) to block moving dislocations is a commonly used
approach for strengthening purposes1–3. This widely adopted “disper-
sion hardening” mechanism, however, often sacriﬁces ductility,
the obstacles lead to stress
because dislocation pile-ups at

concentration, facilitating the nucleation of cracks4–6. We propose here
to replace the conventional crystalline dispersions with amorphous
nanoparticles. This is a likely solution to the problem, because an
amorphous phase and its interface with the matrix have been reported
to act as dislocation sources and sinks7,8, which would help alleviate the

stress concentrations at the obstacles. As such, amorphous nano-
particles would be the dispersion of choice, in delaying damage
nucleation to signiﬁcantly improve ductility and other damage-
sensitive in-service properties such as fatigue resistance.

The question is then how to realize a dense and uniform disper-
sion of amorphous nanoparticles inside the metals. To this end, we
take advantage of additive manufacturing (AM)9–11. This non-
equilibrium processing route and associated complex melt ﬂow have
been known to provide opportunities for tailoring the microstructure,
including the grain morphology, subgrain dislocation structure and
chemical segregation, leading to vastly improved mechanical proper-
ties over those from traditional processing9. For example, we recently
showed that laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) can achieve spontaneous
and intragranular dispersion of microparticles in conventional com-
posite systems12. Herein, we exploit L-PBF to create a new type of
nanocomposite consisting of a metal matrix with uniformly and den-
sely distributed reinforcing amorphous nanoparticles. An in situ nano-
fragmentation process is exploited to spontaneously reﬁne the crys-
talline reinforcing microparticles into amorphous nanoparticles dur-
ing L-PBF (Fig. 1a). For the reinforcing phase, we set three criteria for
the materials selection: (1) high strength and elastic modulus to ensure
the desired strengthening; (2) a melting point within a control window
(~ 3000 K) that is accessible to the L-PBF process, such that the dis-
persions can be turned amorphous via melting, which are then torn
apart during turbulent ﬂuid ﬂow and rapidly quenched; and (3) no
chemical decomposition or extensive reaction with the matrix pool
during the melting of reinforcements13. We integrate Thermo-Calc
software with the latest substance database to evaluate the thermally
stable phases of different metal–ceramic particle systems. The above
criteria led us to a system of simple boron carbide (B4C) reinforced
copper as the ﬁrst model. We demonstrate in the following that L-PBF
produces a high density of amorphous nanoparticles that are
embedded within pure copper grains.

Results
Microstructures and their formation mechanism
High-purity copper powders (average size of ~35 μm) were mixed with
crystalline B4C microparticles (average size of ~4 μm, 12 vol.%). A
porosity-free bulk composite (density: >99.8%) was then built using
L-PBF (Methods). Notably, the B4C microparticles were melted and
transformed into nanoparticles with an average size of ~47 nm (see
Supplementary Fig. 1a for particle size distributions), which are den-
sely and uniformly dispersed in the copper matrix (Fig. 1b). These
nanoparticles are amorphous, as indicated by the X-ray diffraction
(XRD) pattern and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectrum
(Supplementary Fig. 1b, c)14. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD)
imaging of the cross-sectional regions indicates that the copper grains
are equiaxed, with ultraﬁne grains averaging to 0.39 ± 0.14 μm (Fig. 1b).
High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) indicates
the presence of nanocrystals (black regions, sizes of ~2.9 nm) inside the
amorphous nanoparticles (Fig. 1c, d). Observing along the [110] face-
centred cubic (FCC) zone axis via high-angle annular dark-ﬁeld
(HAADF) scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), we ﬁnd
that the lattice spacings of these nanocrystals correspond to copper
(Fig. 1e), which was conﬁrmed by energy-dispersive X-ray spectro-
scopy (EDS) spectrum. Therefore, these fragmentated nanoparticles
are “quasi-amorphous”. We used atom probe tomography (APT) to
study the nanoscale compositions of the amorphous nanoparticles
and the atomic diffusion across the interface (Fig. 1f–h). The nano-
particle composition (B3.89C) is close to B4C, with 8 at% copper
incorporated. Figure 1h indicates very limited diffusion of the B and C
atoms into copper (~5 nm). This is because B–C has strong chemical
afﬁnity such that their robust atomic bonding did not allow the dif-
fusion of individual elements even under molten conditions, as indi-
cated by our ab initial molecular dynamics calculations of the

formation enthalpy of B4C at various temperatures (Supplementary
Fig. 2). On the other hand, copper atoms diffuse into the B4C nano-
particles, forming the nanoscale clusters seen under TEM. Near-edge
X-ray absorption ﬁne-structure (NEXAFS) spectroscopy of the extrac-
ted nanoparticles (Fig. 1i) shows broadened π* peak with a relatively
low intensity, which can be attributed to the amorphous structure15,16.
Thus, amorphous nanoparticles are generated by melting and frag-
mentation of the B4C microparticles upon laser scanning, followed by
rapid quenching, which kinetically inhibits the thermodynamically
favoured crystallization.

The in situ nano-fragmentation of ceramic particles was achieved
by increasing the input energy density of the L-PBF. We ﬁnd that
microparticles are retained at low energy density (86.9 J/m3) but
fragmented as the energy input increased, eventually into nanoscale
particles at 180.6 J/m3 (Fig. 2a). Importantly, the fast Fourier transform
(FFT) images demonstrate that most of the produced ﬁne particles are
amorphous upon rapid solidiﬁcation. To reveal the particle melting
and fragmentation dynamics, we conducted high-ﬁdelity simulations
to track the changes in B4C microparticles, which produced three-
dimensional data at nanoscale and meso-nanosecond time resolutions
(Methods). As shown in Fig. 2b–d, we observe the following micro-
structural changes during a single-track scan. Initially, a laser imping-
ing on the composite powder bed increases the local temperature to a
maximum value of 3800 K, directly melting the B4C microparticles.
Then, the strong and complex ﬂuid ﬂow induced by the large thermal
gradient of L-PBF (reaching 108 K/m, Supplementary Fig. 3) tears the
ceramic droplets apart, gradually turning them into very ﬁne droplets
that are tens of nanometres in size (Fig. 2e). Notably, the above frag-
mentation process operates on the ﬁrst track when the laser directly
irradiates the microparticles. The subsequent laser tracks do not raise
the melt pool temperature to reach the melting point of B4C. Even-
tually, the Marangoni convection-induced intermixing of solidiﬁed
amorphous nanoparticles with copper melt prevents particle
agglomeration12, which facilitates the observed high dispersion uni-
formity. The same melt-quench and fragmentation is expected to
happen in other metal-ceramic particle systems to obtain similar
composite structures. For example, we have achieved B4C amorphous
nanoparticles in pure aluminium using the same in situ nano-
fragmentation strategy (Fig. 2f). We have also conﬁrmed the generality
in other ceramic–copper systems (e.g., CrB2-copper nanocomposites,
Fig. 2g). In all cases, the ceramic particles are fragmented to the
nanoscale without marked changes in their compositions.

Tensile properties and the elimination of printing defects
We employed tensile tests to investigate the mechanical properties
of the L-PBF nanocomposites. Figure 3a shows the representative
tensile responses of the as-printed copper reinforced with three
volume fractions (12%, 8% and 4%) of the amorphous nanoparticles
(ANPs) (hereafter referred to as Cu–ANP). Copper grains show no
obvious texture in the as-built samples, and their sizes decrease
from 7.17 ± 4.48 μm to 0.39 ± 0.14 μm (Supplementary Fig. 4a) with
increasing particle volume fraction inside. A tensile curve for con-
ventional high-strength pure copper with a grain size (~ 400 nm,
Methods) similar to that of Cu-12%-ANP is presented for comparison.
Clearly, Cu–ANPs show much better tensile strengths and strain
hardening beyond plastic yielding, leading to high ductility. Speci-
ﬁcally, Cu-12%-ANP exhibits very high yield and tensile strengths of
729 ± 27 and 1036 ± 35 MPa, respectively, along with relatively large
uniform and total elongations of 7.2% ± 0.4% and 9.7% ± 0.4%,
respectively. This enhanced tensile ductility of Cu-ANPs is further
evidenced by the improvement in true fracture strain, estimated
from the reduction in area at fracture (Supplementary Fig. 5). Pre-
vious AM attempts have also achieved excellent mechanical prop-
erties in other types of advanced alloys, such as titanium-based
alloys, high-strength steels and high-entropy alloys; on a normalized

amorphous nanoparticles do not suffer from this drawback. The
absence of premature failure in Cu-ANP nanocomposites is consistent
with the presence of necking, as predicted by the Considère criterion
(see Supplementary Fig. 6d); however, the Cu-12%-CNP nanocompo-
site fractures before necking occurs, indicating signiﬁcant stress con-
centration. As shown in Fig. 4a, a group of grains after 3% strain is
examined using high-resolution EBSD, which enables a quantitative
cross-correlation-based analysis of strain and stress (Methods). As
observed, the residual elastic strain ﬁeld relative to the reference
region (i.e., the lowest kernel average misorientation value within a
grain) in the Cu–ANP sample exhibits much lower magnitudes and
more uniform distributions across all selected grains, compared with
its crystallized counterpart. For a further precise evaluation of the
deformation compatibility in Cu–ANP, we conducted precession
electron diffraction (PED)-based automated crystal orientation map-
ping (ACOM) via TEM for the 3%-deformed sample, with a mapping
spatial resolution of 1 nm (Fig. 4b). Speciﬁcally, the two-beam bright-
ﬁeld TEM images show random distributions of dislocations inside the
copper grains, and no discernible dislocation pile-ups are observed at
the matrix-nanoparticle interface. The overall dislocation density, as
estimated from the TEM images of the deformed Cu–ANP, is higher
(~1.1 × 1015 m−2) than that in the as-printed state (~2.3 × 1014 m−2), sug-
gesting dislocation multiplication and therefore strain hardening. Note
that the point-to-point misorientation proﬁle reveals a very low local
misorientation across the interface (less than 0.5°, Fig. 4b), indicating a
more uniform spread of the stored dislocations. It appears that the
geometrically necessary dislocations that would otherwise pile-up
near the interfaces have been accommodated via shear transforma-
tions at the surface of the ANPs (to be discussed below). On the con-
trary, in the CNP case dislocations piled up as expected, to accumulate
at the Cu-CNP interface, as evidenced by both the post-deformation
TEM and electron channelling contrast imaging analyses (Supple-
mentary Fig. 9). This ANP-induced stress delocalization at the interface
is the primary mechanism driving stable deformation without pre-
mature failure in the L-PBF nanocomposites.

In situ synchrotron XRD and atomic scale modelling
We also employed in situ synchrotron XRD experiments with crystal
plasticity ﬁnite element (CPFE) modelling (Methods)9. This approach
allows us to dissect the mechanical behaviour of each sample com-
ponent despite the amorphous nature of the nanoparticles. Figure 4c
shows the lattice strain εhkl along the loading direction against the
applied true stress (σ) for several representative {hkl} reﬂections of
copper in different nanocomposites (hollow symbols, 8 vol.% of
nanoparticles). Initially, all reﬂections exhibit elastic deformation, with
slopes differing due to the elastic anisotropy of diffraction planes.
Upon straining, the lattice strain of the {220} reﬂection in both samples
ﬁrst shows a nonlinear trend, turning upwards, and the lattice strain of
the {200} reﬂection deviates from a linear trend in a downward
direction due to the occurrence of load transfer from the soft {220} to
hard {200} reﬂections, revealing the early onset of microplastic yield-
ing. As deformation proceeds, progressive yielding occurs sequentially
from the {111}, {311} to {200} reﬂections. Notably, compared with those
of Cu–CNPs, the crystallographic families of Cu–ANPs are more resis-
tant to softening due to the greater uniform elongation values of the
composites. We calibrate our CPFE model in terms of simulated lattice
strain responses based on in situ diffraction data (solid lines in Fig. 4c).

The stress‒strain curves derived from the CPFE model closely match
the experimental data (Supplementary Fig. 10a). Then, we inversely
determine the constitutive relationships between copper and nano-
particles as a function of applied strain during deformation, the results
of which are displayed in Fig. 4d. Copper in Cu–ANP has a lower initial
yield strength due to the lower initial dislocation density (Supple-
mentary Fig. 10b; a higher dislocation density in Cu–CNP may be
attributed to thermal misﬁt upon sample cooling after heat
treatment23); however, its dislocation accumulation and strain hard-
ening rates are slightly greater. Importantly, the ANPs demonstrate
remarkably improved strain hardening, contributing to most (61%) of
the strain hardening magnitude of Cu–ANP (the true strain ranges
from 1% to 7%). This signiﬁcantly improved hardening is primarily
attributed to the self-hardening (and stiffening) of the ANPs as well as
the associated hardening of the interface-affected zone24. Here, the
ANPs have been rapidly melt-quenched at cooling rates around 108 K/s,
such that many dangling bonds and much excess volume would be
available for bond switching to accomplish shear transformations25.
This latter process accommodates the dislocations running into the
nanoparticles, and relieves the strain incompatibility across the metal-
nanoparticle interface. Hence, ANPs can play a dual role in the tensile
properties of the L-PBF nanocomposites. They themselves dynamically
work harden while simultaneously eliminating excessive dislocation
loops and stress concentrations at the interfaces. In addition, the dis-
location segments that interact locally with ANP at the interface
undergo a thermally activated process with small activation volumes.
This behaviour is reﬂected in multiple stress relaxation tests, which
revealed a physical activation volume (V*) of ~20 b3 for the repre-
sentative Cu-8%-ANP nanocomposite (Supplementary Fig. 11). This
value is comparable to, or even smaller than, those reported in nano-
grained metals (on the order of tens of b3), highlighting the unique
dislocation manipulation behaviour induced by ANPs.
