Keywords:
antibacterial coating; bioinspired hydration; density functional theory;
graphene-based hydrogel; supramolecular structure

Abstract
Natural hydration shells are discovered to play an essential role in the structure and function of biomolecules (deoxyribonucleic
acid, protein, and phospholipid membrane). Hydration layers are also important to the structure and property of artificial graphene-
based materials. Our recent works prove that graphene-based hydrogels are supramolecular hydration structures that preserve
graphene nanosheets from the restacking through hydrophobic force, van der Waals force, and π–π interaction. In this manuscript,
density functional theory and high-performance computing (HPC) are used for modeling and calculating van der Waals force be-
tween graphene nanosheets in water-intercalated AB bilayer graphene structures. A layer of water molecules significantly decreases
the intersheet van der Waals force. A novel hydrogel of graphene oxide–silica gel–zinc hydroxide (GO-SG-ZH) is experimentally
synthesized to demonstrate the advantages of hydrated hydrogel structure in comparison with dry powder structure. The synthesis
of graphene-based hydrogels is a green chemistry approach to attain extraordinary properties of graphene-based nanostructures. An-

806

 Beilstein J. Nanotechnol. 2025, 16, 806–822.
Beilstein J. Nanotechnol. 2025, 16, 806–822.

alytical characterizations exhibited moisture contents, water evaporation rates, three-dimensional structures, elemental composi-
tions, aqueous dispersibility, and antibacterial activities. Hydration shells on graphene-based nanosheets in the hydrogel increase
intersheet distances to prevent the stacking of the nanostructures. Hydration layers in the GO-SG-ZH hydrogel was also lubricative
for direct brush coating on polymer substrates, typically polylactide films. Interfacial adhesion of graphene-based nanosheets on
polylactide substrates made the antibacterial coating stable for several application purposes. In general, supramolecular graphene-
based hydrogels are bioinspired hydration structures to advance nanoscale properties and nanotechnology applications.

Introduction
Biological  cells  are  assemblies  of  biomolecules  that  are
hydrated with water molecules. The cell content includes about
70–95% water that creates an aqueous environment for biologi-
cal processes. Water molecules are bound to biomolecular sur-
faces and participate in the structuring and functioning of bio-
molecules, typically the folding of protein and the twisting of
the double helix of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) [1]. Water
molecules  and  their  hydrogen  bonding  network  function  as
lubricants for biomolecular dynamics. Recent scientific works
have analyzed the important role of hydration shells on DNA,
proteins, and phospholipid membranes [2-4]. The first hydra-
tion shell (about 3.5 Å) at the interface of biomolecules has
considerably slower dynamics than water molecules in the bulk.
Besides, the first water layer on the interface is responsible for
hydration  forces  between  biomolecular  structures [5].  The
rearrangement of water molecules through hydrogen bonding
on  hydrated  surfaces  generates  repulsive  hydration  forces
when  another  surface  perturbs  the  hydration  layers  [6-8].
Hydration shells and hydration forces keep the hydrated struc-
tures stable and functional in the natural concert of biological
processes.

In  the  aspect  of  artificial  nanomaterials,  it  is  proposed  that
hydration also plays an important role in the stability and func-
tionality  of  nanoscale  structures.  Van  der  Waals  forces  are
supramolecular  intermolecular  interactions  that  govern  the
agglomeration of nanomaterials. Carbon nanostructures with
π-conjugated  systems  (fullerene,  carbon  nanotube,  and
graphene) have π–π interactions, a type of van der Waals force,
for supramolecular attraction [9]. Particularly, graphene sheets
with a large surface area and π-conjugated network are likely to
stack  together  through  hydrophobic  agglomeration  and π–π
interaction. Although π–π interactions are generally weaker than
hydrogen bonding, two graphene sheets in face-to-face geome-
try have a large interaction surface area to multiply the van der
Waals force per unit area, resulting in strong binding energy of
total attraction forces. The restacking of graphene-based nano-
sheets, including pristine graphene, graphene oxide (GO), and
reduced graphene oxide (RGO), causes the drawbacks of small
effective  surface  area  and  low  dispersibility  in  media [10].
Several  approaches  have  been  reported  to  prevent  the irre-

versible stacking of graphene-based nanosheets, including elec-
trostatic  repulsion,  nanoparticle  intercalation,  three-dimen-
sional assembly, and surface hydration [10-12]. In our previous
works, a number of graphene-based hydrogels (RGO-SnO2,
RGO-ZnO, and RGO) were synthesized to evidence the revers-
ible  self-assembly  of  graphene-based  nanosheets  thanks  to
water intercalation in the hydrated ensembles [13-17]. There-
fore, supramolecular graphene-based hydrogels with hydration
intercalation and hydration force are quite useful for preserving
and generating graphene-based nanosheets for many applica-
tions.

In this manuscript, we calculated van der Waals forces in bilay-
er graphene structures using density functional theory modeling
(DFT) and dispersion energy correction functional (DFT-D3).
The theoretical work aimed to elucidate the relationship be-
tween  water  intercalation  and  intersheet  binding  energy  in
quantum  mechanical  level.  The  computational  calculations
quantified intersheet distance, van der Waals force, bandgap
energy,  and  formation  energy  of  the  molecular  system  of
bilayer  graphene  intercalated  with  a  water  layer.  In  the
experimental aspect, green chemistry methods were applied
for synthesizing GO nanosheets, rice-husk-derived silica gel
(SG),  nano-silica–zinc  hydroxide  nanoparticles  (SG-ZH),
and graphene oxide–nanosilica–zinc hydroxide nanocompos-
ites  (GO-SG-ZH).  Graphite  oxidation  reaction  in  a  cascade
design  gives  good  efficiency  values  of  energy,  chemical
reaction,  and  reaction  time  [14,15].  The  recycling  of  rice
husk  ash  waste  into  nanosilica  products  is  eco-friendly  and
sustainable  for  circular  economy  [18-21].  Especially,
GO  nanosheets  decorated  with  SG-ZH  nanoparticles  have
hydrophilic surfaces to retain hydration layers in the hydrogel
structure of the GO-SG-ZH nanocomposite. Hydration layers
in  the  GO-SG-ZH  hydrogel  also  function  as  lubricants  at
the nanomaterials interfaces, leading to facile brush coating on
plastic  films  of  polylactide  (PLA).  Dehydrated  GO-SG-ZH
coating  is  adhered  to  the  PLA  substrate  through  interfacial
interactions.  Furthermore,  antibacterial  activities,  coating
stability, and mechanical properties of the nanocomposite mate-
rials were investigated and described in the results and discus-
sion.

807
807

 Methods
Computation method of density functional
theory
First-principles  calculations  based  on  DFT  were  conducted
using the Vienna ab initio simulation software (VASP) and a
high-performance  computing  system  (HPC).  The  projector-
augmented  wave  method  (PAW)  was  implemented  in elec-
tronic structure calculations. Generalized gradient approxima-
tion of Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (GGA-PBE) was used for
describing exchange-correlation energy of electron–electron
interactions. The correction of van der Waals dispersion energy
was applied using the DFT-D3 method proposed by Grimme
[22-24]. The modeling of infinite graphene sheets was extrapo-
lated  from  periodic  supercells.  The  supercell  of  bilayer
graphene structure includes 16 carbon atoms (two graphene
sheets with eight carbon atoms per sheet). The modeling of
water-intercalated bilayer graphene structure used the supercell
of 16 carbon atoms, one oxygen atom, and two hydrogen atoms
(two graphene sheets and one water molecule).

Preparation of graphene oxide from natural graphite
The improved cascade-design synthesis of graphite oxide (GrO)
was reported in our previous papers [15,16]. Briefly, 5 g of raw
material of natural graphite (Shanghai Zhanyun Chemical) was
soaked and agitated in 50 mL of 98% sulfuric acid. The solu-
tion of Mn(VII) compound was prepared by dissolving 10 g of
potassium permanganate in 100 mL of 98% sulfuric acid. The
graphite/H2SO4 suspension was slowly poured into the Mn(VII)
solution. A cooling water bath and an infrared thermometer
were used for controlling the reactor temperature below 55 °C
(the peak of the reactor temperature is about 50 °C). After agita-
tion  in  room-temperature  conditions  for  4  h,  the  graphite/
Mn(VII)/H2SO4 suspension was slowly poured into 360 mL of
water (the exothermic heat increased the reactor temperature to
above 90 °C). After 2 h of agitation, the reaction was mixed
with 150 mL of a 5% H2O2 solution and kept stirring for one
day. After washing to neutral pH, the material was dried and
ground to produce a GrO powder (moisture ≈20%). Next, the
GrO powder was dispersed in water and sonicated for 1 h. After
natural sedimentation overnight, the suspension was decanted to
collect the supernatant dispersion of GO nanosheets.

Preparation of nanosilica from rice husk ash waste
Rice husk ash that was discarded from industrial boilers was
collected for recycling experiments. Our method of nanosilica
synthesis  using  potassium  hydroxide  and  acetic  acid  was
mentioned in a recent paper [21]. Raw material from rice husk
ash waste was dispersed in a 7% potassium hydroxide solution.
The suspension was agitated for 1 h at a temperature range of
80–90 °C. After careful filtration, a clear yellow solution of

potassium silicate was obtained and neutralized with a 15%
acetic acid solution. After that, the suspension of precipitated
nanosilica was incubated overnight and then thoroughly washed
with water. The obtained product of silica gel (SG) was used for
subsequent synthesis and brush coating experiments.

hydroxide hydrogel

Results and Discussion
Density functional theory calculations of
intersheet distances, van der Waals forces
and bandgaps
The van der Waals force between two graphene nanosheets
arises from the π–π interaction between π orbitals of carbon
atoms in one graphene sheet and π orbitals of carbon atoms in
the other graphene sheet. The van der Waals force is responsi-
ble for AB graphene stacking in natural multilayer graphite
[28].  Production  processes  convert  multilayer  graphite  into
single-layer  graphene  sheets  dispersed  in  solvent  medium.
However, after the drying process, solvation shells of graphene
sheets  are  removed,  resulting  in  smaller  distances  between
graphene sheets and larger interaction surfaces. With a short
intersheet distance and large interaction surface area, van der
Waals  forces  between  graphene  sheets  increase  to  a  higher
binding energy which accounts for the restacking of graphene
sheets. The restacking of graphene materials at dry state is the
main cause of lower aqueous dispersibility and reduced surface
area of graphene-based materials in many applications, such as
aqueous dispersions, polymer nanocomposites, and water-based

Beilstein J. Nanotechnol. 2025, 16, 806–822.

paints. Our previous works demonstrated that in graphene-based
hydrogel structures, the intercalation of water molecules be-
tween graphene-based sheets maintains large intersheet dis-
tances and low interaction surface area, which leads to reduced
binding  energy  of  van  der  Waals  force [14,15].  The  simple
method of water intercalation in hydrogel structures is an effec-
tive bioinspired approach to prevent nanosheet stacking and
preserve graphene-based nanostructures.

Herein, DFT calculations were performed to quantify the van
der Waals dispersion interactions in pristine bilayer graphene
and water-intercalated bilayer graphene structures. In natural
multilayer graphite, graphene sheets stack together in an AB
configuration.  Figure 1a  shows  the  modeling  of  a  bilayer
graphene structure that mimics the AB stacking in multilayer
graphite. DFT optimization calculation presented that pristine
bilayer graphene has the formation energy of −9.3778 eV/super-
cell, intersheet distance of 3.459 Å, and van der Waals binding
energy of 0.064 eV/atom (Figure 1a and Table 1). The inter-
sheet distance is comparable to the values reported in other
papers [29-31].  The  bilayer  graphene  structure  has  a  small
bandgap of 0.06 eV which is slightly open in comparison to the
zero bandgap of a single-layer graphene sheet.

Besides, DFT modeling of the water-intercalated AB bilayer
graphene structure was also calculated by HPC. The resulting
formation energy is −10.6414 eV/supercell (Table 1). In the
optimal structure (Figure 1c and 1d), hydrogen atoms of the
water molecule are oriented toward graphene sheets due to the
hydrogen–π interaction. It is noteworthy that the enlarged inter-
sheet distance of 6.626 Å led to the intersheet binding energy of
0.04  eV/atom.  A  layer  of  water  molecules  in  between  two
graphene sheets significantly declined the van der Waals force
by 37.5% (from 0.064 to 0.040 eV). The bandgap of the water-
intercalated bilayer graphene structure increased to 0.09 eV. Al-
though the opening of the bandgap is still small, it is suggested
that the bandgap of the AB bilayer graphene can be further
opened by increasing molecular water layers in the intersheet
spacing as well as the spacing distance. The approach of water
intercalation  in  graphene-based  structures  is  effective  for
lowering van der Waals force and opening the bandgap. There-
fore,  water-intercalated  structures  of  graphene-based nano-
sheets should be experimentally synthesized to ameliorate the
nanostructures and properties for various applications in science
and industry.

Experimentally, GO nanosheets, SG, nanoparticles, and SG-ZH
nanoparticles were synthesized and separately characterized as
exhibited in SEM images in Figure 3a–c. Particularly, artificial
nanocomposites  of  GO-SG-ZH  powder  (Figure 3d–f)  and
GO-SG-ZH hydrogel (Figure 3g–i) were prepared for compara-

macroscopic particle and its microscopic structure. Since the
material was dehydrated, graphene-based nanostructures could
be covalently cross-linked through esterification reaction of
carboxyl  and  hydroxyl  groups  on  GO  nanosheets [38].  The
GO-SG-ZH nanosheets agglomerated and stacked together to
form big particles (size of hundreds of micrometers, Figure 3e).
The GO-SG-ZH particles had low porosity or small spacing be-
tween  graphene-based  nanosheets  (Figure 3f).  Besides,  the
GO-SG-ZH hydrogel was spread on a carbon tape and dehy-
drated for SEM imaging (Figure 3h and 3i). Although GO-SG-
ZH nanosheets agglomerated into microstructures (Figure 3h),
the self-assembly of graphene-based nanosheets was different
from the stacked morphology of the GO-SG-ZH powder. At a
higher  magnification  of  20,000×,  SEM  image  in Figure 3i
revealed  the  porous  structure  with  large  spacing  between
graphene-based  nanosheets.  As  a  result,  the  GO-SG-ZH
hydrogel is a three-dimensional assembly of water-intercalated
graphene-based nanosheets.

Water evaporation characteristics of the GO-SG-ZH hydrogel
were  recorded  and  analyzed  during  drying  processes  in  the
moisture analyzer (MX-50, resolution of 0.01%). Figure 5a de-
scribes the moisture curves during the drying process at 70, 85,
and 100 °C, corresponding to the drying times of 170, 100, and
70 min, respectively. Although the corresponding drying times
were different, the curves of cumulative evaporated water had a
similar  shape  and  amounted  to  1.87  g  (93.5%  moisture,
Figure 5b). The lower drying temperature of 70 °C was suffi-
cient to evaporate the hydration layers in the hydrogel. A scien-
tific report by Khan et al. demonstrated that the drying of apple
tissues at 70 °C is critical to the rupturing of cell membranes,
resulting in dehydration of the biological tissues [32]. In the
drying process, water at the outer surface evaporated first, fol-
lowed by the evaporation of intracellular water. Figure 5c and
5d exhibit the water evaporation rates as a function of drying
time and water content in the GO-SG-ZH hydrogel. In the first
period, the water evaporation rates increased to a plateau of
constant drying rate, corresponding to the evaporation of free
water molecules at the outer surface [39]. Then, the water evap-
oration curves entered into the decreasing rate period where
there is deficiency of free water at the outer surface and water
transport from the interior to the surface. The critical water
content at which the first decreasing rate period began was iden-
tified to be about 40% (the left dashed line in Figure 5d). It is

noticeable that at the water content of 20% (the middle dashed
line in Figure 5d), the water evaporation rates at 70, 85, and
100 °C were approximately half the initial water evaporation
rates at 5 min. There is a second decreasing rate period which
occurred at the critical water content of 4% (the right dashed
line in Figure 5d). Interestingly, in biological tissues, interfacial
water  integrated  in  cell  walls  is  also  about  2–5%  [32].  It
is explained that the significantly slower rates of water evap-
oration  in  the  decreasing  rate  period  are  due  to  water
movement from the interior to the surface and the hydrogen
bonding of interfacial hydration layers on the hydrophilic nano-
structures.

Supramolecular systems with non-covalent interactions and re-
versible cross-links are recognized to provide extraordinary
properties and applications [45-47]. Reversible self-assembly is
an advantage of supramolecular graphene-based hydrogels in
comparison with the powder form [13-16]. Hydration layers in
between  graphene-based  sheets  not  only  reduce  intersheet
binding energy (van der Waals force) but also generate repul-
sive forces for exfoliating the macroscopic assembly into nano-
scale structures especially under external sonication and me-
chanical stimuli. Reversible self-assembly of graphene-based
nanosheets in water is essential to many applications, such as
adsorption, photocatalysis, biosensing, drug delivery, aqueous
paints, and multifunctional coatings [48-50]. Figure 6c exhibits
the aqueous dispersions derived from the sonication of GO-SG-
ZH hydrogel and powder in water (see Supporting Information
File 1, Figure S3). Ultrasound waves vibrated water molecules
and created cavitation in the hydrogel structure, leading to the
exfoliation of graphene-based nanosheets in water. It is notable
that  low  concentrations  (≤50  ppm)  are  necessary  to  obtain
homogenous dispersions. The ultrasonic dispersion of GO-SG-
ZH hydrogels was faster and clearer due to the high content of
water intercalation. The GO-SG-ZH powder contained about
10%  of  water  and  approximate  60%  of  nanosilica  and  zinc
hydroxide nanoparticles, which functioned as spacing layers be-
tween graphene-based nanosheets. Therefore, the ultrasonic
treatment of GO-SG-ZH powder in water also yielded a homo-
geneous  dispersion.  However,  the  aqueous  dispersion  of
GO-SG-ZH  powder  was  not  completely  exfoliated  in  the
aqueous  environment  and  quickly  settled  down.  Stacked
agglomerates of GO-SG-ZH powder at the bottom of the disper-
sion were observed in the micrograph of Figure 6c, while the
micrograph of the dispersion of GO-SG-ZH hydrogel showed
the absence of stacked structures. In Figure 6d, UV–vis spectra
of aqueous dispersions of GO-SG-ZH hydrogel present light
absorption  in  the  ultraviolet  range  (200–400  nm)  that  was
proportional to the colloidal concentrations (50, 40, 30, and
20 ppm). Small absorption peaks at 340 and 360 nm corre-
spond to nanosilica and zinc hydroxide nanoparticles, respec-
tively [21,43]. In addition, hydration lubrication in supramolec-
ular graphene-based hydrogels is important to applications in
paints  and  coatings [51,52].  While  the  GO-SG-ZH  powder

could not be directly used for brush painting, the GO-SG-ZH
hydrogel can be easily coated on various substrates using a
simple brush. In the scientific literature, it is elucidated that
water layers between graphene-based nanosheets significantly
lower the interfacial frictions of the nanomaterials [53-55]. In
this  study,  hydration  lubrication  makes  supramolecular

Antibacterial properties of graphene
oxide–nanosilica–zinc hydroxide in hydrogel
and in coating structures
The EDS analysis in Table 2 showed that the solid nanocom-
posite of GO-SG-ZH hydrogel was composed of 12.81% zinc
atoms (derived from the Zn(OH)2 constituent). ZH nanoparti-
cles and GO nanosheets in the GO-SG-ZH hydrogel are anti-
bacterial and antibiofilm agents with low toxicity for food pack-
aging and biomedical applications [56,57]. The main antibacte-
rial mechanism of GO nanosheets is cell membrane damage
caused by direct contact of GO sharp edges with bacterial mem-
branes [57,58]. The crucial antibacterial activity of ZH nano-
structures is the delivery of Zn2+ ions to disrupt bacterial mem-
branes and intracellular processes [59,60]. Antibacterial activi-
ty of the GO-SG-ZH hydrogel was tested in agar well diffusion
assays (Figure 9). The photographic results showed inhibition
zones against E. coli (Figure 9a) and S. aureus (Figure 9b). The
inhibition zones resulted from the diffusion of ZH nanoparti-
cles and Zn2+ cations from the hydrogel to the surrounding
agar. As the GO-SG-ZH hydrogel is antibacterial, the brush

coating of the GO-SG-ZH hydrogel on PLA films produced an
antibacterial coating on the substrate.

Antibacterial tests of uncoated and coated PLA films are de-
scribed in Figure 10, where the interfaces between PLA films
and agar/E. coli plates are displayed. Before the incubation
process,  E.  coli  bacteria  did  not  grow  to  biofilms
(Figure 10a–c).  After  incubation  at  37  °C  for  24  h,  stripy
biofilms  of E.  coli  bacteria  were  formed  on  the  agar  plates
(Figure 10d–f). While stripy patterns were observed in the areas
of blank PLA film (Figure 10d) and SG/PLA film (Figure 10e),
the GO-SG-ZH/PLA film presented an inhibition zone at the
vicinity of its boundary (Figure 10f). PLA and SG/PLA were
not antibacterial materials, and the GO-SG-ZH coating was
effective against the growth of E. coli biofilm on the coating
surface. The antibiofilm result is attributed to the antibacterial
activities of GO nanosheets and ZH nanoparticles. Regarding
the  antibacterial  mechanism  of  the  nanocomposite  coating,
direct contact of bacterial cells with sharp nanostructures of the
coating is the cause of membrane damage and cell inactivation.

SG/PLA and GO-SG-ZH/PLA films were immersed in an envi-
ronment simulating aqueous food for one month. The stability
of  the  coatings  in  aqueous  environments  was  measured  by
calculating the loss of coating weight. These experimental tests
are  useful  for  studying  packaging  materials  and  chemical
releases over a time period in environments simulating food

[14,27]. Line charts in Figure 11 report the weight losses of SG
(Figure 10a) and GO-SG-ZH/PLA (Figure 10b) coatings after 1,
3, 5, 7, 10 and 30 days in aqueous solutions containing water,
3% acetic acid, 10% ethanol, and 50% ethanol. Both coatings
were quite stable in pure water as the weight losses were insig-
nificant even after 30 days. However, acidic and alcoholic solu-
tions gave more notable effects on coating stability. Especially,
the  weight  losses  of  SG  coating  in  50%  ethanol  were
0.32 mg/cm2 after 3 days and 1.48 mg/cm2 after 30 days. The
high coating weight loss indicated that the coating of silica
nanoparticles was not stable in 50% ethanol solution (equiva-
lent  to  a  fatty  food  environment).  Besides,  the  coating  of
GO-SG-ZH nanocomposite showed weight losses of 0.3 mg/
cm2 after 3 days and 0.62 mg/cm2 after 30 days in 50% ethanol.
Although the coating weight losses were considerable in the
first 3 days, the trend curve became steady in the period from 3
to 30 days. The GO-SG-ZH coating was more stable than the
SG coating on PLA films. As demonstrated in our previous

with nanosilica-based and graphene-based
coatings
The thin coatings of SG and GO-SG-ZH considerably affected
the mechanical properties of plastic films. Tensile testing results
of blank PLA, SG/PLA, and GO-SG-ZH/PLA films are de-
scribed in Figure 12 and summarized in Table 4. Additional
data of measurement values and stress–strain curves are given
in Supporting Information File 1, Table S1, Figure S4, Table

S2, and Figure S5. Our previous paper presented that GO-ZnO
coating on PLA film led to an increase of elastic modulus and a
decrease of tensile elongation [14]. Similar trends were also
noted in the tensile properties of coated PLA films in this study.
Elastic moduli of SG/PLA and GO-SG-ZH/PLA films rose to
2447.08 ± 27.71 MPa and 2232.7 ± 105.52 MPa, which were
respectively 31.89% and 20.34% higher than that of blank PLA
film. Nanosilica and graphene-based nanosheets were nano-
structures with high elastic modulus for reinforcement of PLA
films through load transfer mechanism. High elasticity of SG
and GO-SG-ZH coatings led to the increases in elastic moduli
of the coated films. Besides, considerable decrease of elonga-
tion was observed due to the propagation of cracks from the
coatings to the substrate. The tensile strength of the GO-SG-
ZH/PLA film (54.22 ± 2.86 MPa) was slightly higher than that
of the blank PLA film. The enhancement of tensile strength of
the GO-SG-ZH/PLA film is explained due to the load transfer
from the polylactide substrate to the graphene-based coating
during the tensile process. Effective coating adhesion to the
substrate and high elastic modulus of graphene-based nano-
sheets contributed to the higher tensile properties. Supporting
Information File 1, Figure S6 shows SEM images of surfaces at
the fracture of a GO-SG-ZH/PLA film generated by the tensile
measurement.

Conclusion
Supramolecular  graphene-based  hydrogels  are  bioinspired
structures which are biomimetic to natural hydration structures
of cellular membranes, proteins, and other biomolecules. While
hydration shells participate in the shaping and dynamics of bio-
logical structures, water intercalation in graphene-based hydro-
gels is proposed to reduce intersheet van der Waals interaction,
generate repulsive hydration forces, and facilitate hydration
lubrication of graphene-based nanosheets. DFT calculations
showed  that  a  water  layer  in  AB  bilayer  graphene  enlarges
the  intersheet  distance  from  3.459  to  6.626  Å,  and conse-
quently  leads  to  a  reduction  of  37.5%  in  intersheet  binding
energy of the van der Waals force. In our experiments, sustain-
able  green  chemistry  approaches  are  used  to  synthesize
graphene  oxide,  silica  gel,  nanosilica–zinc  hydroxide,
and graphene oxide–nanosilica–zinc hydroxide nanocompos-
ites. The chemical methods used saved chemical reagents and
production  energy,  converted  rice  hush  ash  waste  into
nanosilica, improved materials quality, and contributed to envi-
ronmental sustainability. The GO-SG-ZH hydrogel is a supra-
molecular hydration structure with the advantages of aqueous
dispersibility, antibacterial activity, and hydration lubrication.
Water evaporation analysis suggested that the last 4% of water
in the GO-SG-ZH hydrogel are interfacial hydration shells on
graphene-based nanosheets. The first water shell is crucially re-
sponsible for primary hydration forces between nanostructures.

Additionally, hydration lubrication is another interesting effect
of water-intercalated graphene-based systems. As graphene-
based nanosheets in the hydrogel structure are in non-stacking
state, they can slide on each other owing to water lubrication
and low interfacial friction. After brush coating and water evap-
oration, the graphene-based coating is adhered to the polylac-
tide substrate through interfacial interactions. The GO-SG-ZH/
PLA films showed antibacterial activity, coating stability, and
enhanced tensile properties. In summary, the supramolecular
hydration structure of graphene-based hydrogels is a prospec-
tive nanotechnology approach to advance nanoscale structures
and interfaces for a variety of applications.

essential  to  overcoming  these  hurdles  and  ensuring 
reproducible clinical performance.

Remaining  Gaps  and  Controversies:  Despite 
remarkable  progress  in  designing  and  preclinically 
validating  hybrid  hydrogels  for  gynecologic  oncol-
ogy,  key  gaps  and  debates  persist.  First,  the  mecha-
nistic  interplay  between  specific  nanomaterials  (e.g., 
graphene  oxide,  PLGA  nanoparticles)  and  the  com-
plex tumor microenvironment remains poorly defined, 
with  conflicting  reports  on  how  hydrogel  stiffness 
and  degradation  by-products  influence  ovarian  ver-
sus cervical cancer cell behaviour. Second, a lack of 
standardized metrics for mesh size, crosslink density, 
and rheological properties hinders direct comparison 
across  platforms  and  laboratories.  Third,  immuno-
genicity  remains  controversial:  although  genipin-
crosslinked  chitosan  matrices  have  been  reported  to 
elicit  minimal  inflammation,  other  studies  document 
macrophage  activation  and  fibrotic  encapsulation 
with similar chemistries. Fourth, the optimal stimuli-
responsive  trigger  (pH,  enzyme,  thermal,  or  light)  is 
still debated, as few head-to-head evaluations exist to 
determine which cue offers the best spatial–temporal 
control in vivo. Finally, the translational gap is strik-
ing—only  a  handful  of  formulations  have  entered 
early‐phase  clinical  trials,  underscoring  challenges 
in  scaling,  sterilization,  regulatory  compliance,  and 
long-term  safety.  Addressing  these  controversies 
through  rigorous  mechanistic  studies,  harmonized 
testing protocols, and coordinated multi-center efforts 
will  be  vital  to  accelerate  the  clinical  translation  of 
hybrid hydrogels in gynecologic cancer care.

Innovations on the horizon

Emerging  technologies  and  materials  offer  potential 
solutions  to  these  challenges.  One  such  innovation 
is  developing  smart  hydrogels  which  can  respond  to 
multiple stimuli, such as pH, temperature, and enzy-
matic activity. They can provide more controlled and 
localized  drug  release,  enhancing  the  precision  of 
cancer  treatments(Yu  et  al.  2022).  Advanced  nano-
including  carbon-based  nanostructures 
materials, 
(graphene  and  carbon  nanotubes)  and  metal–organic 
frameworks  (MOFs),  are  being  explored  for  their 
exceptional  mechanical  properties  and  functional

versatility  (Venkatas  and  Singh  2023;  Nelson  and 
Bissell 2006). These materials can boost the mechani-
cal  strength  and  functional  capabilities  of  hybrid 
hydrogels,  making  them  more  effective  in  clinical 
applications. 3D bioprinting technology is advancing 
the  creation  of  sophisticated  and  customized  hydro-
gel  scaffolds(Varinelli,  et  al.  2023).  It  allows  pre-
cise placement of cells, nanomaterials, and bioactive 
agents  within  the  hydrogel  matrix,  creating  complex 
tissue  constructs  that  closely  mimic  natural  tissues. 
This  technology  could  revolutionize  hybrid  hydrogel 
fabrication,  making  them  more  consistent  and  scal-
able for clinical use. By enhancing the precision and 
scalability  of  these  materials,  3D  bioprinting  holds 
the  potential  to  significantly  improve  the  effective-
ness and accessibility of hybrid hydrogels in medical 
applications(Zhou  et  al.  2021).  Innovations  in  gene 
editing  and  molecular  biology  are  enhancing  hybrid 
hydrogels. Techniques like CRISPR-Cas9 can modify 
the genetic makeup of cells within hydrogels, boost-
ing  their  regenerative  capabilities  and  cancer  resist-
ance. Additionally, incorporating engineered extracel-
lular vesicles (EVs) into hydrogels improves targeted 
drug delivery and tissue regeneration. These advance-
ments  could  significantly  improve  the  effectiveness 
of  hybrid  hydrogels  in  medical  applications,  making 
them more adaptable and powerful for various thera-
peutic uses(Ma et al. 2023).

Future research needs

To  fully  realize  the  potential  of  hybrid  hydrogels  in 
gynecological  cancer  treatment,  further  investigation 
is  needed  in  several  areas.  Comprehensive  studies 
on  long-term  biocompatibility  and  biodegradability 
are vital for safety and efficacy. Research should also 
optimize  the  mechanical  characteristics  of  hydrogels 
to  match  different  tissue  requirements,  focusing  on 
the  effects  of  nanomaterials  and  crosslinking  meth-
ods.  Developing  standardized  fabrication  protocols 
will  ensure  consistency  and  reproducibility,  facilitat-
ing  clinical  translation.  Additionally,  clinical  trials 
are  necessary  to  evaluate  efficacy,  side  effects,  and 
patients’ life quality across diverse populations.

Although separate lines of investigation have dem-
onstrated the feasibility of targeted drug delivery and 
tissue  regeneration  in  gynecologic  settings,  evidence 
for  their  concurrent  implementation  within  a  sin-
gle  hydrogel  platform  remains  scarce.  For  instance, 

folate-conjugated 
doxorubicin–loaded 
liposomal 
hydrogels have been shown to enhance drug accumu-
lation and antitumor efficacy in ovarian cancer mod-
els,  whereas  distinct  growth  factor–laden  hydrogel 
scaffolds  have  successfully  supported  endometrial 
repair in rodent studies. To date, few reports describe 
the  co-encapsulation  of  cytotoxic  and  regenerative 
cues within the same construct, and their performance 
in orthotopic gynecologic cancer models has yet to be 
validated.  Bridging  these  trajectories  by  engineering 
dual-payload  hydrogels  could  enable  simultaneous 
eradication of residual malignancy and restoration of 
normal  tissue  architecture,  representing  a  promising 
frontier for multifunctional platform development.

Preclinical models for evaluating hybrid hydrogels

Preclinical  models  that  most  faithfully  recapitulate 
the  gynecologic  tumor  microenvironment  include 
patient-derived  xenografts  (PDXs)  of  high-grade 
serous  ovarian  and  endometrial  cancers  implanted 
orthotopically  into  immunodeficient  mice,  which 
preserve  native  stromal  architecture  and  ECM  com-
position;  syngeneic  models  such  as  ID8  in  C57BL/6 
mice,  providing  an  intact  immune  milieu  and  peri-
toneal  dissemination;  genetically  engineered  mouse 
models (e.g., MISIIR-TAg) that develop spontaneous 
ovarian  neoplasms  with  desmoplastic  stroma  in  an 
immunocompetent  setting;  and  rapid,  cost-effective 
assays like the chicken chorioallantoic membrane and 
zebrafish  xenografts  for  early  screening  of  hydrogel 
biocompatibility,  angiogenic  potential,  and  matrix 
remodeling. By employing this complementary panel, 
researchers  can  robustly  evaluate  in  vivo  gel  rheol-
ogy,  degradation  kinetics,  controlled  release,  and 
downstream  effects  on  vascularization  and  immune 
infiltration,  thereby  streamlining  translational  devel-
opment of hybrid hydrogels in gynecologic oncology.

methods, and more predictive animal models will be 
essential  to  overcoming  these  hurdles  and  ensuring 
reproducible clinical performance.

Remaining  Gaps  and  Controversies:  Despite 
remarkable  progress  in  designing  and  preclinically 
validating  hybrid  hydrogels  for  gynecologic  oncol-
ogy,  key  gaps  and  debates  persist.  First,  the  mecha-
nistic  interplay  between  specific  nanomaterials  (e.g., 
graphene  oxide,  PLGA  nanoparticles)  and  the  com-
plex tumor microenvironment remains poorly defined, 
with  conflicting  reports  on  how  hydrogel  stiffness 
and  degradation  by-products  influence  ovarian  ver-
sus cervical cancer cell behaviour. Second, a lack of 
standardized metrics for mesh size, crosslink density, 
and rheological properties hinders direct comparison 
across  platforms  and  laboratories.  Third,  immuno-
genicity  remains  controversial:  although  genipin-
crosslinked  chitosan  matrices  have  been  reported  to 
elicit  minimal  inflammation,  other  studies  document 
macrophage  activation  and  fibrotic  encapsulation 
with similar chemistries. Fourth, the optimal stimuli-
responsive  trigger  (pH,  enzyme,  thermal,  or  light)  is 
still debated, as few head-to-head evaluations exist to 
determine which cue offers the best spatial–temporal 
control in vivo. Finally, the translational gap is strik-
ing—only  a  handful  of  formulations  have  entered 
early‐phase  clinical  trials,  underscoring  challenges 
in  scaling,  sterilization,  regulatory  compliance,  and 
long-term  safety.  Addressing  these  controversies 
through  rigorous  mechanistic  studies,  harmonized 
testing protocols, and coordinated multi-center efforts 
will  be  vital  to  accelerate  the  clinical  translation  of 
hybrid hydrogels in gynecologic cancer care.

Innovations on the horizon

Emerging  technologies  and  materials  offer  potential 
solutions  to  these  challenges.  One  such  innovation 
is  developing  smart  hydrogels  which  can  respond  to 
multiple stimuli, such as pH, temperature, and enzy-
matic activity. They can provide more controlled and 
localized  drug  release,  enhancing  the  precision  of 
cancer  treatments(Yu  et  al.  2022).  Advanced  nano-
including  carbon-based  nanostructures 
materials, 
(graphene  and  carbon  nanotubes)  and  metal–organic 
frameworks  (MOFs),  are  being  explored  for  their 
exceptional  mechanical  properties  and  functional

Page 25 of 31

versatility  (Venkatas  and  Singh  2023;  Nelson  and 
Bissell 2006). These materials can boost the mechani-
cal  strength  and  functional  capabilities  of  hybrid 
hydrogels,  making  them  more  effective  in  clinical 
applications. 3D bioprinting technology is advancing 
the  creation  of  sophisticated  and  customized  hydro-
gel  scaffolds(Varinelli,  et  al.  2023).  It  allows  pre-
cise placement of cells, nanomaterials, and bioactive 
agents  within  the  hydrogel  matrix,  creating  complex 
tissue  constructs  that  closely  mimic  natural  tissues. 
This  technology  could  revolutionize  hybrid  hydrogel 
fabrication,  making  them  more  consistent  and  scal-
able for clinical use. By enhancing the precision and 
scalability  of  these  materials,  3D  bioprinting  holds 
the  potential  to  significantly  improve  the  effective-
ness and accessibility of hybrid hydrogels in medical 
applications(Zhou  et  al.  2021).  Innovations  in  gene 
editing  and  molecular  biology  are  enhancing  hybrid 
hydrogels. Techniques like CRISPR-Cas9 can modify 
the genetic makeup of cells within hydrogels, boost-
ing  their  regenerative  capabilities  and  cancer  resist-
ance. Additionally, incorporating engineered extracel-
lular vesicles (EVs) into hydrogels improves targeted 
drug delivery and tissue regeneration. These advance-
ments  could  significantly  improve  the  effectiveness 
of  hybrid  hydrogels  in  medical  applications,  making 
them more adaptable and powerful for various thera-
peutic uses(Ma et al. 2023).

Future research needs

To  fully  realize  the  potential  of  hybrid  hydrogels  in 
gynecological  cancer  treatment,  further  investigation 
is  needed  in  several  areas.  Comprehensive  studies 
on  long-term  biocompatibility  and  biodegradability 
are vital for safety and efficacy. Research should also 
optimize  the  mechanical  characteristics  of  hydrogels 
to  match  different  tissue  requirements,  focusing  on 
the  effects  of  nanomaterials  and  crosslinking  meth-
ods.  Developing  standardized  fabrication  protocols 
will  ensure  consistency  and  reproducibility,  facilitat-
ing  clinical  translation.  Additionally,  clinical  trials 
are  necessary  to  evaluate  efficacy,  side  effects,  and 
patients’ life quality across diverse populations.

Although separate lines of investigation have dem-
onstrated the feasibility of targeted drug delivery and 
tissue  regeneration  in  gynecologic  settings,  evidence 
for  their  concurrent  implementation  within  a  sin-
gle  hydrogel  platform  remains  scarce.  For  instance, 

folate-conjugated 
doxorubicin–loaded 
liposomal 
hydrogels have been shown to enhance drug accumu-
lation and antitumor efficacy in ovarian cancer mod-
els,  whereas  distinct  growth  factor–laden  hydrogel 
scaffolds  have  successfully  supported  endometrial 
repair in rodent studies. To date, few reports describe 
the  co-encapsulation  of  cytotoxic  and  regenerative 
cues within the same construct, and their performance 
in orthotopic gynecologic cancer models has yet to be 
validated.  Bridging  these  trajectories  by  engineering 
dual-payload  hydrogels  could  enable  simultaneous 
eradication of residual malignancy and restoration of 
normal  tissue  architecture,  representing  a  promising 
frontier for multifunctional platform development.

Preclinical models for evaluating hybrid hydrogels

Preclinical  models  that  most  faithfully  recapitulate 
the  gynecologic  tumor  microenvironment  include 
patient-derived  xenografts  (PDXs)  of  high-grade 
serous  ovarian  and  endometrial  cancers  implanted 
orthotopically  into  immunodeficient  mice,  which 
preserve  native  stromal  architecture  and  ECM  com-
position;  syngeneic  models  such  as  ID8  in  C57BL/6 
mice,  providing  an  intact  immune  milieu  and  peri-
toneal  dissemination;  genetically  engineered  mouse 
models (e.g., MISIIR-TAg) that develop spontaneous 
ovarian  neoplasms  with  desmoplastic  stroma  in  an 
immunocompetent  setting;  and  rapid,  cost-effective 
assays like the chicken chorioallantoic membrane and 
zebrafish  xenografts  for  early  screening  of  hydrogel 
biocompatibility,  angiogenic  potential,  and  matrix 
remodeling. By employing this complementary panel, 
researchers  can  robustly  evaluate  in  vivo  gel  rheol-
ogy,  degradation  kinetics,  controlled  release,  and 
downstream  effects  on  vascularization  and  immune 
infiltration,  thereby  streamlining  translational  devel-
opment of hybrid hydrogels in gynecologic oncology.

Advances in hybrid hydrogel design for biomedical 
applications: innovations in drug delivery and tissue 
engineering for gynecological cancers

Abstract  Hybrid  hydrogels  have  emerged  as  mul-
tifunctional  biomaterials  for  targeted  drug  delivery 
and  tissue  engineering  in  gynecologic  oncology.  In 
this  review,  we  summarize  recent  advances  in  the 
design of hybrid hydrogels that combine polymer net-
works with nanomaterials to achieve tunable stimuli-
responsiveness,  enhanced  mechanical  strength,  and 
improved  biocompatibility.  For  example,  preclini-
cal  studies  of  folate‐conjugated  liposomal  doxoru-
bicin have demonstrated enhanced accumulation and 
antitumor  efficacy  in  ovarian  cancer  models,  while 
growth  factor–loaded  hydrogel  scaffolds  have  sup-
ported  endometrial  repair  in  rodent  models.  We

Highlights 
(1)  Hybrid  hydrogels  integrate  poly-
mer  networks  and  nanomaterials  for  tunable,  stim-
uli-responsive  drug  delivery  in  ovarian  and  cervical 
cancer.
(2) Localized implantation ensures sustained chemo-
therapeutic  concentration  at  residual  tumor  sites, 
reducing systemic toxicity.
(3)  Nanoparticle-reinforced  scaffolds  support  pelvic 
tissue  regeneration  post-resection  while  providing 
immunomodulatory cues.

(4)  Multifunctional  platforms  combine  real-time 
imaging  and  chemo-immunotherapy  for  precision

Keywords  Hybrid hydrogels · Drug delivery · 
Tissue engineering · Gynecological cancers

Introduction

Gynecological  cancers  are  malignant  neoplasms  of 
the female reproductive tract, including ovarian, cer-
vical, endometrial (uterine), vulvar, and vaginal can-
cers.  Among  these,  ovarian  and  cervical  cancers  are 
the most prevalent and pose significant health risks to 
women worldwide (Hollis 2023; Nebgen et al. 2019). 
Ovarian  cancer,  often  diagnosed  at  a  late  stage  due 
to  non-specific  symptoms,  remains  the  most  lethal 
gynecological  disease(Karnezis  et  al.  2017).  Cervi-
cal cancer patients usually contracted persistent high-
risk human papillomavirus (HPV), which has seen a 
decline  in  incidence  due  to  screening  programs  and 
HPV vaccination. However, cervical cancer still rep-
resents a major health burden in worldwide low- and 
middle-income  countries  (Burd  2003;  Sharma  et  al. 
2020).

The  treatment  of  gynecological  cancers  typically 
involves a combination of surgery, chemotherapy, and 
radiotherapy  (Ferrall  et  al.  2021;  Koh,  et  al.  2019). 
Despite  advances  in  these  conventional  modalities, 
significant  challenges  remain.  Although  surgical 
resection  effectively  removes  gross  tumor  masses,  it 
often leaves behind microscopic residual disease that 
can lead to recurrence (Kahn et al. 2023; Vergote et al. 
2011).  Chemotherapy,  although  a  cornerstone  in  the 
management of advanced-stage cancers, is associated 
with significant systemic toxicity and the progression 
of drug resistance (Stein et al. 2021; Konstantinopou-
los  et  al.  2015;  Kingnate  et  al.  2021).  Radiotherapy, 
while targeted, can unintentionally provide collateral 
damage  to  adjacent  healthy  tissues,  resulting  in  per-
sistent side effects. Additionally, the heterogeneity of 
tumors and the unique microenvironment of gyneco-
logical  cancers  further  complicate  treatment  strate-
gies,  necessitating  the  progression  of  more  effective 
and less toxic therapeutic options (Herrera et al. 2019; 
Dembo  1992;  Mayadev  et  al.  2022).  Efficient  deliv-
ery to gynecologic tumors leverages both passive and 
active targeting strategies. The enhanced permeability 

and  retention  (EPR)  effect  allows  nanoscale  carri-
ers  to  preferentially  accumulate  in  ovarian  and  uter-
ine  tumors  within  the  peritoneal  cavity  due  to  leaky 
vasculature and impaired lymphatic drainage. Active 
targeting employs ligands—such as folate, RGD pep-
tides,  or  antibodies  against  folate  receptor  α,  HER2, 
or CD44—to promote receptor-mediated endocytosis 
by  cancer  cells.  Physical  guidance  methods,  includ-
ing magnetic field–directed navigation of iron-oxide-
embedded hydrogels and focused ultrasound–induced 
cavitation,  further  enhance  localization  to  pelvic 
lesions.  Stimuli-responsive  triggers  (e.g.,  acidic  pH, 
elevated  MMP  activity,  redox  gradients,  and  hyper-
thermia)  refine  spatial–temporal  drug  release  within 
the  tumor  microenvironment.  These  fundamental 
mechanisms  underpin  the  subsequent  development 
of  hybrid  hydrogel  vectors  tailored  for  gynecologic 
oncology applications.

However, current approaches fail to bridge the gap 
between  these  clinical  limitations  and  precise,  local-
ized  therapy.  For  instance,  residual  microscopic  dis-
ease  after  surgery  can  evade  systemic  chemotherapy, 
and drug-resistant tumor subclones frequently emerge 
when  drug  concentrations  fluctuate  between  sub-
therapeutic  and  toxic  levels.  Hybrid  hydrogels  can  be 
engineered to address each of these issues as follows: 
(1)  Residual  disease  after  surgery:  Hybrid  hydrogels 
can  be  implanted  or  injected  into  the  surgical  bed  to 
form  an  in  situ  depot  that  gradually  releases  chemo-
therapeutics  or  immunomodulators,  thereby  targeting 
microscopic foci that might otherwise remain. (2) Sys-
temic  toxicity  and  drug  resistance:  By  encapsulating 
chemotherapeutic  agents  within  a  polymeric  network, 
hybrid  hydrogels  achieve  sustained,  local  drug  con-
centrations  that  remain  above  the  resistance-threshold 
in tumor cells while sparing healthy tissues from high 
systemic  exposure.  (3)  Collateral  damage  from  radio-
therapy: Hydrogels can be loaded with radioprotective 
nanoparticles  or  antioxidant  compounds  that  release 
selectively in peri-tumoral regions, mitigating damage 
to  adjacent  normal  tissues  during  and  after  radiation. 
(4) Tumor heterogeneity and microenvironmental bar-
riers: Stimuli-responsive hydrogel matrices can exploit 
tumor-specific  cues  (e.g.,  acidic  pH,  elevated  enzyme 
activity) to trigger on-demand drug release, overcom-
ing  barriers  such  as  poor  vascularization  and  hypoxia 
that limit conventional delivery.

At  the  core  of  these  advances  lies  the  integration 
of  nanotechnology  with  well-characterized  polymer 

Vol:. (1234567890) 
 Cell Biol Toxicol          (2025) 41:115  

Page 3 of 31 

  115 

systems.  Specifically,  polyethylene  glycol  (PEG) 
and  chitosan  have  emerged  as  leading  candidates 
for  gynecologic  applications:  PEG-based  hydrogels 
are  renowned  for  their  excellent  biocompatibility, 
“stealth”  properties  (minimized  protein  adsorption), 
and tunable degradation rates. In ovarian cancer mod-
els,  PEG  hydrogels  have  been  formulated  to  release 
cisplatin  over  several  weeks  within  the  peritoneal 
cavity,  maintaining  therapeutic  drug  concentrations 
while reducing nephrotoxicity and myelosuppression. 
Chitosan-based  hydrogels—derived  from  deacety-
lated chitin—offer intrinsic mucoadhesive and hemo-
static  properties  that  are  particularly  advantageous 
for cervical and vaginal delivery. When administered 
intravaginally,  chitosan  matrices  adhere  to  cervical 
mucosa and prolong residence time, improving local 
retention of chemotherapeutics or immunomodulators 
and enhancing uptake by dysplastic epithelial cells.

By  combining 

these  polymers  with 

func-
tional  nanomaterials  (e.g.,  metallic  nanoparticles, 
liposomes,  carbon-based  nanostructures),  hybrid 
hydrogels can be tailored to the mechanical and bio-
logical demands of gynecologic tissues. PEG imparts 
a  hydrophilic,  mesh-like  network  suitable  for  fluid-
rich  peritoneal  environments,  whereas  chitosan  con-
fers  mucoadhesion  and  in  situ  gelation  under  mildly 
acidic vaginal conditions. Such polymer-nanomaterial 
pairings  enable  precise  control  over  swelling  behav-
ior,  degradation  kinetics,  and  drug  release  profiles, 
thereby  addressing  the  specific  clinical  shortcom-
ings  of  surgery,  chemotherapy,  and  radiotherapy  in 
gynecological oncology.

Given the constraints of current therapeutic strate-
gies,  it  is  an  urgency  for  innovative  approaches  that 
can  optimize  therapeutic  outcomes  while  lower  the 
risk of adverse effects. Drug delivery systems specifi-
cally focus on targeting tumor cells, thereby decreas-
ing  systemic  toxicity,  are  of  paramount  importance. 
Similarly, tissue engineering solutions that can facili-
tate  the  regeneration  of  tissues  damaged  by  cancer 
or  its  treatment  are  critical  for  boosting  patient  sur-
vival  and  life  quality  (Fig.  1).  Figure  1  illustrates 
four  complementary  strategies  for  tumor-targeted 
nanotherapy. In panel a, lipid vesicles decorated with 
tumor-specific  antibodies  engage  receptor-mediated 
endocytosis  for  active  targeting;  panel  b  shows  pas-
sive  accumulation  of  nanoparticles  via  the  enhanced 
permeability  and  retention  (EPR)  effect  in  leaky 
tumor  vessels;  panel  c  depicts  magnetic  guidance  of 

chitosan-coated,  5-fluorouracil-loaded  magnetic  nan-
oparticles  under  an  external  magnet  to  concentrate 
the drug at the tumor site; and panel d demonstrates 
focused  ultrasound-induced  cavitation  of  circulat-
ing  microbubbles  to  transiently  disrupt  vascular  bar-
riers  (e.g.,  the  BBB),  thereby  enabling  nanoparticle 
entry—a  mechanism  that  could  be  adapted  to  over-
come  peritoneal  or  pelvic  barriers  in  gynecologic 
cancers. Together, these approaches integrate molec-
ular recognition, physical forces, and barrier modula-
tion  to  enhance  delivery  specificity  and  efficacy,  yet 
each  faces  critical  hurdles—antigen  heterogeneity, 
variable vascular permeability, dosimetry and equip-
ment  logistics  for  external  fields,  and  the  risk  of 
mechanical  tissue  damage—underscoring  the  need 
for multimodal designs and rigorous preclinical vali-
dation.  Nanotechnology  served  as  a  promising  field 
in  this  regard,  giving  novel  strategies  for  both  drug 
delivery and tissue engineering (Ling et al. 2023; Li 
et  al.  2023a).  Nanomaterials,  due  to  their  small  size 
and large surface area, can be engineered to function 
in  molecular  biological  systems,  helping  precise  tar-
geting  and  controlled  release  of  drug  agents  (Cheng 
et  al.  2021;  He  et  al.  2022).  Moreover,  nanomateri-
als can be integrated into scaffold structures for tissue 
engineering, establishing a conducive matrix for cell 
proliferation  and  tissue  regeneration(Bharadwaz  and 
Jayasuriya 2020; Li et al. 2017; Tupone, et al. 2021; 
Grimaudo et al. 2019).

For  drug  delivery,  hybrid  hydrogels  are  engi-
neered for releasing therapeutic agents in a controlled 
way  when  exposed  to  surrounding  stimuli  (e.g.,  pH, 
temperature,  or  enzymatic  activity).  This  ensures 
localized  drug  release  while  minimizing  systemic 
exposure  (Juthi,  et  al.  2023;  Gao  et  al.  2016;  Zhang 
et  al.  2022a;  Mauri  et  al.  2021).  This  delivery  not 
only  enhances  the  therapy  efficacy  but  also  weakens 
side  effects  induced  by  conventional  chemotherapy. 
In  tissue  engineering,  hybrid  hydrogels  can  serve  as 
scaffolds  that  promote  the  growth  and  differentia-
tion  of  cells,  aiding  the  tissue  regeneration  damaged 
by  cancer  or  its  treatments  (Neves  et  al.  2020;  Yang 
et al. 2017). The integration of nanomaterials within 
these hydrogels significantly enhances their mechani-
cal  properties,  rendering  them  ideal  for  load-bearing 
applications.  Furthermore,  nanomaterials  can  be 
functionalized  with  bioactive  molecules  like  pep-
tides,  extracellular  matrix  components,  or  growth 
factors,  which  enhance  cell  adhesion,  proliferation,

only  give  the  necessary  help  for  new  tissue  growth, 
but  also  actively  enhance  the  biological  processes 
involved  in  tissue  regeneration,  resulting  in  better 
clinical outcomes and improved patient recovery.

Hybrid  hydrogels  that  combine  natural  and  syn-
thetic  polymers  with  nanoscale  additives  have  dem-
onstrated  remarkable  versatility  across  tissue‐engi-
neering and drug‐delivery applications. For cartilage 
regeneration,  porous  gelatin  methacrylate–poly(2-
ethyl-2-oxazoline)  scaffolds  loaded  with  kartogenin

hyaluronic acid bioinks have similarly enabled high‐
fidelity  bioprinting  of  osteochondral  constructs,  sup-
porting cell viability and extracellular matrix deposi-
tion under shear forces typical of extrusion processes 
(Dorishetty et al. 2021; Jia and Kiick 2009). In repro-
ductive‐tissue 
engineering,  polysaccharide‐based 
hydrogels  (e.g.,  alginate,  chitosan,  hyaluronic  acid)

 Cell Biol Toxicol          (2025) 41:115  

Page 5 of 31 

  115 

mimic  the  endometrial  niche,  promoting  adhesion, 
proliferation,  and  controlled  release  of  growth  fac-
tors—offering  new  strategies  for  infertility  treat-
ment  and  uterine  tissue  regeneration  (Dorishetty 
et  al.  2021;  Jia  and  Kiick  2009).  Stimuli‐responsive 
designs  further  extend  these  platforms’  functionality 
by  tuning  release  profiles  to  local  cues.  pH-sensitive 
montmorillonite–PVP/PEG  composites  released  cur-
cumin  preferentially  under  acidic,  tumor-mimicking 
conditions  and  enhanced  cytotoxicity  in  MCF-7 
cells  compared  to  free  drug  (Dorishetty  et  al.  2021; 
Jia  and  Kiick  2009).  Magnetic  Fe₂O₃–PEG–agarose 
nanocomposites regulated 5-fluorouracil delivery via 
pH triggers, demonstrating biocompatibility and con-
trolled release in vitro (Dorishetty et al. 2021; Jia and 
Kiick  2009).  Together,  these  studies  highlight  how 
judicious  selection  of  polymer–nanomaterial  combi-
nations  and  crosslinking  methods  can  meet  diverse 
mechanical,  biological,  and  release‐kinetic  require-
ments—while  underscoring  ongoing  challenges  in 
standardizing  metrics,  elucidating  long-term  in  vivo 
performance, and scaling toward clinical translation.

This  review  highlights  the  significant  progress  in 
hybrid hydrogel design and development for biomedi-
cal usage, mainly focusing on drug delivery and tissue 
engineering  in  gynecological  cancer  treatment.  By 
incorporating  nanomaterials  and  advanced  hydrogel 
matrices,  these  hybrid  systems  offer  enhanced  bio-
compatibility,  mechanical  strength,  and  responsive-
ness to stimuli. Their ability to achieve targeted drug 
delivery reduces side effects and improves therapeutic 
outcomes,  which  is  critical  in  reconstructive  surgery 
for  gynecological  cancers.  We  emphasize  key  inno-
vations,  successful  case  studies,  and  future  research 
directions that hold the potential to transform cancer 
treatment approaches.

Hybrid Hydrogels: Composition and Properties

Definition and composition

Hybrid hydrogels are innovative materials that merge 
the  properties  of  traditional  hydrogels  with  those  of 
nanomaterials, creating multifunctional systems ideal 
for advanced biomedical applications (Aliakbarzadeh 
et al. 2024; Ghorbani et al. 2023; Ghahremani-Nasab 
et al. 2025). Hybrid hydrogels are three-dimensional, 
large 
hydrophilic  polymer  networks 

that  retain 

volumes  of  water  while  mimicking  the  extracellular 
matrix  of  native  tissues.  When  these  networks  are 
integrated with nanoscale components—ranging from 
inorganic  nanoparticles  to  polymeric  and  carbon-
based nanostructures—the result is a multifunctional 
platform  that  combines  the  swelling  and  biocompat-
ibility  of  hydrogels  with  the  tailored  properties  of 
nanomaterials  (Pourmadadi  et  al.  2024a,  2024b). 
They are valued for their biocompatibility, flexibility, 
and  ability  to  be  tuned  for  specific  physical  proper-
ties,  rendering  them  appropriate  for  drug  delivery 
and  tissue  engineering  (Wang  et  al.  2021;  Cao  et  al. 
2023).

The  integration  of  nanomaterials  into  hydrogels 
enhances  their  capabilities.  Nanomaterials  including 
nanoparticles,  nanofibers,  and  nanotubes  are  incor-
porated  into  the  hydrogel  matrix  to  impart  unique 
characteristics.  These  include  increased  mechanical 
strength,  responsiveness  to  environmental  changes 
(pH, temperature, or light), and improved drug load-
ing  and  release  profiles  (Qian  et  al.  2022;  Wu  et  al. 
2023; Wang et al. 2024). This combination results in 
a  hybrid  system  where  the  hydrogel  provides  a  bio-
compatible  and  hydrophilic  environment,  while  the 
nanomaterials add functionality, making it possible to 
create  versatile  platforms  for  treating  gynecological 
cancers.  The  increased  mechanical  strength  ensures 
that the hydrogel can withstand physiological stresses 
for  load-bearing  tissues.  Responsiveness  to  environ-
mental  stimuli  permits  the  targeted  release  of  thera-
peutic  agents  upon  encountering  specific  triggers, 
ensuring precise drug delivery towards the tumor site. 
Improved drug loading and release profiles mean that 
higher  doses  of  therapeutic  agents  can  be  incorpo-
rated and transferred in a controlled manner, advanc-
ing the overall efficacy of the treatment. This hybrid 
approach achieves the precise targeting and controlled 
release of drugs, making it a significant advancement 
in  cancer  therapy.  Furthermore,  this  method  mini-
mizes  side  effects  and  maximizes  therapeutic  out-
comes, representing a major step forward in the treat-
ment of gynecological cancers.

These  nanoscale  additives  contribute  to  hybrid 
hydrogel  performance  through  two  complementary 
mechanisms:

Mechanical  reinforcement.  Rigid  nanomaterials 
such  as  carbon  nanotubes  (CNTs),  graphene  oxide 
(GO)  nanosheets  and  silica  nanoparticles  serve  pri-
marily to bolster the hydrogel’s load-bearing capacity

Presentation  of  biological  cues.  In  parallel,  nano-

carriers  can  be  surface-functionalized  through  car-

thiol–maleimide  ligation  to  present  targeting  ligands 
such  as  RGD  peptides,  folic  acid,  or  growth  factors

nanoparticles (gold, iron oxide) further contribute by 
providing protein-binding surfaces for enzyme immo-

bined diagnostic imaging and therapeutic (“theranos-
tic”) functions within a single hydrogel scaffold.

By  treating  mechanical  reinforcement  and  bio-
logical  functionality  as  complementary  yet  distinct 
aspects of hydrogel design, this nuanced composition 
enables the creation of bespoke platforms for targeted 
drug  delivery,  tissue  engineering  and  regenerative 
therapies in gynecological oncology.

Types of hybrid hydrogels

Interpenetrating networks (IPNs) are a type of hybrid 
hydrogel  comprising  two  or  more  polymer  networks 
that  are  physically  entangled  but  not  covalently 
bonded (Li et al. 2023b). This unique structure allows 
each  polymer  network  to  retain  its  individual  prop-
erties  while  augmenting  the  overall  functionality  of 
the  hydrogel.  The  attributes  of  improving  mechani-
cal strength, swelling capacity, and responsiveness to 
environmental  stimuli  make  them  particularly  fit  for 
drug  delivery  and  tissue  engineering  in  gynecologi-
cal cancer therapy. IPNs provide robust and adaptable 
scaffolds  that  support  cellular  activities  and  transfer 
therapeutic agents effectively (Carpentier et al. 2024). 

In the context of drug delivery, IPNs can accommo-
date  high  drug  loads  and  release  them  in  particular 
physiological  conditions,  concerning  pH  changes 
within  the  TME.  This  release-targeted  mechanism 
guarantees  the  delivering  precision  where  needed, 
lessening  systemic  side  effects  and  boosting  treat-
ment  efficacy.  In  addition,  the  enhanced  mechanical 
strength  and  swelling  capacity  of  IPNs  ensure  that 
they reserve their structural integrity, providing con-
sistent and reliable performance throughout the treat-
ment duration(Wang et al. 2014).

For tissue engineering, IPNs offer a versatile plat-
form  for  creating  scaffolds  that  support  cell  activi-
ties. The physical entanglement of polymer networks 
within  IPNs  provides  a  stable  and  conducive  condi-
tion  for  cellular  activities,  promoting  tissue  regen-
eration  and  restoration  (Chang  and  Yeh  2021).  The 
responsiveness of IPNs to environmental stimuli also 
allows for dynamic modulation of the scaffold’s prop-
erties, adapting to the evolving needs of the regener-
ating  tissue.  This  adaptability  is  helpful  for  treating 
gynecological cancer, due to the need of effective and 
sustained  tissue  regeneration  after  surgical  interven-
tions or radiation therapy (Yang et al. 2021).

Moreover, the ability to incorporate bioactive mol-
ecules and nanomaterials into IPNs further enhances 
their  functionality.  Bioactive  molecules  of  growth 
factors and peptides can be integrated into the hydro-
gel  matrix  to  promote  specific  cellular  responses, 
while nanomaterials can impart additional properties, 
such  as  antimicrobial  activity  or  enhanced  mechani-
cal  strength(Mehmood,  et  al.  2023;  Thankam  et  al. 
2022). This multifunctionality makes IPNs an attrac-
tive  option  for  developing  advanced  therapeutic  and 
regenerative  solutions  tailored  to  the  unique  chal-
lenges of gynecological cancer treatment.
Core–shell  structures  are  another 

innovative 
approach  in  hybrid  hydrogel  design(Brunel  et  al. 
2025).  These  structures  consist  of  a  core  material, 
often  a  nanoparticle,  encapsulated  within  a  hydrogel 
shell.  The  core  can  be  made  of  various  nanomateri-
als,  such  as  metallic  nanoparticles  or  quantum  dots, 
providing  unique  functionalities  like  imaging,  heat-
ing, or magnetic responsiveness (Li et al. 2025). The 
hydrogel  shell,  typically  composed  of  biocompatible 
polymers,  controls  the  release  of  therapeutic  agents 
and  ensures  biocompatibility  (Horst  et  al.  2022a; 
Strassburg  et  al.  2017).  Core–shell  hybrid  hydrogels 
are  particularly  beneficial  for  drug-targeted  delivery

IPNs  with  translational  validation.  Beyond  their 
utility  as  in  vitro  mechanobiology  platforms,  IPN 
hydrogels  have  demonstrated  efficacy  in  preclinical 
gynecologic  models.  Horst  et  al.  developed  inject-
able  agarose–collagen  and  alginate–collagen  IPNs 
that  faithfully  reproduce  key  physical  and  biochemi-
cal  cues  of  the  ovarian  tumor  microenvironment, 
with tunable stiffnesses from 0.5 to 5 kPa and colla-
gen concentrations up to 3 mg/mL, enabling mecha-
notransduction  studies  in  epithelial  ovarian  cancer 
cells  (Horst  et  al.  2022a;  Strassburg  et  al.  2017). 
Translating these networks into drug‐delivery depots, 
Sun  et  al.  formulated  an  in  situ  crosslinkable  IPN 
hydrogel  depot  containing  paclitaxel  nanocrystals 
(PNC-gel).  A  single  intraperitoneal  administration 
in  SKOV3-bearing  mice  extended  median  survival 
by 45% compared with Taxol, attributed to sustained 
peritoneal  drug  levels  and  low  systemic  exposure 
(Horst et al. 2022a; Strassburg et al. 2017). Moreover, 
Winer  et  al.  used  F3-targeted  cisplatin-loaded  poly-
acrylamide  IPN  nanoparticles  to  selectively  ablate 
tumor vasculature in both murine and human ovarian 
carcinoma  models,  achieving  rapid  tumor  regression 
and vascular necrosis, even in platinum-resistant lines 
(Horst et al. 2022a; Strassburg et al. 2017).

Core–shell  hydrogels  for  controlled  release,  bio-
degradation  and  imaging.  Core–shell  architectures—
where  a  drug-laden  core  is  enveloped  by  a  degrada-
ble hydrogel shell—offer precise control over release 
kinetics, tunable degradation, and integrated imaging 
functions.  An  injectable  DNA–doxorubicin  hydro-
gel  (“MB-Dox”)  demonstrated  this:  covalent  MB-
Dox  cores  were  encapsulated  in  a  nuclease-degra-
dable  DNA  shell,  permitting  activatable,  trackable 
release  via  photoacoustic  tomography  and  yielding 
a  72.2%  reduction  in  intraperitoneal  ovarian  tumor 
growth versus free DOX in mice (Horst et al. 2022a; 
Strassburg  et  al.  2017).  Likewise,  thermosensitive 
micelle–hydrogel  hybrids  based  on  Poloxamer  407 
and  carboxymethyl  chitosan  provided  an  initial  20% 
burst  release  of  paclitaxel  followed  by  sustained 
delivery  for  20  days,  achieving  64.3%  tumor  inhibi-
tion  in  H22-bearing  mice;  when  loaded  with  fluo-
rescent probes, these constructs also enabled intratu-
moral  imaging  to  confirm  depot  localization  (Horst 
et  al.  2022a;  Strassburg  et  al.  2017).  By  selecting 

hydrolyzable ester linkers or nuclease-sensitive back-
bones,  core–shell  hydrogels  can  be  tuned  for  com-
plete  clearance  within  2–4  weeks,  and  can  incorpo-
rate  contrast  agents—such  as  iron  oxide  for  MRI  or 
gold  for  CT/photothermal  imaging—to  support  non-
invasive monitoring in gynecologic cancer models.

Properties

Firstly,  hybrid  hydrogels  are  characterized  by  bio-
compatibility,  a  fundamental  property  that  allows 
them  to  engage  with  biological  tissues  without  elic-
iting  negative  immune  reactions.  The  hydrophilic 
nature  of  hydrogels,  combined  with  the  inertness  of 
many  nanomaterials,  promotes  cell  behaviors(Zhang 
et  al.  2021;  Sartore,  et  al.  2022).  It  makes  hybrid 
hydrogels  ideal  for  biomedical  fields  for  drug  deliv-
ery  and  tissue  engineering  in  gynecological  cancers. 

The  biocompatibility  of  these  materials  can  be  fur-
ther enhanced by functionalizing them with bioactive 
molecules  or  peptides  that  mimic  the  extracellular 
matrix,  thereby  improving  their  integration  with  the 
surrounding tissue.

Secondly, the mechanical strength of hybrid hydro-
gels  is  vital  for  their  application  in  load-bearing  tis-
sues  and  in  situations  where  structural  integrity  is 
necessary  (Chen  et  al.  2013).  The  incorporation  of 
nanomaterials  containing  carbon  nanotubes,  gra-
phene,  or  silica  nanoparticles  significantly  enhances 
the  mechanical  properties  of  hydrogels.  This  results 
in  materials  that  can  withstand  mechanical  stresses 
and reserve their shape and functionality in dynamic 
physiological environments. In the context of gyneco-
logical cancer treatment, robust hydrogels can provide 
durable  scaffolds  for  tissue  regeneration,  supporting 
the repair and reconstruction of affected tissues.

Thirdly, stimuli-responsive behavior describes how 
hybrid  hydrogels  can  change  physically  or  chemi-
cally when exposed to external stimuli like tempera-
ture,  pH,  light,  or  magnetic  fields  (Wu  et  al.  2010). 
This  property  is  especially  beneficial  for  targeted 
drug  delivery,  enabling  precise  regulation  of  thera-
peutic  agents  triggered  by  external  factors.  pH-sen-
sitive hydrogels can transfer drugs in the acidic con-
dition  of  a  tumor,  ensuring  the  targets  are  delivered 
directly  to  tumor  cells  (Wang,  et  al.  2020)  (Fig.  2). 
This schematic depicts a dual‐responsive drug‐deliv-
ery  platform  in  which  mesoporous  silica  nanoparti-
cles  (MSNs)  bearing  an  acid‐labile,  self-immolative 
polymer  coating  (CS-SIP)  are  homogeneously  dis-
persed  within  a  thermo-sensitive  hydrogel  network 
(Fig. 2). Under normothermic conditions the compos-
ite  remains  a  stable  gel,  entrapping  both  the  MSNs 
and their small-molecule payloads. Upon exposure to 
the  mildly  acidic  tumor  microenvironment,  protona-
tion triggers depolymerization of the CS-SIP shell—
liberating  the  drug-loaded  MSNs—and  concurrently 
cleaves the Boc‐protected end groups on the NHP407 
polymer  chains  to  yield  amine-terminated  SHP407. 
This  deprotection  disrupts  the  hydrogel’s  physical 
crosslinks, accelerating network dissolution and facil-
itating rapid, localized release of both MSNs and pay-
load. By coupling temperature‐induced gelation with 
pH‐triggered cleavage, this system affords minimally 
invasive  administration  followed  by  highly  specific, 
tumor‐site drug liberation while minimizing systemic 
exposure. Specifically, three classes of tumor-relevant

ing  cellular  uptake.  The  integration  of  these  stimuli-
responsive behaviors into hybrid hydrogels enhances 
their  versatility  and  effectiveness  in  drug  delivery 
systems. By incorporating responsive elements, these 
hydrogels can adapt to the dynamic conditions within 
the  body,  providing  a  smart  and  adaptable  platform 
for  cancer  therapy.  This  adaptability  is  particularly 

beneficial for gynecological cancer treatments, where 
targeted  and  controlled  drug  release  can  signifi-
cantly  improve  patient  outcomes  and  reduce  adverse 
effects(Winer et al. 2010).

Characterization  of  Regular  and  Stimuli-Respon-
sive  Hydrogels.  A  comprehensive  suite  of  physico-
chemical  and  mechanical  tests  is  required  to  ensure 
that  both  conventional  and  smart  hybrid  hydrogels 
meet  application‐specific  criteria:  equilibrium  swell-
ing studies to quantify swelling ratio and water con-
tent;  oscillatory  rheometry  for  gelation  kinetics  and 
storage/loss  moduli;  uniaxial  compression  or  tensile 
tests  for  Young’s  modulus  and  yield  strength;  SEM 
or  micro-CT  imaging  to  assess  porosity  and  pore-
size  distribution;  FTIR  and  NMR  analyses  to  verify 
chemical  composition  and  crosslink  density;  DSC 
and TGA for thermal stability; and Flory–Rehner cal-
culations  to  estimate  mesh  size.  Stimuli-responsive 
systems  further  demand  dynamic  evaluation,  includ-
ing  pH-  or  temperature-dependent  swelling/deswell-
ing  cycles  monitored  by  rheometry  under  controlled 
light-  or  redox-triggered  modulus 
environments, 
changes,  and  in  vitro  release  assays  under  each  trig-
ger condition quantified by UV–Vis or HPLC. In situ 
imaging modalities (environmental SEM or confocal 
microscopy)  can  capture  real-time  network  collapse 
or  pore-opening  events  upon  stimulus  application 
(Kulkarni et al. 2023). This multi-modal characteriza-
tion  framework  guarantees  reproducible,  predictable 
performance in both standard buffers and biologically 
relevant microenvironments.

Degradation  Pathways  and  Toxicity  Assessment. 
Hybrid  hydrogels  require  comprehensive  evaluation 
of both their breakdown mechanisms and biocompat-
ibility to ensure safety in clinical settings. As outlined 
by  Pagar  et  al.  (Pagar  et  al.  2022),  degradation  can 
proceed  via  hydrolytic  cleavage  of  ester/amide  link-
ages,  oxidative  scission  by  reactive  oxygen  species, 
photolytic  bond  breakage  under  UV  exposure,  and 
enzymatic  hydrolysis  by  matrix  metalloproteinases. 
Characterization  of  these  pathways  should  employ 
complementary  techniques—gel  permeation  chro-
matography  (GPC)  or  size‐exclusion  chromatogra-
phy (SEC) for molecular‐weight profiling; ^1H/^13C 
NMR,  FTIR,  and  UV–Vis  spectroscopy  for  func-
tional‐group  analysis;  DSC/TGA  for  thermal  stabil-
ity; and LC–MS/MS for identification of intermediate 
and  final  degradation  products.  Forced‐degradation 
studies  under  ICH  Q1A  and  Q3A  stress  conditions

Controlled drug release ranks among the most sig-
nificant  advantages  of  applying  hybrid  hydrogels  for 
cancer therapy. Hydrogels have a porous structure that 
can  encapsulate  diverse  therapeutic  agents,  contain-
ing small molecules, proteins, and nucleic acids(Gao 
et  al.  2016).  By  incorporating  nanomaterials,  the 
release  kinetics  of  these  agents  can  be  finely  tuned 
to  achieve  sustained  or  stimuli-responsive  release 
profiles(Borum  et  al.  2022).  This  release  under  con-
trol  lessens  the  systemic  toxicity  of  chemotherapeu-
tic  agents  and  enhances  their  therapeutic  efficacy  by 
maintaining optimal drug concentrations at the tumor 
site(Ju  et  al.  2013).  In  gynecological  cancers,  this 
approach  can  improve  treatment  survival  and  lower 
the side effects caused by chemotherapy.

Design and synthesis of hybrid hydrogels

Chemical Crosslinking

Chemical crosslinking is a critical technique in form-
ing hybrid hydrogels, providing them with necessary 
structural  integrity  and  functionality  for  biomedi-
cal  applications,  especially  in  gynecological  cancer 
treatment.  This  process  contains  constructing  cova-
lent bonds between polymer chains to obtain a stable 
and durable network. Various methods and materials 
are  employed  to  achieve  chemical  crosslinking,  each 
contributing  unique  properties  to  the  final  hydrogel. 
One of the most widely used methods for chemically 
crosslinking  hydrogels  is  free  radical  polymeriza-
tion (Salahuddin et al. 2021). This technique involves 
generating  free  radicals,  which  initiate  the  polym-
erization  of  monomers  to  form  polymer  chains  that 
subsequently  crosslink  (Moncada  et  al.  2023).  Free 
radicals can be generated using thermal initiators, UV 

light, or chemical initiators. This method is versatile, 
permitting  the  addition  of  diverse  functional  groups 
and  nanomaterials  into  the  hydrogel  matrix.  For 
example,  UV-induced  free  radical  polymerization  is 
often employed to create photo-crosslinked hydrogels 
with  precise  control  over  the  network  structure  and 
mechanical properties(Wang et al. 2023).

Additionally,  click  chemistry  represents  a  highly 
specific and efficient approach to chemical crosslink-
ing.  It  involves  reactions  that  form  covalent  bonds 
between  polymer  chains  with  high  yield  and  under 
mild  conditions.  A  prominent  example  is  the  azide-
alkyne cycloaddition, which facilitates the formation 
of  robust  hydrogel  networks(Wang  and  Zhang  2022; 
Singh  et  al.  2022).  The  specificity  and  efficiency  of 
click  chemistry  make  it  particularly  appropriate  for 
biomedical field where precise control over the hydro-
gel’s architecture and functionality is required. Enzy-
matic crosslinking leverages enzymes to catalyze the 
formation of covalent bonds between polymer chains. 
This method is advantageous for its biocompatibility 
and ability to proceed under physiological conditions. 
For instance, horseradish peroxidase (HRP) can cata-
lyze  the  crosslinking  of  phenol-containing  polymers 
within  hydrogen  peroxide(Chen,  et  al.  2025;  Singh, 
et  al.  2025).  Enzymatic  crosslinking  is  particularly 
useful for creating hydrogels intended for tissue engi-
neering  and  regenerative  medicine,  where  maintain-
ing a biological environment is crucial.

Notably, various materials are employed in chemi-
cal  crosslinking  to  create  hydrogels  with  specific 
properties  (Table  1).  Polyethylene  Glycol  (PEG): 
Known  for  its  biocompatibility,  hydrophilicity,  and 
ease  of  functionalization,  PEG-based  hydrogels  are 
often  crosslinked  using  methods  like  free  radical 
polymerization and click chemistry(Dong et al. 2022; 
Kulkarni et al. 2023). These approaches facilitate the 
production  of  hydrogels  with  designed  mechanical 
and  biological  features,  making  them  ideal  for  drug 
delivery  and  tissue  engineering(Pagar  et  al.  2022). 
Alginate:  This  natural  polymer  is  biocompatible  and 
forms  gels  within  divalent  cations.  Chemical  modi-
fications  allow  for  covalent  crosslinking,  enhancing 
the stability and functionality of the hydrogels, mak-
ing  them  suitable  as  biocompatible  scaffolds(Lin 
et  al.  2020;  Simão  et  al.  2020).  Chitosan:  Derived 
from  chitin,  chitosan  is  frequently  used  in  hydrogel 
formation  due  to  its  biocompatibility  and  biodeg-
radability.  It  can  be  chemically  crosslinked  using
