Second,  atomic-resolution  HAADF  and  annular 
bright  field  (ABF)  images  require  acquisition  in 
STEM mode, where the lattice structure of the mate-
rials is easily damaged by prolonged electron beam 
irradiation. Reducing the operating voltage of the 
TEM can effectively mitigate the damage of electron 
irradiation, but it may also lead to a certain degree of 
reduction in the resolution of electron images.
  (ii)  There  are  limitations  in  using  some  of  the  cur-
rent open electrochemical cells in the in-situ TEM 
experiments due to ineffective battery-performance 
cycles. In many cases, the electrode material dynam-
ics cannot be uncovered during battery’s operation 
over long-term cycling. To address this, an acceler-
ated durability test could be adopted, which should 
aid elucidating the inherent fundamental science of 
structural  transformation  process  over  long-term 
cycling.

  (iii)  For assessing intercalation reactions of the electrode 
nanomaterials, the determination of the transport 
pathways and mechanisms of intercalated ions within 
the host structure is rather difficult, which poses a 
major challenge for understanding the fundamen-
tal principles of the reaction. Current in-situ TEM 
techniques,  when  combined  with  EDX  or  EELS, 
allow the observation of electrochemical reaction 
interfaces, but have limited capabilities to capture 
the movement or transport of intercalated ions within 
the  lattice.  This  difficulty  arises  partly  from  the 
limited resolution of current transmission electron 
microscopes for light elements, making it challeng-
ing to capture intercalated lithium and sodium ions. 
To overcome this, in-situ observation under STEM 
mode should be developed.

  (iv)  While charge transfer plays an important role in elec-
trochemical energy storage, there is a lack of tech-
niques to directly characterize charge density at the 
nano or atomic scale. 4D-STEM offers high temporal 
resolution, enabling the mapping of charge density 
distribution within a sample by analyzing the phase 
changes that occur as the electron beam propagates 
through the sample. 4D-STEM combined with in-situ 
techniques can be utilized to simulate the dynamic 
evolution of interfacial charge density under cycling 
conditions.

  (v)  During  in-situ  TEM  measurements,  exposure  of 
samples to the electron beam may have a significant 

impact  on  the  experimental  results.  High-energy 
electron beams may damage sample structures, par-
ticularly in organic materials and lithium metal, lead-
ing to bond breakage, oxidation, and structural deg-
radation. As the magnification increases, the damage 
caused by the electron beam becomes more severe. 
Therefore, a lower resolution TEM mode is typically 
employed to mitigate the electron beam effect on the 
experimental results during in-situ observation. It is 
particularly important to take appropriate preventive 
measures regarding the effects of the electron beam, 
especially  in  view  of  some  nanomaterials  being 
sensitive to electron beam-induced reactions [73, 
74]. Within this field, increasing imaging speed to 
reduce radiation doses and applying voltages below 
the threshold for radiation damage have proven effec-
tive in mitigating electron beam damage. However, 
the adoption of this strategy could result in a cer-
tain degree of reduction in image resolution. The 
integration  of  cryo-TEM  technology  with  in-situ 
techniques offers a promising solution to electron 
irradiation issues. At extremely low temperatures, 
the  damage  from  electron-beam  can  be  greatly 
reduced. By combining cryo-TEM with in-situ TEM 
techniques, it is expected to obtain more meaning-
ful information on the formation of SEI layer and 
lithium dendrites at the nanoscale.

  (vi)  In-situ TEM can facilitate the high-resolution imag-
ing and spectroscopic data collection, but the analy-
sis of such data is complex and time-consuming. For 
instance, hundreds of SAED and HRTEM images can 
be collected in investigating the structural evolution 
of electrode materials. However, analyzing and pro-
cessing each image may take several months. The use 
of AI-aided data analysis can effectively address this 
challenge. AI is powerful in analyzing visual data, 
such as morphological images, satellite imagery, and 
video footage. The application of machine learning 
algorithms facilitates the automatic indexing of elec-
tron diffraction patterns, alongside the classification 
of image or spectral features and the spatial mapping 
of elemental distributions. This approach greatly 
enhances the efficiency and accuracy of data inter-
pretation in electron microscopy, enabling advanced 
structural and compositional analyses.

 (vii)  In-situ TEM experiments are typically conducted 
under applied potentials to study electrochemical 
reactions, but the actual overpotential that drives the 
electrochemical reactions is highly sensitive to the 
contact conditions between the electrode materials 
and the electrolyte. Consequently, it is challenging to

While some advancements have been achieved in the 
development and application of in-situ TEM technology 
in the research field of electrochemical energy storage 
systems, the fundamental understanding of the interfacial 
nanostructures at atomic-scale remains challenging. Wu 
et al. has recently demonstrated the ability to gain ensem-
bled-averaged atomic insight into dynamic and oscillatory 
lattice strains of nanomaterials under fuel cell operation 
condition by in-situ high-energy XRD coupled pair distri-
bution function analysis [10], which points to the potential 
viability of atomic-scale visualization of dynamic lattice 
strains  of  electrode  materials  under  battery  operating 
conditions. The development of advanced combinations 
of imaging, diffraction, and spectrometry techniques in 
in-situ TEM probing of interfacial structures is promis-
ing for enabling the visualization of morphological evo-
lution, chemical composition changes, and phase trans-
formation mechanisms of electrode nanomaterials during 
electrochemical reactions. These advances will drive the 
development of advanced electrochemical energy storage 
technologies. With continuous advancement of electron 
microscopy techniques, the in-situ detection capabilities 
are anticipated to further improve nanoscale and atomic-
scale resolution and reveal new insights into fundamental 
correlation of the dynamic interfacial structures with the 
electrochemical energy storage performances in practical 
applications.

Chen et al. Stem Cell Research & Therapy          (2025) 16:343 
https://doi.org/10.1186/s13287-025-04456-6

Stem Cell Research & Therapy

MiR-145 encapsulated small extracellular 
vesicles inhibit colorectal cancer progression 
by downregulating fascin actin-bundling 
protein 1 expression

Yanxia Chen1,2,6, Meijuan He3, Lei Cui4, Jianguo Zhang1, Hanpeng Huang3* and Zhimin Tao1,2,5*

Abstract
Background  Drug degradation poses a significant challenge in the pursuit of effective gene therapies for cancers.

Methods  Here we have developed a bioactive nanosized composite that utilizes human umbilical cord 
mesenchymal stem cells (hucMSCs) derived small extracellular vesicles (sEVs), to carry tumor suppressor miR-145 
alongside erbium-doped rare earth nanoparticles (ErNPs). This approach not only enhances in vivo delivery but 
also facilitates real-time fluorescence tracking of nucleic acid drugs in the near infrared (NIR) II window. With this 
technique, we are able to realize and visualize the effective inhibition of colorectal cancer (CRC) progression in a 
xenografted murine model.

Results  Our results revealed that the efficient loading of miR-145 into sEVs could be achieved through a dynamic 
combination of sonication and electroporation. The resulting miR-145-encapsulated sEVs (i.e., miRNA@sEVs) exhibited 
a profound ability to hinder tumor growth by effectively downregulating the expression of fascin actin-bundling 
protein 1 (FSCN1), both in vitro and in vivo. Additionally, the circulation half-time of miRNA@sEVs was measured to 
be ~ 4 h and the fluorescence at the tumor sites reached a peak intensity at ~ 8 h after intravenous injection of sEVs 
particles. Finally, the fluorescent signals of miRNA@sEVs were predominantly localized in the mouse liver and spleen, 
with substantial accumulation in tumors.

Conclusions  Our results illuminated the excellent biosafety of miRNA@sEVs and their high accumulation in tumors, 
leading to efficient suppression of tumor progression. This research heralds a promising advancement in gene 
therapy, paving the way for more effective and safer treatment options.

Clinical trial number  Not applicable.

Keywords  Small extracellular vesicles, MicroRNA, Colorectal cancer, Fascin actin-bundling protein 1, Near-infrared II 
fluorescence

Introduction
Colorectal  cancer  (CRC)  is  one  of  the  most  prevalent 
malignancies  worldwide.  While  its  incidence  typically 
rises  with  age,  an  alarming  trend  shows  that  younger 
adults  are  increasingly  at  risk  as  well  [1].  In  the  United 
States,  CRC  tragically  remains  the  second  leading  cause 
of  cancer-related  deaths,  with  153,020  new  cases  diag-
nosed  and  52,550  death  tolls  in  2023  [2].  The  carcino-
genesis of CRC is characterized by a series of progressive 
genetic  changes  through  multiple  pathways,  leading  to 
tumor  formation,  growth,  migration  and  local  or  dis-
tant metastasis, often resulting in diagnoses at advanced 
stages  when  treatment  options  become  very  limited  [3, 
4].  Conventional  treatments  for  CRC  include  surgery, 
chemotherapy,  and  immunotherapy,  playing  essential 
roles in combating this disease. In addition, gene therapy 
is  emerging  as  an  innovative  alternative.  Targeting  the 
frequently  altered  TP53  and  KRAS,  this  cutting-edge 
approach offers hope for many facing CRC [5]. This gene 
intervention  holds  promise  as  a  safe  and  reliable  treat-
ment  strategy  with  reduced  side  effects,  lighting  a  path 
forward  in  the  quest  for  effective  cancer  treatments  in 
clinical settings [6].

MicroRNA (miRNA) as a non-coding small RNA mol-
ecule  that  regulates  gene  expression,  can  interfere  with 
specific oncogenic pathways [7]. Among the most studied 
miRNAs in CRC, miR-145 has been identified as a potent 
suppressor  of  tumorigenesis,  progression,  and  metasta-
sis, which intricately engages with various tumor-specific 
pathways,  including  KRAS  and  P53  signaling  [8].  The 
expression  level  of  miR-145  was  found  significantly  cor-
related with poor prognosis of patients with a diversity of 
malignant tumors, including colorectal, gastric, and ovar-
ian cancers [9, 10]. Simultaneously, the level of miR-145 
in the blood plasma predicted the CRC risk in the general 
population, making it a practical biomarker in early diag-
nosis of CRC [11]. However, the gene targets of miR-145 
can  be  multiple,  as  the  primary  target  in  CRC  progres-
sion remains elusive, which may otherwise enrich thera-
peutic regimen greatly.

As  many  gene  therapy  techniques  require  viral  vec-
tors  (e.g.,  adeno-associated  virus)  to  carry  therapeutic 
nucleic  acids,  it  raises  concerns  of  immunogenicity  and 
cytotoxicity  in  clinical  contexts.  Alternatively,  non-viral 
formulations,  primarily  composed  of  lipids  and  poly-
mers,  have  emerged  as  safe  and  effective  vehicles  for 
delivering  genetic  substances.  Among  those  biocompat-
ible  materials,  extracellular  vesicles  (EVs)  are  a  group  of 
membraned  particles  secreted  by  most  types  of  living 
cells.  They  exhibit  a  range  of  physicochemical  proper-
ties,  such  as  different  sizes  and  densities,  and  biological 
characteristics  related  to  their  diverse  origins  and  the 
resulting surface and interior compositions [12]. EVs can 
be categorized into small EVs (sEVs), measuring less than 

200  nm  in  diameter,  and  medium/large  EVs  that  exceed 
this size [13]. Often referred to as exosomes, sEVs possess 
a typical ‘cup-shaped’ structure and exist in most biologi-
cal  fluids,  including  saliva,  blood,  and  urine  [14].  Their 
surfaces are enriched with transmembrane proteins that 
are capable of relocation within the cellular matrix, facili-
tating  the  exchange  of  materials  and  signaling  between 
cells  [15].  Compared  to  artificially  synthesized  particles 
of  similar  size,  sEVs  own  naturally  derived  membrane 
structures  of  lipid  bilayer,  so  offering  many  unmatched 
features  as  a  delivery  platform,  including  low  immuno-
genicity,  non-toxicity,  exceptional  biocompatibility  and 
stability [16].

In this study, we utilized sEVs derived from hucMSCs 
as  gene  carriers.  Those  sEVs  were  loaded  with  miR-145 
and ErNPs for in vivo miRNA delivery and fluorescence 
tracking. The employment of ErNPs as an NIR II emissive 
fluorescent  probe  provided  an  unprecedented  imaging 
window  for  biological  tissues  [17].  Compared  to  tradi-
tional NIR I dyes, which have an emission wavelength of 
650–900 nm, ErNPs emit a peak wavelength at 1540 nm. 
This  allows  deeper  tissue  penetration  with  minimized 
spontaneous  fluorescence,  so  enabling  precise  localiza-
tion  of  the  transported  particles  in  murine  CRC  mod-
els.  Concurrently,  this  study  validated  the  interaction 
between  the  tumor  suppressor  miR-145  and  its  cancer-
ous  targets  in  CRC,  shedding  light  on  the  anti-cancer 
mechanisms of gene therapies.

Materials and methods
Human CRC tissue samples

Sixty-two  CRC  samples  (24  rectum  and  38  colon  tis-
sues)  were  clinically  diagnosed  and  histopathologically 
confirmed at theAffiliated Hospital of Jiangsu University 
(AHJU)  between  March  2023  and  February  2024,  and 
preserved  at  -80  °C,  together  with  their  corresponding 
paracancerous  tissues.  All  cancerous  tissues  were  his-
tologically  adenocarcinomas  surgically  removed  from 
patients  that  received  no  prior  treatment.  Patient  infor-
mation  was  summarized  in  Table  S1.  Informed  consent 
was  acquired  from  patients  and  ethical  approval  was 
obtained from the research ethics committees of AHJU.

Isolation, characterization and culture of hucMSCs

HucMSCs  were  isolated  as  previously  reported  [18,  19]. 
In  brief,  following  approval  from  the  Research  Ethics 
Committee  of  AHJU  and  with  informed  consent  from 
patients,  fresh  umbilical  cord  tissues  were  obtained. 
HucMSCs  were  isolated  using  the  tissue  block  adhe-
sion  method  and  cultured  in  an  alpha  minimum  essen-
tial  medium  (α-MEM,  Invitrogen,  USA)  with  10%  fetal 
bovine serum (FBS, Gibco, USA). The isolated hucMSCs 
were characterized as reported [20].

HucMSCs  were  transferred  to  a  10  cm  culture  dish 
with  the  number  of  1 × 106  cells.  When  the  cell  density 
reached  50–70%  confluence  in  1–2  days,  the  medium 
was  replaced  with  α-MEM  containing  10%  EV-depleted 
FBS for 8 mL/dish. Then the cells were cultured at 37 °C 
in the incubator with 5% CO2 for 48 h. Next, the super-
natant  from  the  cell  culture  of  hucMSCs  was  collected 
and centrifuged at 1,500 g for 20 min at 4 °C to remove 
cell  debris.  Subsequently,  centrifugation  was  continued 
at  10,000  g  for  30  min  at  4  °C  to  eliminate  cell  organ-
elles.  The  supernatant  was  then  transferred  to  100  kDa 
molecular  weight  cut-off  (MWCO)  ultrafiltration  tubes 
(Millipore, USA) and centrifuged at 1,500 g for 30 min at 
4 °C for multiple times until the concentration of vesicles 
reached  100×  of  original  solutions,  i.e.,  the  volume  of 
the  concentrated  solution  is  1/100  of  the  initial  amount 
when cell supernatant was first collected. Next, the con-
centrated solution was transferred to high-speed centri-
fuge  tubes  and  centrifuged  at  4  °C,  100,000  g  for  1.5  h 
(Beckman, USA). Then the supernatant was carefully dis-
carded, and fresh PBS was added to the tubes to wash the 
precipitate, followed by centrifugation again at 4 °C and 
100,000  g  for  1.5  h.  After  centrifugation,  the  hucMSC-
derived sEVs were obtained as precipitates. To character-
ize,  transmission  electron  microscopy  (TEM)  (Hitachi,

Western blot

Total  proteins  in  cells,  sEVs  and  tissues  were  extracted 
using radioimmunoprecipitation assay (RIPA) lysis buffer 
containing protease inhibitors. Proteins of equal quantity 
in each group were separated by sodium dodecyl sulfate-
polyacrylamide  gel  electrophoresis  (SDS-PAGE),  fol-
lowed by transfer of the gel onto a polyvinylidene fluoride 
(PVDF)  membrane.  After  the  transfer,  the  membrane 
was blocked with 5% skim milk for 2 h. Subsequently, the 
PVDF membrane was incubated overnight with primary 
antibodies  specific  to  each  protein  at  4  °C,  including 
anti-Alix,  anti-TSG101,  anti-CD9,  anti-Calnexin  (1:500, 
Cell  Signaling  Technology,  USA),  anti-FSCN1  (1:1000, 
Abcam,  USA),  and  anti-GAPDH  (1:3000,  Abcam,  USA). 
Later, the PVDF membrane was incubated with a horse-
radish  peroxidase  (HRP)-labeled  secondary  antibody 
(1:2000) (Vazyme, China). After washing, the membrane 
was detected by chemiluminescence imaging instrument 
(GE, USA).

qRT-PCR analysis

Trizol  lysis  buffer  was  employed  to  extract  mRNA  from 
cells  and  tissues.  The  exosomal  RNA  purification  kit 
(Qiagen,  Germany)  was  utilized  to  isolate  miRNA  from 
sEVs,  and  the  reverse  transcription  kit  (Vazyme,  China) 
was used for reverse transcription of miRNA and mRNA. 
Subsequently, QuantStudio 3 was employed for qRT-PCR 
analysis.  The  primer  sequences  used  in  the  experiment 
were shown in Table 1.

Transfection of miRNA and plasmids

All  the  miRNA  mimics,  miRNA  inhibitors  and  negtive 
control (NC) used in the experiment were obtained from 
Genepharma  Co.,  Ltd.,  China.  The  synthetic  miRNA 
comprised of 21-base pair nucleotides. NC has a scram-
bled  sequence  of  nucleotides  that  undergoe  random 
rearrangement (i.e., in a shuffling order) while maintain-
ing  the  same  length  and  GC  content  as  the  miR-145. 
Cells  were  seeded  in  6-well  plates  (2 × 105  cells/well). 
When the cell density reached 60–70%, cells were trans-
fected  with  miRNA  and  plasmid  using  Lipofectamine 
2000  (Invitrogen,  USA)  in  serum-free  medium  accord-
ing  to  the  manufacturer’s  instructions.  Firstly,  the  origi-
nal  culture  medium  was  gently  discarded  and  the  cells 
were  washed  twice  with  fresh  PBS. Then  0.5  mL  of  cul-
ture  medium  without  FBS  was  added,  and  the  cell  plate 
was cultured in the cell incubator for 1–2 h. During the 
incubation,  the  transfection  reagent  was  prepared,  as  5

Dual-luciferase reporter gene analysis

Human  CRC  cell  lines  HCT116  and  SW480  were  pur-
chased  from  Institute  of  Biochemistry  and  Cell  Biol-
ogy  at  the  Chinese  Academy  of  Sciences  (Shanghai, 
China)  and  cultured  in  Dulbecco’s  Modified  Eagle’s 
Medium  (DMEM)  containing  10%  FBS  at  37°C  with  5% 
CO2.  The  dual-luciferase  reporter  plasmids  were  con-
structed  by  inserting  the  wild-type  (WT)  or  mutant 
(MUT)  3’-untranslated  region  (3’UTR)  of  FSCN1  into 
the GP-miRGLO vector. The WT plasmid contained the 
putative  miR-145  binding  sites,  while  the  MUT  plas-
mid  carried  site-directed  mutations  in  the  seed  regions. 
The  experiments  were  conducted  in  four  groups,  each 
with  three  replicates  (n = 3).  The  groups  were  FSCN1-
WT  plasmid + miR-145  mimics  negative  control  (NC), 
FSCN1-WT  plasmid + miR-145  mimics,  FSCN1-MUT 
plasmid + miR-145  mimics  NC,  and  FSCN1-MUT  plas-
mid + miR-145  mimics.  Plasmids  were  transfected  into 
the  corresponding  cells.  Following  transfection,  100  µL 
of  1  ×  passive  lysis  buffer  (PLB)  was  added  to  the  cells. 
After thorough lysis, the cell suspension was transferred 
to Eppendorf (EP) tubes and placed under a biochemical 
luminescence detector (Turner Biosystems, USA), where 
the  first  reading  was  recorded.  To  each  tube,  50  µL  of 
reaction  termination  solution  was  added,  gently  mixed, 
and then retested, recording the fluorescence signal ratio, 
followed by statistical analysis.

Cell counting kit-8 (CCK-8) for viability tests

Cells  from  each  treatment  group  were  seeded  into 
96-well  plates,  with  2 × 103  cells  per  well.  Each  group 
had  6  replicates,  and  the  plates  were  then  incubated  in 
a  cell  incubator  for  24–96  h.  Every  24  h,  one  plate  was 
taken out. The original culture medium was carefully dis-
carded, and the plate was washed with fresh PBS. Subse-
quently, 100 µL of fresh culture medium containing 10% 
CCK-8 detection reagent was added to each well, and the 
plate was incubated in the dark for 2 h in the incubator. 

The absorbance of each well was then measured using a 
microplate reader at the wavelength of 450 nm.

Cell migration assay

Cells  were  resuspended  in  serum-free  medium,  adjust-
ing  the  cell  concentration  to  2.0 × 105  cells/mL.  Then, 
200  µL  of  cell  suspension  was  added  to  the  upper  layer 
of the chamber (sterile transwell with 8.0 μm pore poly-
carbonate  membrane  insert,  purchased  from  Corning, 
USA),  while  600  µL  of  cell  culture  medium  containing 
10% FBS was added to the lower layer. The culture plate 
was  then  placed  in  the  incubator  for  16  h.  After  PBS 
washing,  the  chamber  was  fixed  with  4%  paraformalde-
hyde  for  20  min,  followed  by  staining  with  0.5%  crystal 
violet for 10–15 min. Unmigrated cells in the upper layer 
were carefully removed with cotton swabs, and the num-
ber of migrated cells was observed and counted under a 
microscope.

Cell invasion assay

The  matrix  gel  was  pre-melted  on  ice  and  diluted  with 
serum-free medium at a ratio of 1:4. Then, 50 µL per well 
was  added  to  the  upper  layer  of  the  chamber  at  37  °C 
for 30 min to solidify the gel for later use. The cells were 
resuspended  in  serum-free  culture  medium,  where  the 
cell  concentration  was  adjusted  to  2.0 × 105  cells/mL. 
Then, 200 µL of cell suspension was added to the upper 
layer of the chamber, while 600 µL of cell culture medium 
containing  10%  FBS  was  added  to  the  lower  layer.  The 
culture  plate  was  then  placed  in  the  cell  incubator  for 
24  h.  After  PBS  wash,  the  chamber  was  fixed  with  4% 
paraformaldehyde  for  20  min,  followed  by  staining  with 
0.5%  crystal  violet  for  10–15  min.  Non-invasion  cells 
in  the  upper  layer  were  carefully  removed  with  cotton 
swabs,  and  the  number  of  invading  cells  was  observed 
and counted under a microscope.

Cell colony formation assay

Cells  were  seeded  into  3.5  cm  cell  culture  dishes  with 
1 × 103  cells  per  dish  and  then  cultured  in  a  cell  incu-
bator.  The  growth  status  and  density  of  the  cells  were 
monitored  under  a  microscope  on  a  daily  basis.  When 
significant  cell  colony  formation  was  observed,  cell  cul-
ture was immediately halted. After washing with PBS, 4% 
paraformaldehyde  was  used  for  fixation  for  20  min,  fol-
lowed by 0.5% crystal violet staining for 10–15 min. The 
staining  solution  was  then  discarded,  and  the  unbound 
staining  solution  was  rinsed  away  using  PBS.  The  cells 
were  left  to  air  dry  at  room  temperature.  The  size  and 
number of cell colonies were recorded. A cell count > 50 
was considered a positive colony, and the number of cell 
colonies in each group was calculated.

Statistical analysis

All  data  presented  in  this  article  were  presented  as 
mean ± standard  deviation  (SD).  Statistical  comparisons 
between  two  groups  were  analyzed  by  Student’s  t-test, 
while multiple group comparisons were analyzed by two-
way  ANOVA  using  GraphPad  Prism  8.3.0  (GraphPad, 
San  Diego,  CA,  USA).  *p < 0.05,  **p < 0.01,  ***p < 0.001, 
****p < 0.0001.

Preparation and characterization of miRNA-encapsulated 
sEVs (miRNA@sEVs)

Freshly  extracted  sEVs  and  miRNA  mimics  were  thor-
oughly  mixed  in  a  centrifuge  tube,  resulting  in  a  final 
concentration  of  1 × 1010/mL  sEVs  and  100  nM  miRNA 
mimics. The centrifuge tube was placed in the ice water, 
and  the  tip  sonication  parameters  were  set  as  500  V, 
2 kHz, 20% amplitude, 6 cycles, with 5 s pulse/3 s pause 
(QSonicator  500,  SONICS,  USA).  This  process  was 
repeated twice with a 2-min interval on ice to cool down. 
Next,  the  solution  was  transferred  to  an  electrode  cup, 
and the electroporation conditions were set to 110 V and 
940  µF,  using  the  CUY21EDIT  II  electroporator  (BEX, 
Japan).  After  electroporation,  the  mixture  was  centri-
fuged  at  100,000  g  for  2  h  to  remove  unbound  miRNA, 
resulting in the precipitation of miRNA@sEVs.

Fluorescent labeling of miRNA@sEVs

6.4  mg/mL  sEVs  and  1  mg/mL  ErNPs  were  incubated 
in  the  dark  at  37  °C  for  30  min.  ErNPs  were  purchased 
from  Nirmidas  Biotech,  USA,  and  well  characterized 
as  reported  [21].  Basically,  they  were  synthesized  as 
α-phase  Er-doped  NaYF4  nanocrystal  and  functional-
ized  with  PEG-NH2  group  to  give  off  enhanced  bright 
downconversion fluorescence upon excitation at 980 nm 
(size = ~ 14 nm; λex/λem=980 nm/1540 nm). Subsequently, 
the  mixture  was  placed  in  an  ultrasonic  water  bath  and 
sonicated  for  3  min.  Then,  the  liquid  was  transferred  to 
100  kDa  MWCO  ultrafiltration  tubes  and  centrifuged 
at  1,500  g  for  30  min  at  4  °C  to  remove  unbound  dyes. 
We also investigated the possible dye leakage in the fresh 
cell-free  media  over  time  after  sEVs  were  stained  by 
ErNPs. Specifically, the fluorescence of the newly stained 
miRNA@sEVs  was  recorded  as  the  initial  fluorescence 
intensity and kept incubated at 37 °C up to 24 h. The sam-
ples  were  taken  at  different  time  points  and  transferred 
to  the  ultrafiltration  tube  and  centrifuged  at  1500  ×  g 
for  30  min  to  separate  the  dye  stained  sEVs  and  super-
natant. The fluorescence of supernatant was measured by 
the DeepVision NIR-II in vivo imaging system (Nirmidas 
Biotech, USA). The fluorescence intensity of the obtained 
supernatant  at  each  time  point  was  normalized  to  the 
initial  fluorescence  intensity,  obtaining  the  cumulative 
release of dyes from stained sEVs as a function of time.

Validation of miR-145 expression and its gene targets

A total of 62 human CRC tissue samples were previously 
extracted  and  preserved,  and  the  expression  of  miR-145 
in each pair of cancerous and paracancerous tissues was 
retrospectively  examined  using  qRT-PCR.  The  results 
indicated  that  the  miR-145  expression  was  significantly 
lowered  in  CRC  tissues  compared  to  that  in  adjacent 
(paracancerous)  tissues  (Fig.  1A).  Consequently,  miR-
145  overexpression  and  knockdown  were  performed 
in  colorectal  carcinoma  derived  cell  lines  HCT116  and 
SW480,  respectively.  As  a  result,  in  comparison  to  the 

control,  overexpression  of  miR-145  significantly  inhib-
ited  cell  proliferation,  colony  formation  and  migration/
invasion  capabilities.  Reversely,  knockdown  of  miR-145 
promoted those cellular activities (Supplementary File 1: 
Figures S1 and S2). Those results integrated that miR-145 
may play a suppressive role in the CRC progression.

through  databases  including  miRDB,  TargetScan,  miR-
TarBase and miRWalk. The top 10 targets were identified 
with  the  highest  prediction  probabilities  by  intersecting 
these datasets (Fig. 1B), and these predictions were vali-
dated in HCT116 and SW480 cells (Fig. 1C). The results

Preparation and characterization of miRNA@sEVs

To  obtain  efficient  and  stable  loading  of  miRNA  into 
sEVs,  various  methods  were  implemented  to  assess  and 
improve  the  loading  efficiency.  These  methods  included 
direct  incubation,  electroporation,  sonication,  electro-
poration followed by sonication, and sonication followed 
by  electroporation,  respectively.  The  qRT-PCR  was  uti-
lized  to  validate  the  loading  efficiency  when  miRNA 
expression  in  each  group  was  measured  and  compared. 
Compared  to  the  direct  incubation,  the  electropora-
tion  resulted  in  a  2.6-fold  increase  of  miR-145  loading, 
the  sonication  had  a  2.2-fold  increase,  the  electropora-
tion plus sonication achieved a 5.6-fold increase, and the 
sonication  followed  by  electroporation  attained  a  5.9-
fold increase. Collectively, there was yet statistical differ-
ence  of  miR-145  loading  efficiency  in  terms  of  different 
sequential  orders  when  combining  sonication  and  elec-
troporation (Fig. 3A).

We  then  characterized  the  physicochemical  and  bio-
logical  properties  of  miRNA@sEVs.  Before  and  after 
miR-145  loading  using  sonication  in  combination  with 

electroporation, sEVs consistently expressed surface pro-
tein markers such as CD9, TSG101 and Alix, but no intra-
cellular  Calnexin  (Fig.  3B).  TEM  images  revealed  that 
miRNA@sEVs maintained a cup-shaped vesicle structure 
and remained intact during modification (Fig. 3C). NTA 
results  indicated  that  the  loading  method  had  minimal 
impact on the size and zeta potential of sEVs, measuring 
a diameter of (157.6 ± 1.5) nm (Fig. 3D) and zeta potential 
of (-17.3 ± 0.2) mV.

To  further  validate  the  successful  loading  of  miR-145 
into  sEVs,  the  interaction  between  miRNA@sEVs  and 
its  intracellular  target  FSCN1  was  then  examined.  First, 
miRNA@sEVs (6.4 mg/mL sEVs + 0.5 µM miR-145) were 
added  to  HCT116  and  SW480  cells  for  48  h,  and  RNAs 
and proteins were then extracted from the cells to detect 
changes of FSCN1 at both gene and protein levels. Con-
currently,  the  untreated  group,  the  group  treated  with 
sEVs  (6.4  mg/mL)  alone,  the  group  directly  added  with 
miR-145 mimics (0.5 µM), and the group transfected with 
miR-145 mimics (0.5 µM) using Lipofectamine 2000, des-
ignated as miR-145 (lipo), were set up in the same experi-
ments  for  comparison.  Our  findings  revealed  that  the 
gene  and  protein  expression  of  FSCN1  in  the  miRNA@
sEVs group and the group transfected with miR-145 were 
significantly lowered compared to those in the untreated 
group  (Fig.  3E  and  F),  demonstrating  a  notable  tumor-
suppressing effect that inhibited cell proliferation, colony

In vivo profiles of miRNA@sEVs

We  investigated  in  vivo  profiles  of  miRNA@sEVs  in 
murine cancer models. NIR-II fluorescent probes ErNPs 
were  adopted  to  stain  sEVs  or  miRNA@sEVs,  and  their 
fluorescent  properties  were  measured  to  determine  the 
dye  concentration  and  physical  stability  (Supplementary 
File  1:  Figure  S6A).  Firstly,  the  fluorescent  linear  range 
of  ErNPs  was  examined.  The  original  solution  of  ErNPs 
was diluted at ratios of 1:1, 1:2, 1:5, 1:10, 1:20, 1:50, 1:100, 
1:200,  and  1:500  in  PBS.  The  NIR-II  small  animal  live 
imaging instrument was applied to measure the fluores-
cence intensity versus each concentration at λex/λem=980 
nm/1540  nm.  The  results  showed  that  the  fluorescence 
intensity of ErNPs increased linearly when the concentra-
tion  fell  in  the  range  of  0–1  mg/mL.  Thus,  1  mg/mL  of 
ErNPs was determined for the working concentration in 
the following experiments.

Subsequently,  1  mg/mL  ErNPs  were  incubated  with 
sEVs  and  miRNA@sEVs,  respectively,  and  the  labeled 
particles were transferred to ultracentrifugation tubes at 
different time points (i.e., 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, and 24 h after 
labeling), followed by thorough PBS washing and fluores-
cence determination of ErNPs-labeled sEVs or miRNA@
sEVs. The fluorescence intensity of the obtained superna-
tant at each time point was normalized to the initial fluo-
rescence  intensity  of  ErNPs-stained  sEVs  or  miRNA@
sEVs,  and  the  cumulative  release  of  ErNPs  from  stained 
particles  was  obtained  over  time.  The  results  demon-
strated  that  the  initial  release  of  ErNPs  from  stained 
sEVs or miRNA@sEVs showed a linearly increasing trend 
over time but finally reached a plateau after 15 h release 
(Supplementary File 1: Figure S6B). Thereby, for later ani-
mal  experiments,  1  mg/mL  ErNPs  were  first  incubated 
with  sEVs  and  miRNA@sEVs,  respectively,  for  > 15  h  to 
ensure the staining stability (i.e., no further dye leakage). 
Afterwards, ErNPs-sEVs and ErNPs-miRNA@sEVs were 
prepared  and  injected  into  mice  bearing  HCT116  sub-
cutaneous tumors through the tail vein. At time of injec-
tion, the dimension of tumors reached 0.8–0.9 cm in all 
groups.

The in vivo images of mice at various time points were 
illustrated  in  Fig.  4A.  Concurrently,  venous  blood  was 
collected  from  mice  to  assess  the  pharmacokinetics  of 
sEVs  and  miRNA@sEVs  (Fig.  4B),  while  the  accumula-
tion  of  sEVs  and  miRNA@sEVs  at  the  tumor  sites  was 
monitored over time (Fig. 4C). Our findings revealed that 
ErNPs-sEVs  and  ErNPs-miRNA@sEVs  exhibited  com-
parable  circulation  time  (i.e.,  4.0 ± 0.4  h  and  4.1 ± 0.2  h). 

Following  injections,  fluorescent  accumulation  at  the 
tumor  sites  increased,  reaching  a  peak  at  ~ 8  h  when 
the  fluorescence  intensity  attained ~ 1.5  times  the  ini-
tial value. After mice were sacrificed, major organs were 
examined  ex  vivo  to  investigate  the  biodistribution  of 
injected  particles.  These  results  indicated  that  the  fluo-
rescent signals of ErNPs-sEVs and ErNPs-miRNA@sEVs 
were predominantly localized in the liver and spleen. By 
normalizing  the  fluorescence  intensity  of  each  tissue  to 
that of the liver as the largest uptake upon tail vein injec-
tion, it was observed that the tumors in the ErNPs-sEVs 
group  and  ErNPs-miRNA@sEVs  group  accounted  for 
(15.4 ± 3.1)%  and  (20.7 ± 3.0)%  of  liver  uptake,  respec-
tively,  although  no  statistical  difference  was  noticed 
between  the  two  groups  (p > 0.05)  (Fig.  4D).  All  the 
results  pointed  out  that  the  incorporation  of  miR-145 
into sEVs via electroporation and sonication in our study 
kept  the  membraned  structure  intact,  minimizing  the 
impact  on  its  in  vivo  profiles,  including  pharmacokinet-
ics, tumor accumulation and biodistribution.

Discussion
In this study we first verified that miR-145 was an effec-
tive  tumor  suppressor  in  clinical  samples  from  patients 
with  CRCs,  and  it  exerted  its  tumor-inhibitory  effect  by 
downregulating its primary target FSCN1. Then, we uti-
lized sEVs derived from hucMSCs as delivering carriers to 
encapsulate miR-145 and enhanced the loading efficiency 
of miR-145 in sEVs by employing a strategic combination 

of sonication and electroporation techniques. The result-
ing  miRNA@sEVs  demonstrated  exceptional  biocom-
patibility,  which  contributed  to  prolonged  circulation 
in  the  bloodstream  and  increased  accumulation  within 
tumors.  Consequently,  these  nanoscaled  miRNA@sEVs 
showed  substantial  suppression  of  tumor  progression 
both  in  vitro  and  in  vivo  by  effectively  downregulating 
the expression of FSCN1 protein.

Recent research suggests that miR-145 is implicated in 
various  malignant  tumors  by  regulating  oncogenes  and 
signal  transduction  related  to  cell  proliferation,  angio-
genesis,  tumor  progression,  metastasis,  and  therapeutic 
resistance  [22].  For  instance,  miR-145  has  been  identi-
fied as a diagnostic marker for chondrosarcoma, where it 
may inhibit the tumor progression by downregulating the 
expression of FSCN1 [23]. Similarly, miR-145 was found 
to be downregulated in hepatocellular carcinoma, reduc-
ing cancer cell proliferation by targeting insulin receptor 
substrate  1  [24].  Moreover,  miR-145  can  suppress  non-
small cell lung cancer by downregulating its dual targets, 
GOLM1 and RTKN [25].

One  miRNA  may  target  multiple  gene  transcripts 
within one specific cancer type, and the primary targets 
can vary in different stages of the same cancer or across 
different  types  of  cancers  [26].  In  human  CRCs,  miR-
145 may modulate a pool of gene targets at each step of

tumor  development  [27].  For  example,  miR-145-5p,  one 
form of mature miR-145, suppresses cell growth, metas-
tasis,  and  epithelial-mesenchymal  transition  in  CRC  by 
targeting  cell  cycle-associated  protein-3  (CDCA3)  [28]. 
Also,  miR-145  inhibits  the  invasion  and  migration  of 
CRC cells by targeting the twist family bHLH transcrip-
tion factor 1 (TWIST1) [29]. However, conflicting results 
have  been  reported.  MiR-145  may  bind  directly  to  and 
suppress  AF9,  decreasing  expression  of  gluconeogenic 
genes  and  promoting  glycolysis,  potentially  leading  to 
carcinogenesis  and  CRC  development  [30].  Moreover, 
while  miR-145-5p  was  found  tumor  suppressive  in  the 
early  stages  of  CRC,  it  promoted  metastasis  in  the  late 
stages by regulating AKT signaling [31]. Further research 
is needed to clarify whether and how miR-145 can bind 
its various gene targets and regulate tumor development 
during different stages of CRC.

Here we delineated that miR-145 deliverd by hucMSC-
derived  sEVs  primarily  targeted  FSCN1  and  effectively 
lowered  its  expression  in  CRCs,  thereby  inhibiting  cell 
proliferation,  colony  formation,  migration  and  invasion, 
which  eventually  led  to  substantial  tumor  suppression. 
Notably,  the  interaction  between  miR-145  and  FSCN1 
has  been  reported  in  several  malignant  tumors,  where 
FSCN1 expression was negatively correlated to miR-145 
[32, 33]. Specifically downregulated by certain long non-
coding RNA inhibition [34] or by promoter hypermethyl-
ation [35], the loss of miR-145 expression, which directly 
interacts  with  3’-untranslated  region  of  FSCN1  messen-
ger  RNA,  upregulates  FSCN1  expression  at  the  mRNA 
and posttranscriptional levels, so promoting tumor pro-
gression  [36,  37].  Our  results  here  validated  the  role  of 
miR-145/FSCN1  axis  in  CRC  progression,  which  stood 
well in line with those reports.

Highly  conserved  across  species,  human  FSCN1  pro-
tein  is  widely  expressed  in  various  organs,  which  cross-
links  actin  microfilaments  into  well-structured  bundles, 
providing rigidity and stability for cytoskeleton remodel-
ing and cell adhesion/migration [38]. Aberrantly elevated 
levels  of  FSCN1  have  been  found  in  a  variety  of  cancer 
types,  closely  associated  with  promoted  cell  prefiltra-
tion,  migration  and  invasion,  and  neovascularization, 
thus being recognized as a poor prognostic indicator and 
a  potential  druggable  target  [39–41].  In  prostate  cancer 
high expression of FSCN1 induces cytoskeleton reorgani-
zation, aggregating actin bundles into filamentous pseu-
dopodia,  therefore  promoting  migration,  invasion  and 
lymph  node  metastasis  [42].  Alternatively,  FSCN1  con-
tributes  to  lung  adenocarcinoma  development  through 
activation  of  PI3K/AKT  signaling  pathway,  stimulat-
ing  cell  proliferation  and  inhibiting  cell  apoptosis  [43]. 
In  hepatoblastoma,  FSCN1  activates  the  Wnt/β-catenin 
pathway  by  stabilizing  the  entry  of  β-catenin  into  the 
nucleus  and  driving  the  transcription  of  oncogenes 
[44].  Nevertheless,  with  regards  to  the  ensuing  FSCN1-
mediated  tumor  progression  in  CRC,  it  requires  further 
investigation to explore the exact mechanism or pathway 
following miR-145 regulation.

Derived  from  their  parental  cells,  sEVs  possess  high 
biocompatibility  and  low  immunogenicity  due  to  their 
endogenous  origin.  Their  surface  proteins  help  evade 
immune  detection,  reducing  clearance  by  the  mononu-
clear  phagocyte  system.  HucMSC-derived  sEVs  inherit 
the  homing  characteristics  of  parental  cells  and  can 
actively recognize the tumor microenvironment through 
adhesion  molecules  such  as  integrins  [45].  In  contrast, 
artificial  particles  at  similar  nano  to  micro  scale,  lipo-
somes  for  example,  albeit  surface  modification  such  as 
tunable PEGylation may reduce immune recognition, can 
still  provoke  an  array  of  immune  responses  and  induce 
local  or  systemic  toxicity  [46].  At  the  same  time,  the 
targeting  capacity  of  liposomes  relies  on  the  enhanced 
permeability  and  retention  (EPR)  effect,  whereas  tumor 
vascular  heterogeneity  may  greatly  limit  their  efficien-
cies [47]. Furthermore, cell-derived sEVs and synthesized 
liposomes can both efficiently carry xenobiotic drugs for 
delivery,  while  sEVs  own  unique  therapeutic  pleiotropy 
as it can  inherit biologically active molecules  from their 
parental cells. For this reason, with similar efforts to load 
exogenous  cargos  of  pharmaceutical  interest  into  both 
drug  carriers,  endogenous  substances  in  sEVs  can  be 
exploited  to  take  synergistic  effects  for  enhanced  treat-
ment [48].

Efficiently  loading  therapeutic  substances  (such  as 
chemical  drugs  and  exogenous  nucleic  acids)  into  sEVs 
and precisely delivering them to the specific target in the 
body may govern the effectiveness of cancer therapy. To 
begin, gene cargos can be encapsulated into sEVs through 

direct  or  indirect  method.  The  direct  method  employs 
physical or/and chemical techniques to import the cargo 
directly  into  sEVs,  including  incubation,  electropora-
tion,  sonication,  extrusion  and  freeze-thaw  cycles.  In 
contrast,  the  indirect  loading  first  integrates  the  gene 
into  the  donor  cells  through  gene  transfection  and  co-
incubation,  followed  by  the  secretion  and  isolation  of 
sEVs  [49].  In  this  study  we  selected  sEVs  derived  from 
hucMSCs  as  the  delivery  platform  to  encapsulate  miR-
145 via a combination of sonication and electroporation. 
Compared  to  direct  incubation  with  very  low  efficiency, 
this combinational method achieved a 5.9-fold improve-
ment of miRNA loading, much higher than electropora-
tion  or  sonication  alone.  This  loading  capacity  was  also 
superior to our previous result when miR-193 was loaded 
into hucMSC-derived sEVs via sonication with optimized 
energy input [18]. Simultaneously, encapsulation of miR-
NAs by sEVs protected them from immature degradation 
before reaching the target, exerting tumor suppression to 
the best of their capacities [18]. Put together, sEVs prove 
themselves as exceptional gene drug delivery vehicles in 
cancer therapy.

To  date,  NIR-II  fluorescence  bioimaging  has  found 
widespread  applications  in  the  biomedical  field,  with 
single-walled  carbon  nanotubes,  quantum  dots,  gold 
nanoparticles,  and  rare  earth  nanoparticles  commonly 
implemented as contrast agents. Compared to NIR-I, the 
NIR-II  fluorescence  imaging  window  offers  higher  spa-
tial resolution and allows deeper tissue penetration [50]. 
To monitor and track the circulation of miRNA@sEVs in 
vivo in a real-time manner, we utilized ErNPs as a tracer 
probe, examining the pharmacokinetics and tumor accu-
mulation  of  miRNA@sEVs.  Our  results  indicated  that 
miR-145 encapsulation had no noticeable impact on the 
pharmacokinetics  of  husMSC-derived  sEVs,  displaying 
a  circulation  half-life  of  approximately  4  h,  consistent 
with  our  previous  findings  [47].  Similarly,  the  presence 
or  absence  of  miR-145  did  not  significantly  alter  the 
accumulation  of  sEVs  at  tumor  sites,  showing  an  initial 
increase  followed  by  a  gradual  decline  until  clearance 
from the body, aligning with our earlier reports [18, 47]. 
Importantly, miR-145 loaded and delivered by sEVs suc-
cessfully  inhibited  tumor  progression  by  downregulat-
ing FSCN1 expression in the xenografted murine model 
of  human  CRC.  Those  results  further  demonstrated  the 
excellent biocompatibility, low immunogenicity, high sta-
bility,  and  minimized  toxicity  of  sEVs  as  a  delivery  plat-
form  of  bioactive  materials,  such  as  therapeutic  nucleic 
acids.

Conclusion
In  this  study,  we  fabricated  miRNA-encapsulated  sEVs 
using  a  combination  of  sonication  and  electroporation. 
We  employed  ErNPs  as  an  NIR-II  fluorescence  tracer 

Chen et al. Stem Cell Research & Therapy          (2025) 16:343  for  miRNA@sEVs,  allowing  us  to  elucidate  their  bio-
logical  profiles  in  vivo,  including  the  circulation  time, 
biodistribution,  and  tumor  accumulation.  Our  results 
demonstrated  that  miRNA@sEVs,  after  effectively  load-
ing  of  miR-145  into  sEVs,  greatly  inhibited  the  progres-
sion of CRC by downregulating the expression of FSCN1 
as  its  primary  target.  This  study  offers  a  new  strategy 
that  utilizes  sEVs  as  a  biosafe  and  reliable  delivery  plat-
form, enabling non-invasive real-time monitoring of gene 
therapy during tumor treatment under an NIR-II fluores-
cence regimen.

title: Conductive biological materials for in vitro models: properties and sustainability implications.

sections.heading: fulltext
sections.text:
Gelatin is a natural biopolymer derived from collagen, pri-
marily extracted from animal connective tissues such as 
skin, bones, and tendons. It is produced through the partial 
hydrolysis of collagen, resulting in long chains of amino 
acids, including a high glycine concentration, proline, and 
hydroxyproline. Gelatin is renowned for its biocompatibility, 
biodegradability, and non-toxic nature, making it highly suit-
able for various medical and pharmaceutical applications. 
One of its distinctive properties is its ability to form a gel 
when cooled and melt when heated, which proves invaluable 
in controlled drug delivery and tissue engineering. Also, 
gelatin’s high water absorption capacity makes it ideal for 
applications requiring hydration and moisture retention, such 
as wound healing and hydrating formulations [53].

sections.heading: fulltext
sections.text:
The conductive polymers can be added to the biomaterial 
scaffold in a similar fashion, with PEDOT:PSS, polyaniline 
and polypyrrole often used for this purpose, due to their 
unique combination of conductivity, biocompatibility, and 
mechanical flexibility. These polymers can be integrated 
into hydrogels, electrospun scaffolds, or films to enhance 
the bioelectrical properties of in vitro models. For example, 
PEDOT:PSS has been used in cardiac patches and neuronal 
scaffolds to provide electrical cues that mimic in vivo con-
ditions [70]. Though as often as these additives have been 
utilized in tissue engineering endeavors, their use is now 
beginning to be questioned due to possible implications of 
the biodegradability of these materials. As such, wanting to 
still utilize the beneficial conductive capabilities of these 
materials, researchers have now begun to tailor these materi-
als to the desired traits. One clear example of this is the elim-
ination of the use of the PSS component in the PEDOT:PSS 
polymer. In its readily available form, PEDOT:PSS relies on 
the PSS component to enable its solubility in water, though 
this component is responsible for the poor biofunctionality 
and biodegradability of the material [39, 71]. Novel efforts 
have been made to eliminate this reliance on the PSS com-
ponent, by synthetizing PEDOT nanoparticles (NPs). These 
NPs are synthetized via a mini-emulsion polymerization 
reaction by means of a surfactant with a negatively charged 
polyelectrolyte, with poly(diallyldimethylammonium chlo-
ride) solution (PDADMAC) and hyaluronic acid (HA) as 
two named examples [39, 72, 73].

•  Bio-based  graphene  production:  Graphene,  a  widely 
used highly conductive material, is traditionally pro-
duced using chemical vapor deposition (CVD) or Hum-
mers’ method, both of which involve hazardous reagents. 
Newer techniques use plant-derived precursors and enzy-
matic methods to synthesize biocompatible and environ-
mentally friendly graphene [106, 107].

hydroxyproline. Gelatin is renowned for its biocompatibility, 
biodegradability, and non-toxic nature, making it highly suit-

One of its distinctive properties is its ability to form a gel 
when cooled and melt when heated, which proves invaluable 
in controlled drug delivery and tissue engineering. Also, 
gelatin’s high water absorption capacity makes it ideal for 
applications requiring hydration and moisture retention, such 
as wound healing and hydrating formulations [53].

The conductive polymers can be added to the biomaterial 
scaffold in a similar fashion, with PEDOT:PSS, polyaniline 
and polypyrrole often used for this purpose, due to their 
unique combination of conductivity, biocompatibility, and 
mechanical flexibility. These polymers can be integrated 
into hydrogels, electrospun scaffolds, or films to enhance 
the bioelectrical properties of in vitro models. For example, 
PEDOT:PSS has been used in cardiac patches and neuronal 
scaffolds to provide electrical cues that mimic in vivo con-
ditions [70]. Though as often as these additives have been 
utilized in tissue engineering endeavors, their use is now 
beginning to be questioned due to possible implications of 
the biodegradability of these materials. As such, wanting to 
still utilize the beneficial conductive capabilities of these 
materials, researchers have now begun to tailor these materi-
als to the desired traits. One clear example of this is the elim-
ination of the use of the PSS component in the PEDOT:PSS 
polymer. In its readily available form, PEDOT:PSS relies on 
the PSS component to enable its solubility in water, though 
this component is responsible for the poor biofunctionality 
and biodegradability of the material [39, 71]. Novel efforts 
have been made to eliminate this reliance on the PSS com-
ponent, by synthetizing PEDOT nanoparticles (NPs). These 
NPs are synthetized via a mini-emulsion polymerization 
reaction by means of a surfactant with a negatively charged 
polyelectrolyte, with poly(diallyldimethylammonium chlo-
ride) solution (PDADMAC) and hyaluronic acid (HA) as 
two named examples [39, 72, 73].

meta.title: Conductive biological materials for in vitro models: properties and sustainability implications.

raw:
In vitro models (2025) 4:89–110 
https://doi.org/10.1007/s44164-025-00088-5

OPINION PAPERS

Conductive biological materials for in vitro models: properties 
and sustainability implications

Aleksandra Serafin1,2 · César R. Casanova3,4 · Arvind K. Singh Chandel1 · Rui L. Reis3,4 · Joaquim Miguel Oliveira3,4 · 
Maurice N. Collins1,2,5 

Received: 17 December 2024 / Revised: 13 March 2025 / Accepted: 1 April 2025 / Published online: 24 April 2025 
© The Author(s) 2025

Abstract
The integration of conductive biological materials into in vitro models represents a transformative approach to advancing 
biomedical research while addressing critical sustainability challenges. Traditional materials used in tissue engineering and 
disease modeling are often environmentally detrimental, derived from non-renewable resources, and limited in their ability 
to replicate the dynamic properties of native tissues. Conductive biological materials bridge this gap by offering a unique 
combination of biodegradability, sustainability, and functional properties, such as bioelectricity and biocompatibility, that 
are essential for mimicking physiological environments. Herein, the development and current applications of biodegradable 
conductive materials, including advanced polymers such as polyaniline and polypyrrole, carbon-based nanocomposites, and 
renewable biopolymers derived from lignin and cellulose, are overviewed. These materials not only reduce the ecological 
footprint of biomedical research but also enable the precise simulation of electrical signaling in tissues, such as cardiac, 
neural, and muscular systems, thereby enhancing the physiological relevance of in vitro models. Their integration into three-
dimensional (3D) tissue constructs, organ-on-chip platforms, and bioprinting technologies facilitates the development of 
patient-specific models, paving the way for personalized therapeutic and diagnostic applications. In addition to advancing 
biomedical precision, these materials align with global efforts to implement circular economy principles in research, promot-
ing resource efficiency and waste reduction. By combining environmental responsibility with state-of-the-art functionality, 
conductive biological materials are redefining the future of in vitro 3D models and research, accelerating innovation in regen-
erative medicine, drug development, and disease modeling while fostering a sustainable framework for scientific discovery.

Keywords  Biodegradable materials · Conductive materials · In vitro models · Sustainability

Introduction

In recent years, sustainability has become a critical focus 
in biomedical research, with growing concerns over the 
environmental impact of traditional practices and materials 

[1]. The biomedical industry generates an estimated 5.9 
million tons of waste annually, with a substantial portion 
being non-biodegradable or hazardous to the environment 
[2].  Materials  such  as  petroleum-based  polymers  like 
polystyrene and polyethylene are one such example, as

they pose significant environmental concerns due to their 
non-biodegradability and high carbon footprint [3]. These 
polymers dominate biomedical applications, particularly 
in cell culture platforms, scaffolds, and laboratory con-
sumables, contributing substantially to plastic waste accu-
mulation. It is estimated that more than 80% of biomedical 
plastics, such as those used in in vitro models, are derived 
from petroleum-based sources, contributing to environ-
mental degradation [3]. For instance, polystyrene, which 
is commonly used in Petri dishes and cell culture plates, 
is a significant source of non-recyclable biomedical waste 
and contributes to microplastic contamination in marine 
and terrestrial [4], raising alarms about their long-term 
ecological consequences. With these statistics in mind, the 
push for more sustainable alternatives in research materi-
als has never been more urgent.

For example, while polylactic acid (PLA), a biodegrad-
able  polymer  derived  from  renewable  sources  such  as 
corn starch, is often considered sustainable, its production 
requires intensive agricultural practices involving high water 
usage, fertilizer application, and land occupancy. Moreo-
ver, PLA biodegradation is not always straightforward, as 
it requires industrial composting conditions with specific 
temperature and humidity levels, which are not always avail-
able in standard waste management systems [2]. Therefore, 
a comprehensive life cycle analysis (LCA) approach must 
be applied to ensure that material choices contribute to sus-
tainability rather than shifting the environmental burden to 
another life cycle stage.

Conductive biological materials present an innovative 
solution by providing environmentally friendly options that 
integrate biological systems with conductive properties, 
offering both sustainability and enhanced functionality for 
in vitro models [5]. Such type of materials holds the poten-
tial to reduce the ecological footprint of biomedical research 
while improving the accuracy and relevance of experimental 
models in disease modelling and therapeutic development.
Sustainable and conductive materials are of importance 
to the future of in vitro models due to their ability to address 
both environmental and scientific challenges associated with 
electrical stimulation of cells for enhanced tissue regenera-
tion [6]. As the field progresses, there is a growing need 
for more accurate and physiologically relevant models to 
study complex biological systems which may often involve 
electrical stimuli for healing and regeneration or electrically 
induced triggering in the case of drug release systems [7]. 
Traditional in vitro models often rely on synthetic materials, 
which are now known to contribute significantly to environ-
mental degradation. For instance, an estimated two million 
tons of medical plastic waste is generated annually, with 
much of it originating and attributed to biomedical research 
materials [8]. This growing environmental burden neces-
sitates the development of sustainable alternatives.

Sustainable materials offer an eco-friendly solution, par-
ticularly biodegradable polymers and naturally sourced raw 
materials. These materials reduce the ecological footprint 
of biomedical research and can also be engineered to pos-
sess specific mechanical and biological properties, to display 
enhanced biocompatibility and tissue-like functionality [8]. 
A recent study demonstrated the use of plant-derived mate-
rials like cellulose nanocrystals for creating scaffolds that 
mimic the extracellular matrix, with potential as an in vitro 
model for tissue engineering and organ model trials [7]. By 
replacing petroleum-based plastics with sustainable materi-
als such as these, a pathway to lower waste and reduced 
reliance on non-renewable resources can be achieved [9, 10]. 
However, using biologically derived materials alone may 
not be the solution as the whole life cycle of the materials 
must be assessed through robust and emerging life cycle 
analysis models which take into account the production, 
usage, and end of life of materials used in vitro models in a 
so-called cradle-to-grave approach. A significant challenge 
in applying LCA to biomedical materials is the high energy 
consumption required for processing and sterilization and 
the emissions associated with transportation, particularly 
for materials sourced from different geographical locations. 
Additionally, end-of-life disposal methods, such as incin-
eration or landfill deposition, can negate the sustainability 
benefits if not managed appropriately [11].

Meanwhile, integrating conductive materials is essential 
for improving the functionality of in vitro models. As men-
tioned, conductivity is crucial for simulating electrical sign-
aling in tissues, particularly for models of the heart, nervous 
system, and muscle tissues [12]. Research has shown that 
when incorporated into in vitro models, conductive polymers 
like polypyrrole and polyaniline can enhance cellular behav-
ior, including differentiation and proliferation, by providing 
electrical cues that more closely replicate in vivo conditions 
[13]. These materials can also be used in organ-on-a-chip 
systems, where conductivity allows for better mimicry of 
the physiological environments necessary for drug testing, 
disease modeling, and sensing applications [14]. From a 
scientific perspective, developing sustainable and conduc-
tive materials offers significant advantages and associated 
challenges. These materials promote ecological responsi-
bility and enable more accurate, reproducible, and versatile 
in vitro models that better mimic the dynamic electrical and 
mechanical environments found in living organisms. As the 
push for sustainability in research grows, these materials 
will be pivotal in shaping the future of biomedical science, 
offering a path toward more efficient, ethical, and environ-
mentally conscious research practices [15].

The significant challenges that our modern society faces 
when treating different health problems are posed by the 
heterogeneity of the diseases and the need for cost-effec-
tive  tools  for  pre-clinical  and  clinical  research  [16].  In 

 In vitro models (2025) 4:89–110 

91

pre-clinical research, the existing validation studies involve 
mostly 2D cell culturing methods, which are time-consum-
ing and present only a narrow view of what is happening 
in the human body [17, 18]. Similarly, animal models are 
expensive and associated with poor reproducibility, thus 
not cost-effective and sustainable [19, 20]. In turn, in vitro 
3D models are more cost-effective biomimetic microphysi-
ological systems that have been developed as technological 
platforms to better recapitulate the physiological and patho-
logical conditions of human diseases, thus potentially pre-
senting a superior translational value [21, 22]. The in vitro 
3D models involve multidisciplinary approaches combin-
ing materials science and engineering, biology, microfluid-
ics, cell engineering and biology, and medicine. This new 
technological platform can help redesign research studies to 
be used for drug testing/discovery/validation and develop-
ment of new diagnostic solutions as an example [23, 24]. 
As tunable biotechnological tools, in vitro 3D models can 
allow patient-specific models to be developed [25]. These 
can help predict individual responses to treatments and aid 
in the development of targeted therapies benefiting diagnos-
tic and therapeutic interventions in personalized medicine 
approaches [25]. In order to better realize these technologies, 
(bio)materials currently used in the fabrication of in vitro 
models play a critical role as artificial extracellular matrices 
(aECM). The presence of such type of aECM components 
in in vitro models allows for cell adhesion, migration, and 
remodeling, enabling the in vitro formation of organized 
tissue structures and cellular phenotypes that more closely 
resemble those found in vivo [26]. In particular, hydrogel 
materials can better mimic the physiological complexity and 
microenvironment of native tissues, including biomechani-
cal properties, ECM interactions, microarchitecture, sign-
aling cues, conductivity, and reproducibility [27]. Thus, it 
is important to properly select the (bio)materials that best 
match the complexity of ECM of human tissues to be emu-
lated. Of course, the (bio)materials selection process still 
poses major challenges not only due to the limited number 
of materials available and processibility, biodegradability, 
biocompatibility, and biofunctionality requirements but also 
due to other possible constraints associated with transfer-
ability to the clinics [28, 29].

Herein, we will overview the current developments and 
discuss the future perspectives involving conductive materi-
als used as aECM and functionalization strategies in in vitro 
3D models.

In vitro 3D models

In vivo, cells exist in a dynamic 3D environment, interacting 
with extracellular matrix (ECM) components and neighbor-
ing cells. Traditional 2D cell cultures, while widely used, 

cannot fully capture these complex interactions, often lead-
ing to inaccurate or non-predictive data, necessitating fur-
ther animal testing [30]. Alternatively, 3D in vitro models 
provide a more realistic approach to replicating tissue struc-
ture and function, making them essential for drug testing and 
biological studies. The significance of these models in these 
fields cannot be overstated. Hydrogels, which imitate the 
hydrated structure of the extracellular matrix (ECM), play 
a crucial role in these models [31]. Composite hydrogels, 
which combine synthetic and natural components, improve 
these systems’ mechanical strength and biological function-
ality. These advancements facilitate better cell interactions 
and create more physiologically relevant conditions. Despite 
considerable progress, challenges persist in fully replicat-
ing the complexity of human tissues. Recent developments 
in bioprinting and composite hydrogel technologies show 
promise but are still evolving [32–34].

Many in vitro 3D models have been created to replicate 
human tissues in a better biomimicry manner, see Fig. 1. 
These include cellular spheroids, organoids, cell-laden bio-
mimetic constructs, and organ-on-chip technological plat-
forms, amongst others. Among these, spheroids and orga-
noids are especially popular because they enable cells to 
grow and self-organize in a three-dimensional environment, 
resembling actual tissues’ structural and functional charac-
teristics [31]. Organoids, derived from stem cells or tissue 
fragments, can differentiate into various cell types. This 
capability enables them to serve as more accurate models for 
studying tissue behavior, drug screening, and disease [35]. 
Traditional extracellular matrix (ECM) -based matrices, like 
Matrigel®, have been used to support tissue structures but 
have limitations, such as variability between batches. Recent 
advancements have aimed at engineering biomaterials that 
offer better environmental control, allowing for more pre-
cise cell interactions and improved tissue formation [35, 36]. 
While organoids do not wholly replicate the complexity of 
natural tissues, their ease of assembly and ability to capture 
cellular diversity make them a valuable alternative to two-
dimensional cultures and animal models [37, 38].

In organ-on-chip platforms, conductive materials are cru-
cial in enabling real-time monitoring and electrical stimula-
tion of tissue constructs as shown in Fig. 2. For instance, 
cardiac  organ-on-chip  models  integrate  microelectrodes 
fabricated using conductive polymers like polyaniline or 
polypyrrole to simulate the electrophysiological behavior of 
cardiac tissues. These materials help replicate native elec-
trical signaling, enhance cell alignment, and support func-
tional contractions of cardiomyocytes. A notable example 
includes a heart-on-chip system embedded with poly(3,4-eth-
ylenedioxythiophene) polystyrene sulfonate (PEDOT:PSS) 
electrodes, facilitating continuous electrical stimulation and 
allowing for high-throughput drug screening application 
[39, 40]. Additionally, graphene-based biosensors have been 

 92 

In vitro models (2025) 4:89–110

incorporated into organ-on-chip devices to measure real-
time electrochemical responses, improving the detection of 
cellular functions in neural and cardiac models [41]. These 
advances allow for better mimicking of physiological condi-
tions and facilitate precise drug efficacy testing.

Conductive bioinks represent a significant advancement 
in bioprinting technologies, particularly for engineering 
neural and cardiac tissues. These bioinks, composed of bio-
compatible conductive polymers like polypyrrole or carbon 
nanotubes, enable printed constructs to support electrical 
conductivity while maintaining high cell viability. For exam-
ple, a study demonstrated the use of a polypyrrole-alginate 
composite bioink to fabricate 3D-printed neural scaffolds 
with enhanced conductivity and improved neural differen-
tiation [42–44]. In another application, graphene-infused 
bioinks  have  been  utilized  to  print  cardiac  patches  that 
mimic the conductive properties of native myocardial tissue, 
significantly improving electrical signal propagation in vitro 
[43]. Such conductive bio-inks are particularly beneficial for 
applications requiring electromechanical stimulation, such 
as muscle tissue regeneration and neural network formation.
Composite hydrogels are increasingly recognized for their 
enhanced functionality and relevance in scientific matrices. 
Composite hydrogels provide a versatile and practical plat-
form for advancing 3D in vitro models by incorporating ele-
ments such as drugs to influence cell behavior, additional ECM 

components to enhance mechanical properties, and biomole-
cules to improve biological activity [45]. The development of 
innovative sustainable materials for in vitro models has recently 
gained significant attention due to their potential to minimize 
environmental impact and enhance biocompatibility, see Fig. 3 
[46]. These materials are derived from renewable sources and 
offer advantages such as biodegradability, reduced toxicity, and 
economic feasibility. Below are some key examples of sustain-
able materials being developed or used in in vitro models:

Biodegradable polymers

Biodegradable polymers are increasingly used as scaffold 
materials in tissue engineering and in vitro models. Plant-
derived materials are sustainable, biodegradable, and often 
biocompatible. They are gaining traction as alternatives to 
synthetic polymers in in vitro models.

Commonly  utilized  plant-based  systems  include  the 

following:

Polylactic acid (PLA)

Polylactic acid (PLA), derived from renewable resources like 
corn starch, is a biodegradable and biocompatible polymer, 
making it highly suitable for creating scaffolds for in vitro

famous for producing scaffolds that support cell growth and 
tissue regeneration [46, 47].

Cellulose and cellulose derivatives

Cellulose, obtained from plant fibers, is a widely utilized 
scaffold material due to its biocompatibility and biodegra-
dability. Nanocellulose, a form of cellulose with nanoscale 
dimensions, has shown promise in creating highly porous 
and flexible scaffolds for 3D cell cultures, tissue engineer-
ing, and drug delivery [48].

Agar and agarose

Agar  and  agarose,  extracted  from  seaweed,  are  natural 
polysaccharides used to create hydrogels that mimic the 
extracellular matrix in vitro models. These hydrogels sup-
port cell culture by providing a customizable environment 
with adjustable stiffness and porosity. Agarose, known for 
its higher gel strength, is often preferred for tissue engineer-
ing and drug testing. The ability to tailor these materials 
makes them ideal for mimicking different tissue types and 
studying various biological processes. Agar and agarose are 
biocompatible, cost-effective, and widely used in biomedical 
research [49].
