Approaches for mitigating nanotoxicity refer to strategies 
used  to  minimize  or  prevent  the  harmful  effects  of 
ENMs  on  human  health  and  the  environment.  Since 
nanotoxicity is largely influenced by the physicochemical 
properties  of  the  ENMs,  and  generally  results  in  ROS 
generation, the key toxicity mitigation strategies include

Characterizing ion release kinetics of ENMs is important

Antioxidants

ENMs  exert  toxicity  through  multiple  interconnected 
mechanisms.  For  example,  the  accumulation  of  ROS 
has  been  shown  to  be  linked  to  oxidative  stress  [245]. 
Naturally  occurring  antioxidants  in  living  organisms  are 
often  insufficient  to  mitigate  nanotoxicity  due  to  their 
limited dissolution and rapid degradation. Therefore, the 
addition  of  enzymatic  and  non-enzymatic  antioxidants 
like  SOD,  CAT,  POX,  MDHAR,  DHAR,  and  APX, 
ascorbic  acid,  phenolic  compounds,  alpha-tocopherols, 
and  alkaloids  has  been  employed  to  alleviate  ROS 
generation.  These  antioxidants  are  often  covalently 
linked, encased in crosslinked nanogels to enhance their 
stability  and  effectiveness  [246].  Eugenol  is  commonly 
used  in  the  synthesis  and  stabilization  of  various  ENMs 
[229].  In  Amaranthus  tricolor,  ascorbic  acid  was  found 
to  reduce  phytotoxicity  caused  by  multi-walled  carbon 
nanotubes  by  scavenging  ROS,  reducing  apoptosis, 
improving  growth,  and  minimizing  leaf  necrosis  [247]. 
Additionally,  synthesizing  Cu  ENMs  using  ascorbic  acid 
has been shown to improve their stability [248].

sections.heading: Experimental section
sections.text:
Experimental section  Materials and methods A stacked flower-like SnO₂ nanostructure was fabricated by altering the molar ratio of CTAB and keeping the temperature of tin chloride (Sn⁴⁺) constant. The organic components were then eliminated by calcination. The hydrothermal method was used for synthesis, as shown in Fig.  1 29 . 
 Fig. 1 ( a ) Hydrothermal synthesis of SnO 2 , and ( b ) Device fabrication methodology. 
 First, in a beaker filled with 100 ml of distilled water, hydrated tin chloride (Sn⁴⁺), CTAB (at an SnO: CTAB wt% ratio of 100:20), and urea (CH₄N₂O) were dissolved while being continuously stirred with a magnetic stirrer. The resulting mixture was then heated in a hot air oven for 24 h at 120 °C and placed in an autoclave lined with Teflon. Impurities were then eliminated by centrifugation using ethanol and deionised water. The final product was dried overnight at 100 °C in an oven. Using a mortar and pestle, the dried materials were crushed into a fine powder before being calcined for 6 h at 400 °C as displayed in Fig.  1 a. The same procedure was applied to the following Table  1 . 
 Table 1 Summary of the preparation of tin oxide nanoparticles. Name of the samples Material (Wt %) Reaction time (hrs.) Temperature (°C) Sn 4 +  (Wt %) CTAB (Wt %) SnO-1 100 0 24 120 SnO-2 100 6 24 120 SnO-3 100 11 24 120 SnO-4 100 16 24 120 SnO-5 100 20 24 120 
  Device fabrication Figure  1 b shows the SnO₂ thin-film device fabrication process. Ethyl cellulose and a mortar and pestle were used to grind the synthesized SnO₂ nanopowder into a paste. The doctor blade method was then used to apply this paste to an FTO substrate, and it was annealed for an hour at 350 °C. After annealing, a thin layer of PEDOT: PSS, which acts as the hole-collecting layer was coated by spin-coating for 30 s at 3000 revolutions per minute (rpm) and then letting it dry for 10 min. The electrical connections were manually applied to the sensor using silver paste, as seen in Fig.  1 b.

title: Toxicity of fluorescent silica nanoparticles in brine shrimp and their implications as food ingestion markers.

sections.text:
Methods for observing zooplankton feeding are often limited by their small body size. Fluorescent 
silica nanoparticles (FSNPs) offer a promising alternative because of their bright fluorescence, 
photostability, and observability without the need for sophisticated equipment. To assess their 
potential as fluorescent markers, their physical properties, toxicity, and marking efficiency were 
ascertained using brine shrimp (Artemia franciscana) as a model marine zooplankton. The FSNPs 
were spherical, 64.0 ± 3.9 nm in diameter, and with stable dispersion in seawater. Acute toxicity 
tests showed no significant mortality or immobility in brine shrimp nauplii within 24 h of exposure to 
various FSNP concentrations. Ingested FSNPs exhibited bright luminescence along the gut passage 
under ultraviolet light, with marking efficiency increasing with FSNP concentration. An optimal 
concentration of 16 mg/L provided high fluorescence brightness without affecting locomotion or 
feeding rates. Food facilitated the clearance of FSNPs from the gut, and no observable FSNPs adhered 
to the outer surfaces of the shrimp. However, prolonged or repeated exposure to FSNPs at 16 mg/L 
reduced survival over time. These findings indicate that FSNPs are an effective, nontoxic marker for 
short-term studies of marine zooplankton feeding behavior, providing a valuable tool for ecological 
research.

Keywords  Feeding behavior, Fluorescence, Silica nanoparticle, Tracking, Zooplankton

One major challenge in observing the feeding behavior of zooplankton, especially at the individual level, stems 
from their minuscule body size. A conventional method used so far to study zooplankton feeding is measuring 
the remaining food over a certain period after providing a known amount1–3. The quantity of food consumed 
was  calculated  based  on  the  final  concentration  of  residual  algal  cells  after  feeding  or  the  amount  of  carbon 
or pigments as a proxy for food. The primary results are generally the characteristics of the whole population 
or  sample  group  tested,  and  mathematical  or  statistical  techniques  are  applied  to  infer  those  of  individual 
plankton2,3. Food ingestion can be simply observed under a microscope by mounting plankton on a glass slide 
and their transparent bodies allowing for the observation of food particles traveling through the gut passage4,5. 
However, this method inevitably disturbs or harms the subject which might not reflect its normal behavior. More 
advanced approaches have been developed, in which the test animals must be fixed onto a needle or holder, 
which allows their behavior to be observed either from a video recorded via a macro lens or by electrochemical 
techniques6,7.  It  assesses  not  only  the  feeding  activity  at  the  individual  level  but  also  other  physiological 
characteristics. However, it requires sophisticated apparatus and is not affordable.

Nanotechnology is rapidly becoming a tool in many research areas, including aquatic science. For instance, 
researchers  can  track  the  movement  trajectories  of  small  zooplankton  employing  quantum  dots  (QDs),  a 
fluorescent semiconductor nanocrystal, as well as apply image processing and tracking softwares8,9. The surface 
of  the  QDs  is  modified  for  adherence  to  the  plankton  body,  and  the  tagged  plankton  can  be  located  under 
ultraviolet (UV) light. However, the QDs have not been used to observe feeding activity. Alternatively, in several 
studies, test animals have been allowed to ingest micro or nanoscale fluorescent plastic beads, enabling tracking 
through their digestive tracts10–12. However, their potential toxicity limits their use, as these studies often focus 
on ecotoxicity rather than feeding behavior tracking.

Fluorescent  silica  nanoparticles  (FSNPs)  are  nanosized  silica  particles  that  incorporate  fluorescent  dye 
molecules  within  their  matrix.  They  present  a  promising  alternative  for  observing  the  feeding  behavior  of 
zooplankton owing to their excellent fluorescence brightness and photostability. This characteristic is attributed 
to  the  numerous  dye  molecules  packed  into  a  small  area  within  the  matrix,  which  protects  the  fluorophores 
from oxygen-induced fluorescence bleaching, thus prolonging their usability13,14. In addition, when used in vivo, 
FSNPs prevent direct contact between potentially harmful fluorophores and organisms15. The surface silanol 
groups (≡ Si-OH) also allow for easy modification, enabling cross-linking with biomolecules to act as biosensors, 
achieving specific targeting of certain cells or tissues13,16,17.

One  major  concern  when  applying  marking  materials  in  live  organisms  is  their  potential  toxicity.  Silica 
nanoparticles (SNPs) in their crystalline form are highly toxic and thus are rarely used in biological applications, 
unlike amorphous silica, which is less toxic and more compatible with biological systems18. However, ambiguities 
remain  regarding  the  toxicity  of  amorphous  SNPs,  even  in  the  same  test  organisms19–21.  Among  aquatic 
organisms, the toxicity of SNPs against crustacean zooplankton has mostly been examined in the freshwater flea, 
Daphnia magna, as a representative organism, with varied results22. However, their impacts on other species, 
especially marine zooplankton, have been reported infrequently.

Several factors should be considered when selecting markers for applicability in small animals23. This study 
focused on four key aspects to evaluate the potential of FSNPs as markers for tracking feeding behavior in the 
brine shrimp (Artemia franciscana), which is a nonselective filter feeder, as a representative model for marine 
zooplankton. First, the FSNPs should be able to disperse well in the medium (seawater) to ensure that the target 
organisms can equally access them. Second, they must be nontoxic and do not interfere with normal behavior at 
their working concentration. Third, they must emit a distinct signal that is easily detectable. Finally, they must 
pass through the digestive tract simultaneously with the ingested food and be excreted along with the feces.

molecules  within  their  matrix.  They  present  a  promising  alternative  for  observing  the  feeding  behavior  of 
zooplankton owing to their excellent fluorescence brightness and photostability. This characteristic is attributed 
to  the  numerous  dye  molecules  packed  into  a  small  area  within  the  matrix,  which  protects  the  fluorophores

FSNPs prevent direct contact between potentially harmful fluorophores and organisms15. The surface silanol 
groups (≡ Si-OH) also allow for easy modification, enabling cross-linking with biomolecules to act as biosensors, 
achieving specific targeting of certain cells or tissues13,16,17.

One  major  concern  when  applying  marking  materials  in  live  organisms  is  their  potential  toxicity.  Silica 
nanoparticles (SNPs) in their crystalline form are highly toxic and thus are rarely used in biological applications, 
unlike amorphous silica, which is less toxic and more compatible with biological systems18. However, ambiguities 
remain  regarding  the  toxicity  of  amorphous  SNPs,  even  in  the  same  test  organisms19–21.  Among  aquatic

Several factors should be considered when selecting markers for applicability in small animals23. This study 
focused on four key aspects to evaluate the potential of FSNPs as markers for tracking feeding behavior in the

their working concentration. Third, they must emit a distinct signal that is easily detectable. Finally, they must 
pass through the digestive tract simultaneously with the ingested food and be excreted along with the feces.

Results
Physical characteristics of the FSNPs
FSNPs were spherical with a diameter of 64.0 ± 3.9 nm (n = 90) (Fig. 1a). At an excitation wavelength of 365 nm, 
the  wavelength  of  the  UV  lamp  used,  their  maximal  emission  wavelength  was  614  nm  when  dispersed  in 
distilled or seawater (Fig. 1b). When the FSNPs were exposed to an excitation wavelength of 460 nm, which is 
the maximal excitation wavelength of the Rubpy dye incorporated in the NPs, the peak emission wavelengths 
were 614 and 617 nm for those dispersed in distilled and seawater, respectively. The average zeta potential of 
FSNPs in seawater (pH 8.2, conductivity 55.57 mS/cm) was − 59.69 ± 10.67 mV (n = 3), which falls within the 
range for good dispersion stability in the medium24.

Acute toxicity
No  apparent  sign  of  acute  toxicity  was  detected  in  the  brine  shrimp  nauplii  treated  with  a  range  of  FSNP 
concentrations  for  24  h  (Table  1),  with  no  differences  in  mortality  or  immobility  between  the  tested  groups 
(mortality:  χ2  =  10.65,  df = 11,  P = 0.473;  immobility:  χ2  =  9.03,  df = 11,  P = 0.619).  However,  after  48  h,  the 
mortality  varied  significantly  within  the  FSNP-treated  groups  (χ2  =  22.99,  df = 11,  P = 0.018),  but  not  when 
compared  to  the  control.  The  immobility  at  48  h  did  not  differ  markedly  among  all  treatments  (χ2  =  13.33, 
df = 11, P = 0.273).

Appropriate FSNP concentration for tracking
Fluorescence due to FSNPs was observed at all tested concentrations. It was observed only in the gut, indicating 
that the FSNPs could not attach to other body parts (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Video 1). The marking efficiency 
was markedly enhanced with an increase in FSNP concentrations until 4 mg/L (Fig. 3a). The presence of food 
did not affect the marking efficiency, but interacted with FSNPs (Table 2).

The  fluorescence  brightness  of  the  marked  individuals  was  influenced  by  FSNP  concentration  and  the 
presence of food (Table 2). The brightness score elevated with an increase in FSNP concentration until 16 mg/L; 
it was greater under the condition of food absence than presence (Fig. 3b). Based on these findings, 16 mg/L 
FSNPs was identified as the optimal concentration (representing the lowest concentration that achieved high 
marking efficiency and fluorescence intensity) and was subsequently used in the following experiments.

Effects on locomotion
The average movement speeds of brine shrimp in the 16 mg/L FSNP suspension (n = 46) and those in the control 
(n = 42)  were  3.20 ± 1.06  and  3.22 ± 1.10  mm/s,  respectively,  which  were  not  significantly  different  between 
the  treatments  (W = 968.0,  P = 0.990).  Similarly,  the  average  distances  traveled  in  30  s  were  95.89 ± 31.92  and 
96.44 ± 33.06  mm  for  the  FSNP-treated  and  control  groups,  which  were  not  markedly  different  (W = 968.0, 
P = 0.990).

through the gut passage (Fig. 6a and c) and were excreted simultaneously with the feces (Fig. 6b and d). However, 
it  seemed  that  the  DAPI  from  the  ingested  yeast  also  stained  the  nuclei  of  the  epithelial  cells,  resulting  in 
numerous small blue luminescence dots dispersed throughout the gut.

Chronic toxicity
In  the  chronic  toxicity  test  conducted  with  16  mg/mL  FSNPs  under  different  exposure  conditions  over  14 
days, the lethal time 50 (LT50) values for brine shrimp in the 3-hour intermittent exposure, 6-hour intermittent 
exposure, and continuous exposure groups were 12.8, 11.5, and 8.9 days, respectively. The LT50 for the control 
group (artificial seawater without FSNPs) was not calculated, as 71% of brine shrimp remained alive at the end 
of the experiment. Significant differences in survival curves were observed among the treatment groups (χ² = 
27.4, df = 3, P < 0.001; Fig. 7). Brine shrimp exposed to FSNPs under all treatment conditions exhibited shorter 
lifespan compared to the control group (Supplementary Table 1). When analyzing survival during the first 6 days 
of exposure, significant differences were also detected among the treatment groups (χ² = 13.0, df = 3, P = 0.005). 
However,  only  the  continuous  exposure  group  showed  significantly  lower  survival  compared  to  the  control, 
while the 3-hour and 6-hour intermittent exposure groups did not differ significantly from the control during 
this initial period (Supplementary Table 1).

Throughout the experiment, more than 70% of brine shrimp in the continuous exposure group exhibited 
fluorescence under UV light at each observation point (every 48 h). In contrast, in both the 3-hour and 6-hour 
intermittent exposure groups, fluorescence was detected within 30 min after FSNP administration but was no 
longer detectable after 48 h seawater renewal.

Tests in adults
Fluorescence due to ingested FSNPs can be seen in the abdomen of the adult shrimp (Fig. 8 and Supplementary 
Video 2), while their feces remained as small pellets at the bottom of the container. The average times that the 
shrimp abdomens began to fluoresce after FSNP exposure were 14.4 and 18.8 min for males (n = 25) and females 
(n = 21), respectively. However, they were not significantly different between the sexes (W = 285, P = 0.601). The 
average times that the fluorescent feces appeared due to the excretion of ingested FSNPs were similar between 
males and females (W = 275.5, P = 0.775), which were 38.2 and 39.0 min after providing FSNPs, respectively.

Discussion
The application of FSNPs synthesized using the water-in-oil reverse microemulsion technique has been successful 
as an internal marker in fruit flies, demonstrating several benefits such as bright fluorescence, photostability, 
and low toxicity15. This study reports that these NPs were well-dispersed in seawater, as indicated by the zeta 
potentials. They exhibited low toxicity during short-term exposure and could be traced through the gut passage

attributable to variations in NP characteristics such as size, surface chemistry, and preparation techniques.

This study used baker’s yeast as the food source for brine shrimp, rather than their natural diet of microalgae, 
to avoid confounding luminescence signals from the algal chlorophylls (664 and 647 nm for chlorophyll a and 
b, respectively), which have fluorescence peaks close to those of FSNPs (614–617 nm)32. Our results indicated 
that ingested food could reduce the fluorescence signal observed in the gut of brine shrimp. However, at the 
optimal concentration of 16 mg/L, the presence of food no longer had a significant effect on the signal of FSNPs 
(Fig.  3b).  It  should  be  noted  that  a  semi-quantitative  scoring  method  in  our  study  was  performed  to  assess 
fluorescence brightness, as it allowed for a practical and efficient evaluation of a large number of individuals 
under  a  stereomicroscope.  Additionally,  all  observations  were  conducted  by  the  same  examiner  to  minimize 
observer bias and ensure consistency. For more precise and quantitative assessments, imaging systems coupled 
with  fluorescence  intensity  measurements  and  tracking  software,  as  applied  in  previous  studies8,9,  could  be 
utilized in future work. Regarding feeding rate, our findings indicated that FSNPs did not influence the shrimp 
feeding rate. However, it is important to note that yeast is not an ideal diet for brine shrimp because the rigid 
cell walls hinder digestion33. The feeding rates observed in our experiments were low because some yeast cells 
remained undigested and were excreted intact, as indicated by the fluorescence image (Fig. 6b).

Clogging  and  accumulation  of  small  particles  in  the  digestive  tract  are  crucial  factors  to  be  considered 
when assessing the suitability of FSNPs as a feeding marker. Such NPs might block the gut passage and impede 
nutrient  assimilation,  resulting  in  abnormal  feeding  behavior  and  mortality,  as  reported  previously11.  Our 
results indicated that most brine shrimp could egest FSNPs within 15 min for nauplii and 40 min for adults, 
concurrently  with  the  ingested  food,  as  evidenced  by  the  luminescent  fecal  pellets.  This  expulsion  time  was 
similar to previous findings, in which the time for ingested food to travel through the gut passage of brine shrimp 
was ~ 30 min, regardless of the body size34. However, under the food absence condition, the excretion of the NPs

results have been reported before as the pressure from recently ingested food particles is required to expel the

been explained by the naturally produced chitinous membranes in the midgut to encase anything consumed, 
preventing the food from passing through the gut too quickly35.

Adherence of different types of NPs to the surfaces or appendages of microcrustaceans has been observed, 
including nanoplastics8,9,12. This adherence has been attributed to the surface charges of both the NPs and the 
organisms10. For instance, the use of QDs to track the movements of water fleas required a modification of the 
NP surface to have a positive charge or coated with biotin, facilitating the biotinylation of the water flea cuticle8,9. 
In contrast, in our study, fluorescence microscopy observations revealed that FSNPs were localized exclusively 
in the digestive tracts of brine shrimp, without adherence to other body parts. The zeta potentials of FSNPs in 
seawater indicated a negative charge, mirroring that of the microcrustacean cuticle8. This same charge likely 
prevents the FSNPs from adhering to or penetrating the tissues of brine shrimp due to electrostatic repulsion.

Brine  shrimp  are  nonselective  filter  feeders  that  ingest  particles,  including  food  and  even  sand  grains, 
< 50 μm37. Consequently, FSNPs can be ingested and accumulated in the gut. Although fluorescent micro and 
nanoplastics used have exhibited fluorescence in the gut, which was similar to the objective of our study, they are 
toxic to brine shrimp and have been used to test their negative effects from an environmental perspective rather 
than for feed tracking10,12. Our study demonstrated that a low concentration of FSNPs at 16 mg/L effectively 
allowed  the  observation  of  their  feeding  behavior—using  a  stereomicroscope  for  nauplii  and  with  the  naked 
eye for adults; it showed no adverse impacts on the brine shrimp in our investigations. Thus, we opted for this 
concentration to avoid the excessive use of FSNPs and to reduce the potential negative effects.

By simultaneously providing DAPI-stained yeast and FSNPs as food, we confirmed that both co-travel during 
gut transit and are expelled with normal feces. However, we observed numerous blue dots along the gut wall, 
likely from DAPI molecules binding to the DNA in the nuclei of the epithelial cells. This finding suggests that 
conventional dye staining of food items may not be appropriate for tracking feeding behavior, as the dye can also 
stain the cells, potentially interfering with observations and posing a toxicity risk.

Although  no  acute  toxicity  was  observed,  our  additional  chronic  toxicity  experiments  indicated  that 
continuous and repeated exposure to FSNPs at 16 mg/L induced significant mortality over time. LT50 values of 
FSNPs from our study were similar to those previously reported for A. salina, where LT50 values of 18.8 and 17.9 
days were observed following exposure to SNPs at concentrations of 5 and 10 mg/L, respectively30. Two possible 
mechanisms may account for this delayed toxicity. First, while FSNPs could be excreted from the digestive tract, 
continuous exposure resulted in their persistent presence in the gut, potentially causing blockage that impaired 
food digestion and assimilation, ultimately leading to starvation11. Second, toxic effects of FSNPs as discussed 
earlier  may  emerge  with  repeated  or  prolonged  exposure19,22.  This  could  explain  the  significant  increase  in 
mortality observed in the 3-hour and 6-hour intermittent exposure groups after 6 days, despite the absence of 
detectable accumulation following depuration.

Although this study demonstrated the effects of FSNP exposure on brine shrimp through behavioral and 
survival  assessments,  it  did  not  include  biochemical  or  molecular  biomarkers,  which  could  provide  deeper 
insights into the underlying mechanisms of toxicity. Previous studies have shown that exposure to NPs can alter 
enzymatic  activities  related  to  oxidative  stress  and  detoxification  pathways  in  Artemia,  including  glutathione 
S-transferase (GST), catalase (CAT), and cholinesterase (ChE)38,39. For example, Gambardella et al.39 reported 
that  metal  oxide  NPs  significantly  altered  GST  and  ChE  activities,  even  in  the  absence  of  acute  mortality, 
highlighting their importance in xenobiotic metabolism and neurotoxicity assessment. Similarly, Varó et al.38 
found that amino-modified polystyrene NPs induced oxidative stress and modulated gene expression related 
to  development  (clap),  molting  (cstb),  stress  response  (hsp70),  and  immunity  (proPO  and  lysozyme)  in  A. 
franciscana. Additionally, transcriptomic analyses have shown that exposure to SNPs can affect genes involved 
in stress response and cuticle renewal in aquatic invertebrates40. These findings suggest that prolonged FSNP 
exposure may plausibly affect cellular and molecular pathways in Artemia, even in the absence of apparent acute 
toxicity. Therefore, future studies incorporating gene expression and enzymatic biomarkers would be valuable 
for confirming the mechanistic basis of FSNP-induced stress and toxicity.

Conclusions
This  study  demonstrated  that  FSNPs  present  a  promising  tool  for  observing  the  feeding  behavior  of  marine 
zooplankton. They showed excellent dispersion stability in seawater and exhibited low acute toxicity. Critically, 
they were effectively ingested and expelled by the brine shrimp, allowing for a clear observation of the feeding 
processes without adhering to the shrimp’s outer surfaces or causing significant adverse effects. Our findings 
indicate that FSNPs can be utilized to track the passage of ingested food through the gut, providing valuable 
insights into the feeding behavior of zooplankton. FSNPs at 16 mg/L were sufficient to mark the shrimp without 
affecting  their  locomotion  during  short  time  exposure.  However,  prolonged  or  repeated  exposure  negatively 
affected survival, indicating potential long-term risks. The presence of food facilitated the clearance of FSNPs 
from their digestive tract. Their ease of observation under UV light makes them particularly useful for such

Materials and methods
Nanoparticle characterization
FSNPs were synthesized according to the method outlined by Songvorawit, et al.15 using the water-in-oil reverse 
microemulsion  technique,  and  Rubpy  dye  (tris  [2,2′-bipyridyl]ruthenium[II]  chloride)  as  a  fluorophore.  The 
NPs  were  examined  under  a  JEM-1400  transmission  electron  microscope  (TEM;  JEOL,  Tokyo,  Japan),  and 
their  size  was  measured  from  the  TEM  images  employing  the  ImageJ  software  version  1.53o  (NIH,  USA; 
https://imagej.nih.gov/ij). Since this study used FSNPs suspended in saline water, their dispersion stability was 
examined in artificial seawater (ASTM D1141-98, pH 8.2) utilizing a Nano ZSP zeta-sizer (Malvern Panalytical, 
Great Malvern, England). Emission spectra were examined employing a Duetta™ fluorometer (Horiba Scientific, 
Kyoto, Japan) at excitation bands of 365 and 460 nm, which corresponded to the UV light wavelength used to 
track animal behavior in this study and the maximal excitation wavelength of Rubpy dye, respectively14. The 
maximal emission wavelength of the FSNPs was calculated using a moving average based on five data points.

Test animals and handling
Commercial  brine  shrimp  (Artemia  franciscana)  cysts  (American  Eagle,  USA)  imported  from  the  Great  Salt 
Lake, USA were purchased from a local supplier in Bangkok, Thailand. They were hatched in artificial seawater 
at 25–26 °C under continuous aeration and illumination. For rearing adult shrimp, nauplii (shrimp larvae) were 
transferred into an 8 L tank and raised in filtered natural seawater (3% salinity) at 25–26 °C under continuous 
aeration and a light intensity of 1,600 lx (fluorescent lamp) under a 12/12 h illumination cycle. Artificial food 
(composition unknown, branded as N.P. Guppy, Thailand) purchased from a local seller in Bangkok, Thailand, 
was provided every other day, and the adults were obtained 3 weeks after hatching.

Euthanasia was performed utilizing the two-step method (immersion in 5% ethanol for 5 min and then 10% 
formalin) per the AVMA guidelines41. The experimental protocol was approved by the Animal Care and Use 
Committee of the Faculty of Science, Chulalongkorn University (Protocol Review No. 2423018).

Acute toxicity test
Nauplii,  18–24  h  post-hatching,  were  transferred  into  24-well  plates  containing  1–1,024  mg/L  of  FSNP 
suspension  in  artificial  seawater  (2  mL  of  suspension  and  10–20  nauplii  per  well)  and  cultured  at  25–26  °C 
under a light intensity of 1,600 lx (fluorescent lamp) with a 12/12 h light/dark cycle. Brine shrimp grown in 
artificial seawater without FSNPs were used as a control. Mortality and immobility were checked at 24 and 48 h 
after exposure. A nauplius was considered dead if its appendages stopped moving within 10 s. Immobility was 
identified when a nauplius remained with moving appendages in situ for 10 s and was calculated by dividing 
the number of immobile (but still alive) individuals by the total number of living individuals. A mortality rate 
in the 24-h period of less than 10% was considered valid for the control group. Each treatment was conducted 
in eight replications.

Test for the appropriate FSNP concentration for tracking
To ensure that all tested brine shrimp were ready to eat the food provided, 15–30 nauplii, 24–36 h after hatching 
were used. They were incubated in 2 mL of FSNP suspension in 24-well plates for 1 h at 25–26 °C in the dark under 
two conditions: food presence (1 × 106 cells/mL of baker’s yeast) or food absence. They were then euthanized. 
The fluorescence due to FSNP intake, which was visible through the body wall, was inspected under a stereo 
microscope coupled with a UV lamp set to 365 nm. To minimize observer bias, the same examiner conducted 
all observations throughout the experiment. The fluorescence brightness was scored on a scale ranging from 0 
to 2: 0 = no, 1 = slight, and 2 = bright fluorescence (Fig. 2). The marking efficiency was calculated following the 
formula described previously15,42, as shown in Eq. (1):

Persistence of FSNPs in brine shrimp
A  depuration  experiment  was  conducted  under  food  presence  or  absence.  Baker’s  yeast  powder  was  used  as

110 μm net. Next, 5–10 nauplii were transferred into each well of a 24-well plate containing 2 mL of seawater 
and  1 × 106  cells/mL  baker’s  yeast.  After  euthanasia,  the  fluorescence  of  FSNPs  consumed  by  the  nauplii  was 
observed under a stereo microscope equipped with a UV lamp and an Axioscope 5 fluorescence microscope 
(ZEISS, Oberkochen, Germany) at 0, 15, 30, 45, and 60 min, as well as 2, 4, 8, 12, and 24 h. The number of nauplii 
with observable FSNPs was counted irrespective of the fluorescence brightness. Under food absence, the entire 
experiment was conducted with the same procedure, but without yeast. Each treatment was conducted in eight 
replications.

To examine whether FSNPs moved along with the ingested food, another experiment similar to the depuration 
described above was conducted by providing brine shrimp nauplii with DAPI-stained baker’s yeast as food and 
FSNPs simultaneously. The nauplii were then examined under a fluorescence microscope.

Chronic toxicity test
Based  on  the  results  of  the  appropriate  FSNP  concentration  experiment,  a  concentration  of  16  mg/L  FSNPs 
was used for the chronic toxicity test. Brine shrimp nauplii (18–24 h post-hatching) were transferred to 250 mL 
Erlenmeyer flasks containing 150 mL of artificial seawater under continuous aeration, with 10 nauplii per flask. 
They were fed with artificial food, and both seawater and food were renewed every 48 h. Three treatment groups 
were performed: (1) continuous exposure to FSNPs, (2) 3-hour exposure to FSNPs every 48 h, and (3) 6-hour 
exposure to FSNPs every 48 h. In treatments (2) and (3), nauplii were exposed to FSNPs prior to the renewal of 
seawater and food. The experiment was conducted over a period of 14 days. A control group was maintained 
in artificial seawater without FSNPs. Rearing conditions and mortality assessment criteria were consistent with 
those used in the acute toxicity test. Each treatment was conducted in nine replications.

Test with adult brine shrimp
Adult brine shrimp, 25 males and 24 females, were used to evaluate whether FSNPs could be applied to developed 
stages. The sexes were determined by the presence of a clasping organ (male) and brood sac (female). The shrimp 
were randomly selected from an aquarium and transferred into 24-well plates filled with 2 mL of baker’s yeast 
suspension  (1 × 106  cells/mL),  one  individual  per  well.  They  were  dark-acclimatized  for  30  min.  The  FSNP 
suspension was then added to each well to reach a final NP concentration of 16 mg/L. Observations were made 
every 5 min under UV light to detect the appearance of abdominal fluorescence, followed by further monitoring 
until luminescent feces were detected, indicating complete gut passage of the ingested FSNPs.

Statistical analyses
Because our data did not meet the assumption for parametric statistics, nonparametric statistical analyses were 
used in all tests. The effects of FSNP concentration on mortality and immobility were ascertained by applying 
the  Kruskal–Wallis  test;  Dunn’s  test  was  used  for  pairwise  comparison.  The  effects  of  FSNP  concentration, 
the presence or absence of food, and their interaction with the marking efficiency or fluorescence brightness 
of  the  marked  individuals  were  analyzed  employing  the  aligned  rank  test.  Feeding  rates  in  the  presence  and 
absence of FSNPs were corrected for the rate of yeast autolysis in the control group and then compared by the 
Wilcoxon rank-sum test. The effects of depuration time, the presence or absence of food, and their interactions 
were analyzed using the aligned rank and Dunn’s tests. Locomotion data for shrimp treated with FSNPs were 
compared  with  the  control  utilizing  the  Wilcoxon  rank-sum  test. The  number  of  times  that  the  abdomen  of 
adult brine shrimp exhibited luminescence and the number of  times that  the fluorescent feces appeared due 
to the excretion of FSNPs were compared between sexes using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. LT50 was analyzed 
using probit analysis in SPSS version 28.044. All other statistical analyses were performed using the base, ARTool, 
combinate, dplyr, survival, survminer, and tidyverse packages in R, version 4.3.045.

By doping oxide semiconductors, such as transition metal-
doped SnO2 (TM-SnO2) or earth rare-doped SnO2 nano-
particles, one targets a wide range of applications, including the
use of self-cleaning surfaces (SCS). In this regard, one can
mention the use of doped SnO2 nanoparticles, which recently
gained attention due to antibacterial activity. Studies have
shown that these nanoparticles can inhibit the growth of
various bacterial species, including Gram-positive and Gram-
negative bacteria,9,10 given that doping enhances antibacterial
activity; the highest values reported in the literature are also

reactive oxygen species (ROS), being responsible for the anti-
bacterial eﬀect of TM-SnO2 nanoparticles.14 ROS have a strong
ability to oxidize a wide range of organic-based materials, such
as pollutants, bacteria, cancer cells, and viruses. When doped
oxide semiconductors are used as self-cleaning surfaces, the
ROS generated on the surface can cause oxidative stress in
bacterial cells, destroying cell walls, DNA, and relevant
proteins.6 The research of new materials with SCS activity is of
extreme importance, especially aer the COVID-2019 pandemic.
In this scenario, we can highlight the use of Cu-doped oxide
semiconductor with high antibacterial activity while it is irra-
diated with UV light.15 However, UV light is not feasible for
creating self-cleaning and antibacterial surfaces in typical
indoor conditions, with negligible UV light exposition. There-
fore, it is necessary to search for alternatives aiming at to
increase antimicrobial response in a dimly illuminated envi-
ronment. Also, no previous investigation has been carried out to
evaluate the inuence of doping enrichment of the surface and
the onset of a secondary phase on the antibacterial activity of
the system, indicating a knowledge gap.

In this study, we aim to investigate the synthesis and char-
acterization of Cu-doped SnO2 nanoparticles, with emphasis on
structural, morphological, and vibrational properties plus
antibacterial activity against Escherichia coli (ATCC® 33876) and
Staphylococcus aureus (ATCC® 25923) in a dark environment.
We also explore the possible mechanisms by which Cu-doping
contributes to enhance the antibacterial activity of the as-
synthesized SnO2 nanoparticles. Our ndings are expected to
contribute to the development of novel materials for self-
cleaning surfaces with high antibacterial activity.

2 Experimental details

Cu-doped SnO2 nanocrystals were synthesized using the poly-
meric precursor method (Pechine's method), using tin chloride
monohydrate
hexahydrate
(Cu(NO3)3$6H2O), ethylene glycol (C2H4(OH)2) and citric acid

(SnCl2$H2O),

copper

nitrate

(C6H8O7)as reactive chemicals. More details about the used
synthesis protocol have been described in the literature.16 X-ray
diﬀraction (XRD) measurements were performed using
a Rigaku MiniFlex 600 X-ray diﬀractometer equipped with Cu
Ka radiation (l = 1.5418 Å) and scanning in the 2q range of 20–
80°. Scanning electron microscope (SEM) images were obtained
using a Zeiss microscope, model EVO10, and JEOL Scanning
Electron Microscopy (SEM) model JSM 7001F, where X-ray
energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) is implemented to deter-
mine the chemical composition of the samples. Transmission
images were obtained using
electron microscopy (TEM)
a Talos™ F200i commercial microscope. Fourier-transform
infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) measurements were carried out
(samples pressed in KBr pellet) using a Bruker VERTEX 70 FT-IR
spectrometer, scanning in the wavenumber range of 450–
−1. Room temperature Raman spectra were recorded
4000 cm
using a Horiba Labram HR Evolution spectrometer equipped
with the 532 nm laser line. The agar disc-diﬀusion testing
method (DDTM) was used to evaluate the inhibition zone (IZ)
associated with the S. aureus and E. coli species. The DDTM is
made up of a xed amount (5 mg) of Cu-doped SnO2 nanocrystal
impregnated on lter paper discs (6 mm of diameter), which are
placed on the surface of a Petri dish culture medium (Mueller–
Hinton agar) containing the appropriate bacterium (S. aureus or
E. coli). Aer placing the paper discs, the Petri dish was placed
in an incubation chamber kept at 35 °C for 24 and 48 hours for
E. coli and S. aureus, respectively, with the in vitro tests per-
formed in triplicate (×3).

3 Results and discussions

XRD patterns of undoped and Cu-doped SnO2 nanoparticles are
shown in Fig. 1(a). The main crystalline phase is linked with the
rutile tetragonal unit cell SnO2 phase, as indicated by the main
peaks found at 26.5°, 33.8°, 37.9° and 51.7° associated with the
(110), (101), (200) and (211) plane reections, respectively.
However, additional peaks at 35.5° and 38.7° were observed in
copper concentrations starting from 20%, which have been
respectively linked with the (111) and (022) planes of the
secondary CuO phase; the latter suggesting that the solution
limit is lower than 20 mol%, this being due to the detection
limit of the technique.

To determine the structural parameters the XRD patterns
were analyzed using Rietveld renement
implemented in
EXPGUI, a graphical user interface for GSAS soware,8 where
a Lorentzian peak shape (S) was used to model the diﬀraction
peaks proles, S = X/cos q + Y tan q, with the rst term repre-
senting the Lorentzian Scherrer whereas the second term
describes the strain broadening. A typical t is shown in
Fig. 1(b), where the open black circles are the recorded experi-
mental data, the solid red line is the theoretical curve, and the
solid green line at the bottom is the diﬀerence between them.
Table 1 displays the structural parameters extracted from the
Rietveld renement. The lattice constants for the undoped SnO2
nanoparticles are a = b = 4.7339 Å and c = 3.1894 Å, giving
a unit cell volume of 71.374 Å3. However, the unit cell volume
shows an increasing tendency as the Cu-content increases,

constant (0.9), the mean crystallite size (hDiXRD) of the Cu-doped
SnO2 nanoparticles was calculated from Scherrer's broadening
contribution. The results are shown in Fig. 1(c), where one can
see the decreasing trend (from ∼9 nm to ∼5 nm) as the Cu
content increases. Fig. 1(c) emphasizes (horizontal orange color
strip) the SnO2 exciton Bohr diameter, which is around 5.4 nm,2
meaning that a quantum connement eﬀect cannot be ruled
out for the samples, as it will be explained below.

SEM and EDS measurements were performed in some of the
samples to determine their chemical composition. Fig. 2
shows the SEM image and its corresponding EDS map for the
undoped (upper panel) and 30 mol% Cu-doped SnO2 (lower
panel). The SnO2 nanocrystals exhibit a curious morphological
characteristic, akin to dried sludge-like formations, which is
a result of the high-temperature production method. Mean-
while, or the 30 mol% Cu-doped a more porous structure is
observed, which could be correlated with the CuO structure. To
make an elemental characterization, a small and homoge-
neous structure was chosen from both samples (see dashed
lines in Fig. 2) and the EDS analysis was performed on it. For
the undoped SnO2, the EDS spectrum (see right-hand side of
Fig. 2) displays the characteristic X-ray peaks located at 0.52
keV and 3.4 keV, expected for the O Ka and Sn La, respectively.
No additional characteristic X-ray peaks are observed, con-
rming the single SnO2 crystalline phase observed by XRD.
However, for the Cu-doped samples, two additional X-ray
peaks are seen located at 0.93 and 8.04 keV; respectively
associated with the characteristic Cu La and Cu Ka x-rays. The
calculated Cu/(Cu + Sn) weight ratio collected in Table 1, was
obtained by deconvolution of the characteristic X-ray peaks,
performed in the internal EDS soware. The results are
consistent with the nominal increase of Cu-content used in the
Cu-doped nanocrystals synthesis.

In addition, TEM images were recorded and corroborated
with the crystallite size obtained from the XRD analyses.
Fig. 3(a) shows a representative high-resolution TEM (HRTEM)

a representative TEM image of the recorded micrographs used

5 Conclusions

In this study, we report on the plausible use of Cu-doped SnO2
nanoparticles to create self-cleaning surfaces. In this regard, we
have systematically studied the inuence of the Cu-dopant
within SnO2 nanoparticles (NPs). The synthesis process
involved the preparation of a polymer solution containing
precursors of both copper and tin ions (precursor polymeric
method), with the copper concentration varying from 0 to

30 mol%. X-ray diﬀraction (XRD) was performed to analyze the
crystal structure of the synthesized nanoparticles. It was found
that the lattice constants increased with increasing Cu content,
which is in good agreement with the diﬀerence in ionic radii
between Cu and Sn-ions. Fourier transform infrared measure-
ments showed vibrational modes (O–H, C–H, and C–O) at the
expected positions. However, a shi to higher values was
observed for the skeletal Sn–O band. This suggests a change in
the reduced mass associated with the entry of Cu-ions. Raman
measurements were performed on all samples to investigate any
changes in their vibration properties as the amount of Cu
content was increased. Furthermore, a signicant antibacterial
eﬀect over the CuO has been detected through a bioassay. The
disc-diﬀusion testing method (DDTM), performed with two
bacterial species (S. aureus and E. coli), was used to assess the
inhibition of bacteria growth. It was found that the DDTM data
scales with cell viability, the latter analyzed using the Hill
equation, from which both lethal dose 50 (LD50) and bench-
mark dose (BMD) were extracted. The ulterior functionalization
of this type of metal oxide powder can be used for self-cleaning
surfaces protocols.

bacterial eﬀect of TM-SnO2 nanoparticles.14 ROS have a strong
ability to oxidize a wide range of organic-based materials, such
as pollutants, bacteria, cancer cells, and viruses. When doped
oxide semiconductors are used as self-cleaning surfaces, the
ROS generated on the surface can cause oxidative stress in
bacterial cells, destroying cell walls, DNA, and relevant
proteins.6 The research of new materials with SCS activity is of
extreme importance, especially aer the COVID-2019 pandemic.
In this scenario, we can highlight the use of Cu-doped oxide
semiconductor with high antibacterial activity while it is irra-
diated with UV light.15 However, UV light is not feasible for
creating self-cleaning and antibacterial surfaces in typical
indoor conditions, with negligible UV light exposition. There-
fore, it is necessary to search for alternatives aiming at to
increase antimicrobial response in a dimly illuminated envi-
ronment. Also, no previous investigation has been carried out to
evaluate the inuence of doping enrichment of the surface and
the onset of a secondary phase on the antibacterial activity of
the system, indicating a knowledge gap.

In this study, we aim to investigate the synthesis and char-
acterization of Cu-doped SnO2 nanoparticles, with emphasis on
structural, morphological, and vibrational properties plus
antibacterial activity against Escherichia coli (ATCC® 33876) and
Staphylococcus aureus (ATCC® 25923) in a dark environment.
We also explore the possible mechanisms by which Cu-doping
contributes to enhance the antibacterial activity of the as-
synthesized SnO2 nanoparticles. Our ndings are expected to
contribute to the development of novel materials for self-
cleaning surfaces with high antibacterial activity.

3 Results and discussions

XRD patterns of undoped and Cu-doped SnO2 nanoparticles are
shown in Fig. 1(a). The main crystalline phase is linked with the
rutile tetragonal unit cell SnO2 phase, as indicated by the main
peaks found at 26.5°, 33.8°, 37.9° and 51.7° associated with the
(110), (101), (200) and (211) plane reections, respectively.
However, additional peaks at 35.5° and 38.7° were observed in
copper concentrations starting from 20%, which have been
respectively linked with the (111) and (022) planes of the
secondary CuO phase; the latter suggesting that the solution
limit is lower than 20 mol%, this being due to the detection
limit of the technique.

were analyzed using Rietveld renement
implemented in

describes the strain broadening. A typical t is shown in
Fig. 1(b), where the open black circles are the recorded experi-
mental data, the solid red line is the theoretical curve, and the
solid green line at the bottom is the diﬀerence between them.

In this study, we report on the plausible use of Cu-doped SnO2

have systematically studied the inuence of the Cu-dopant

method), with the copper concentration varying from 0 to

pandemic, and the use of nanoparticles has been shown as a plausible option for this purpose. In the

5 Conclusions

In this study, we report on the plausible use of Cu-doped SnO2
nanoparticles to create self-cleaning surfaces. In this regard, we
have systematically studied the inuence of the Cu-dopant
within SnO2 nanoparticles (NPs). The synthesis process
involved the preparation of a polymer solution containing
precursors of both copper and tin ions (precursor polymeric
method), with the copper concentration varying from 0 to

30 mol%. X-ray diﬀraction (XRD) was performed to analyze the
crystal structure of the synthesized nanoparticles. It was found
that the lattice constants increased with increasing Cu content,
which is in good agreement with the diﬀerence in ionic radii
between Cu and Sn-ions. Fourier transform infrared measure-
ments showed vibrational modes (O–H, C–H, and C–O) at the
expected positions. However, a shi to higher values was
observed for the skeletal Sn–O band. This suggests a change in
the reduced mass associated with the entry of Cu-ions. Raman
measurements were performed on all samples to investigate any
changes in their vibration properties as the amount of Cu
content was increased. Furthermore, a signicant antibacterial
eﬀect over the CuO has been detected through a bioassay. The
disc-diﬀusion testing method (DDTM), performed with two
bacterial species (S. aureus and E. coli), was used to assess the
inhibition of bacteria growth. It was found that the DDTM data
scales with cell viability, the latter analyzed using the Hill
equation, from which both lethal dose 50 (LD50) and bench-
mark dose (BMD) were extracted. The ulterior functionalization
of this type of metal oxide powder can be used for self-cleaning
surfaces protocols.

drying process, incorporating 10 wt. % HAp and 2 wt. % CGF as optimal additives. Comprehensive 
characterization, including XRD, FT-IR, TGA, SEM, and analysis of porosity, swelling, degradation, 
and biomineralization, confirmed the formation of a porous polymer matrix with favorable properties. 
The optimal PVA/CMC/HAp/CGF scaffold demonstrated compressive strength of 12 MPa, porosity 
of 72%, swelling of 1860%, and biodegradation of 43% over 21 days, while the PVA/Alg/HAp/CGF 
scaffold exhibited a compressive strength of 8.1 MPa and porosity of 79%. Both scaffolds showed good 
biomineralization in SBF and a favorable cell viability rate (OD) in MTT toxicity tests, with an OD of 
1.483 and 1.451 for PVA/CMC/HAp/CGF and PVA/Alg/HAp/CGF scaffolds, respectively. These findings 
suggest that the PVA/CMC/HAp/CGF nanocomposite scaffold is a promising candidate for bone tissue 
engineering applications. By adding hydroxyapatite and magnetic clay modified with graphene oxide 
to the polymer scaffold, the mechanical properties of the scaffold are increased, appropriate porosity 
and swelling values are obtained, and desirable cell viability is achieved.

Keywords  Magnetic nanoclay, Hydroxyapatite, Nanocomposite scaffold, Graphene oxide, Bone tissue 
engineering

Failure  of  tissues  and  organs  due  to  damage,  congenital  disabilities,  and  aging  is  becoming  the  main  issue 
of  human  body  health  all  over  the  world.  Bones  are  one  of  the  strongest  and  primary  tissues  of  the  body, 
maintaining  the  surrounding  soft  tissues1.  Regarding  synthetic  scaffolds  that  promote  bone  tissue  repair,  the 
dual role of bone tissue engineering (BTE) scaffolds in interacting with the extracellular matrix and providing 
load-bearing capacity is a challenge. This research aims to investigate the use and processing of several materials 
and  hierarchical  architectures  to  simulate  the  structure  of  natural  bone  tissues  so  that  they  may  function  as 
bioactive artificial scaffolds2. It is widely believed that designing and preparing new tissues is one of the most

effective and efficient ways that tissue engineering can accelerate bone regeneration during the healing process3. 
A new strategy for repairing bones has emerged that is based on tissue engineering. As a result of its use of 
biomaterial scaffolds along with cells and growth factors, it can induce the formation of new bone tissues while 
reducing the risks associated with autologous bone grafts4. Bone tissue is a composite of approximately 70% 
nano-hydroxyapatite and 30% collagen. Wet collagen and the accumulation of mineral crystals penetrate each 
other and form a mineral fiber on a scale of several hundred nanometers. The primary role of bone is to provide 
a  structural  framework  and  mechanical  strength,  regulate  blood  pH,  and  maintain  calcium  and  phosphate 
levels for metabolic processes5. It is desirable to design a biocompatible composite that can mimic the natural 
extracellular bone matrix and accelerate new bone regeneration6. If the dispersed phase used in the composite is 
nanoparticles, the composite material will be a nanocomposite. Natural bone is an example of a nanocomposite 
composed of two major phases, organic and inorganic, at the nanoscale7. Polymer-based nanocomposites are 
attractive  due  to  their  ability  to  create  porous  architectures  and  biodegradability.  The  ease  of  manipulating 
structures  with  precise  tuning  of  physicochemical  properties  is  an  advantage  of  polymer  nanocomposites 
for  tissue  engineering  applications  such  as  dental,  bone,  and  neural  engineering8.  Nanocomposites  made  of 
polymeric materials and additives are potential materials for constructing bone scaffolds9.

Polymers for making hydrogels include natural and synthetic polymers. Natural polymers are mainly natural 
components  that  prepare  scaffolds  with  high  biocompatibility,  biodegradability,  and  natural  cell  adhesion. 
Recently, synthetic polymers have been widely used to make bone tissue engineering scaffolds because they have 
high mechanical properties and long life. Carboxymethyl cellulose is a biocompatible and biodegradable anionic 
polymer that can create a strong ionic cross-link in the scaffold10 and increase the biochemical characteristics 
of porosity, swelling, and degradation. Cellulose is mainly used for various biomedical applications11. Among 
natural polysaccharides, alginate biopolymer is also widely used as a biomaterial for bone tissue engineering. 
Alginate is one of the most well-known substances, and it has the property of forming a suitable scaffold that can 
be useful for the treatment of organ failure and loss. Alginate consists of guluronic acid and mannuronic acid 
and is used in tissue engineering due to its biocompatibility, non-toxicity, abundance, and low price12. Alginate 
hydrogels can increase minimal protein absorption due to their hydrophilic property13. Sodium alginate is anionic 
and can be dissolved in water. Hydroxyl groups can cause strong interactions between sodium alginate and other 
polymers through hydrogen bonding14. Alginate benefits osteoblast growth due to its functional groups, such 
as hydroxyl and carboxyl, and increases the efficiency of implant substrates. Due to its high degradation rate in 
cell culture, its use in biomedical applications is limited. To improve alginate’s biocompatibility and mechanical 
properties, its combination with synthetic polymers and clay minerals was investigated15. Given the disadvantages 
of  natural  polymers,  such  as  poor  solubility  in  common  solvents,  their  low  mechanical  properties,  and  poor 
stability in physiological environments, There have been numerous studies conducted on the physicochemical 
properties of composite polymers, which have proven to be effective in overcoming the disadvantages of natural 
polymers16. Blending polymers is a potential method for improving mechanical flexibility17. Polyvinyl alcohol 
is a hydrophilic semi-crystalline synthetic biopolymer containing many hydroxyl groups, and it can also form 
hydrogen  bonds  with  free  water  molecules18.  Polyvinyl  alcohol  is  biocompatible  and  has  high  mechanical 
strength, low toxicity, large surface area, and good chemical stability; in a clinical setting, its use is possible to 
construct membranes, repair tissues, and construct biomaterials16. By synergistically combining the bioactive 
properties of nanoparticles and the properties of polymers, composite materials create scaffolds that provide an 
optimal environment for cell proliferation, differentiation, and cell adhesion19. Various natural and synthetic 
fillers  are  used  as  strengthening  agents  to  improve  polymer  scaffolds’  mechanical  properties  and  bioactivity. 
Clay is considered one of the mineral fillers that will enhance the biological and mechanical properties of the 
scaffold  significantly,  and  it  has  already  been  studied  in  bone  cement  processing20.  Clay  can  be  essential  in 
bone regeneration and repair, increasing osteoblast differentiation and apatite deposition20. Also, the graphene 
oxide filler is highly compatible with the polymer matrix due to the attendance of polar groups on the surface 
of  this  material. The  high  exceptional  area  ratio  and  antibacterial  properties  make  GO  a  promising  material 
for developing bone tissue’s antimicrobial and antiviral surface21. GO is exfoliated from graphite and contains 
epoxide, carboxylic, and carbonyl ketone groups in its structural plane. Graphene and graphene-based materials 
have been investigated in various fields, such as bioimaging, biosensors, cancer treatment, drug delivery, and 
tissue engineering. Unique properties such as thermal conductivity, mechanical strength, high surface area, ease 
of operation, flexibility, biocompatibility, and antibacterial activity make it suitable for biological applications. 
GO has osteoconductive and osteoinductive ability to regulate osteoblast differentiation22,23. Also, this substance 
can force stem cells to undergo osteogenic differentiation even without adding a growth factor24. Hydroxyapatite 
contains basic elements such as calcium and phosphate, essential for bone growth. HAp particles increase cell 
proliferation and adhesion and improve bone tissue conduction23. Hydroxyapatite has unique properties, such 
as excellent biocompatibility and low toxicity25. Combining ceramic filler and polymer matrix in one material 
produces  composites  with  polymer  plasticity  and  calcium  phosphate  bioactivity26.  Scaffolds  containing  HAp 
have stronger mechanical properties and higher cell proliferation than scaffolds containing TCP, which gives 
them a better function in bone regeneration in the early stages27. Nanoparticle content can be used to modify the 
properties of polymer nanocomposites28. Various magnetic nanoparticles have been developed recently for use 
in biological applications. Among these nanoparticles, iron oxide nanoparticles (Fe3O4) have biocompatibility 
and  good  performance  for  medical  applications.  Many  researchers  have  shown  that  the  magnetic  properties 
of Fe3O4 nanoparticles make it an ideal material for cell isolation and drug delivery, which also increases the 
effect of bone induction. Several studies have shown that integrating Fe3O4 nanoparticles with polymer fibers 
solves the compaction problem and improves their stability in biological applications29. The research fabricates 
nanocomposite  scaffolds  using  CMC,  Alg,  PVA,  magnetic  clay  nanoparticles  modified  with  graphene  oxide 
(CGF), and natural hydroxyapatite (HAp) to enhance mechanical properties. Characterization involved XRD, 
FT-IR, TGA, and SEM analyses, assessing porosity, swelling, degradation, and biomineralization, and the MTT

test  evaluated  cell  viability.  In  bone  tissue  research,  the  composites  studied  mainly  combine  a  natural  and 
synthetic polymer and an additive, each of which can only be used to improve one property. In this study, two 
biopolymers are compared in terms of the composition of scaffolds. Two additives are also used: HAp can be 
used to improve biomineralization, and CGF is a combination of several materials that can give many favorable 
properties to the polymer composite for use as a polymer scaffold.

Having  the  required  mechanical  properties  is  one  of  the  most  important  properties  that  bone  tissue 
replacement  scaffolds  must  possess.  In  addition  to  having  the  required  mechanical  properties,  the  scaffolds 
should possess other characteristics required by bone tissue, such as porosity, biocompatibility, swelling, and 
non-toxicity. A significant aspect of the research is that in addition to increasing compressive strength, attention 
has been paid to maintaining the required porosity of the bone tissue. A combination of graphene oxide, clay, 
hydroxyapatite, and the magnetic material Fe3O4 has been used in this research as a new material. As a result of 
the combination of graphene oxide with clay, the compressive strength of the scaffold was increased significantly, 
and the presence of HAp led to an increase in biomineralization of the scaffold, whereas Fe3O4 had a positive 
effect on the viability of the cells. The properties of natural bone differ significantly based on its type. For example, 
the compressive strength of cancellous bone ranges from 2 to 20 MPa. As a result, it is important to consider 
the scaffold’s mechanical properties when designing scaffolds for bone reconstruction and fracture healing to 
ensure a successful outcome30. It has been found that the scaffold that was prepared in this study has compressive 
strength within the acceptable range for cancellous bone. It is important to  emphasize that the porosity of a 
hydrogel is a significant factor that profoundly affects the fate of bone cells31. A series of interconnected pores 
in this hydrogel facilitate the migration of cells, the permeability of nutrients, the removal of waste materials, 
and the penetration of blood vessels and nerves32. The porosity of cancellous bone ranges from 30 to 70%33. The 
porosity of the scaffolds prepared for this study is within an appropriate range for cancellous bone scaffolds. 
The prepared scaffolds had appropriate degradation rates because replacing the manufactured tissue with the 
original tissue would have to occur within a proper biodegradation range. Also, they exhibited a high degree of 
cell viability.

Materials and methods
Materials
Sodium alginate (Na-Alg) polymer with a molecular weight of 12,000–40,000 Da from Sigma Aldrich, sodium 
carboxymethyl  cellulose  with  a  molecular  weight  of  70,000  g/mol  and  a  deacetylation  degree  of  90%  from 
Samchun, Korea, and polyvinyl alcohol with a molecular weight of 72,000 g/mol and a hydrolysis degree of 95% 
from  Merck  were  used  in  this  study.  Potassium  hydrogen  phosphate  (KH2PO4),  sodium  hydroxide  (NaOH), 
and  25%  glutaraldehyde  as  cross-linkers  were  obtained  from  Merck.  The  acids  used  in  this  study,  including 
hydrochloric  acid  (HCl)  37%,  phosphoric  acid  (H3PO4),  acetic  acid  (CH3COOH)  100%,  and  sulfuric  acid 
(H2SO4) 98%, were all obtained from Merck. Cloisite 30B clay was organically modified to be the clay used in 
the study, obtained from Southern Clay Company. K2HPO4.3H2O, KCl, NaCl, Na2SO4, MgCl2.6H2O, NaHCO3, 
CaCl2.2H2O, and TRIS salts prepared simulated body fluid purchased from Merck. Iron (II) chloride, Iron (III) 
chloride, KMnO4, and H2O2 were used to modify clay.

Synthesis of graphene oxide
To prepare graphene oxide using the modified Hummer method. First, 3 g of graphite powder was added to 
the H2SO4/H3PO4 mixture (40:360 ml), and then 18 g of KMnO4 was added and stirred at 50 °C for 14 h with 
100 rpm by a magnetic stirrer. The temperature of the resulting mixture was reduced to 25 °C, and then 30% 
H2O2 was added to it, making the mixture light brown and stirred for 20 min. A centrifuge was used to separate 
the mixture, and several washes were done with distilled water to reach a neutral pH. In a vacuum oven, 24 h of 
drying time was spent at 70 °C on the synthesized graphene oxide34. Graphene oxide was synthesized in black 
and in powder form.

Preparation of magnetically modified clay
To prepare magnetically modified clay, 1 g of synthesized graphene oxide (GO) was sonicated in 100 mL of water 
for 35 min, while 2 g of Cloisite 30B clay was sonicated in 100 mL of water for 20 min. A solution of iron(III) 
chloride and iron(II) chloride in a 1:2 molar ratio was then added to the GO-clay mixture, which was heated 
and stirred at 90 °C for 20 min. The resulting mixture was gradually combined with a 4 M sodium hydroxide 
solution and stirred for 50 min. Finally, the modified clay was separated from the solution, washed several times 
with distilled water, and baked at 105 °C for 4 h.

Preparation of natural hydroxyapatite (HAp) powder
The  chicken  femur  was  cleaned  entirely  of  meat  and  remaining  materials  to  prepare  natural  hydroxyapatite 
powder  and  then  boiled  for  45  min  in  boiling  water.  The  cleaned  bones  were  placed  in  a  furnace  for  3  h  at 
900 °C with a nitrogen atmosphere. After the set time, the bones are removed from the oven, cooled to room 
temperature,  and  then  powdered  once  they  are  at  room  temperature.  The  production  efficiency  of  natural 
hydroxyapatite powder is 58%, and the product is white35.

Preparation of nanocomposite scaffold
The  nanocomposite  scaffolds  were  prepared  using  natural  polymer  materials,  PVA,  hydroxyapatite  extracted 
from  natural  bone,  and  modified  clay  using  a  simple  mixing  method.  For  the  preparation  of  the  scaffold,  a 
solution of 2 wt. in the first step. % of a natural polymer in distilled water was prepared by dissolving the polymer 
in the water and stirring the solution until the polymer was fully dissolved. It was also possible to prepare a 
solution of polyvinyl alcohol by dissolving PVA in distilled water at a temperature of 70 °C to prepare a solution

and the mixer was turned on for 12 h. 0.5 v/v % of glutaraldehyde was added to the prepped solution in 5%

CGF is included. The particles were evenly dispersed in the solution after adding CGF and then subjected to 
ultrasonic treatment for two hours. The solution was transferred into a falcon tube and dried using a freeze-
dryer. After drying, the samples were washed with a 2 wt. % NaBH4 solution and a 2 wt. % NaOH solution to 
neutralize any unreacted glutaraldehyde and excess acetic acid. The samples were then dried once more. The

Characterization of scaffolds
Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) study
To examine the functional and chemical properties of HAp, Fe3O4, GO, clay, Cloisite 30B/GO/Fe3O4, Alg, CMC, 
PVA, and their interactions, we performed FTIR analysis on the prepared nanocomposite scaffolds. Infrared 
spectra of the samples, mixed with KBr powder, were recorded using a Bruker Tensor 27 spectrophotometer 
(Germany). This FTIR instrument offers a measurement resolution of 0.1 cm⁻1, and its readings are based on 
absorbance.

X-ray diffraction (XRD) study
XRD  analysis  evaluated  the  crystallinity  of  PVA,  CMC,  Alg,  HAp,  clay,  and  C30B/GO/Fe3O4  samples  and 
the  prepared  nanocomposite  scaffolds.  The  analysis  was  performed  using  a  Krisallofex  D500  diffractometer 
(Siemens, Germany), which employed Cu-Kα radiation at 25 mA, operating at 40 kV, and scanned over a range 
of 4–80°. The device had a scan step of 0.05° and a measurement accuracy of 0.04 deg/sec.

Morphology study of scaffold samples by SEM analysis
The  scaffolds  were  prepared  by  freeze-drying  and  then  coated  with  a  thin  layer  of  gold  after  being  cut  into 
thin sheets. Once the samples were positioned in the microscope, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images 
(MIRA3, TESCAN, Brno, Czech Republic) were used to examine the morphology of the scaffolds. Furthermore, 
the  presence  and  distribution  of  phosphorus  and  calcium  elements  within  the  nanocomposite  scaffold  were 
analyzed using energy-dispersive X-ray (EDX)  mapping. A voltage  of 30  kV was applied to the SEM device. 
Also, to image the amount of cell culture by SEM, uniform pieces of the scaffolds were cut and immersed in 70% 
ethanol solution for 30 min for sterilization. In the next step, the samples were washed three times with PBS to 
remove excess ethanol and then transferred to a 6-well cell culture plate. A cell plate with a density of 50,000 cells 
per cell plate was then used to culture the MSCs on scaffolds. As a final step, the samples were cultured in an 
FBS medium with 1% penicillin–streptomycin and 10% DMEM in an incubator for 72 h. They were incubated 
for 72 h at 37 °C. After this time, the supernatant of all the wells of the 6-well plate was removed, and after 
washing with PBS, they were fixed with 2.5% glutaraldehyde for 20 min. After removing the fixative solution,

Mechanical properties study
The  mechanical  properties  of  the  scaffold  samples  were  evaluated  by  measuring  the  compressive  strength 
prepared by freeze-drying. To assess the material’s compressive strength, cylinder samples measuring 12 mm in 
height and 6 mm in diameter were cut. During a compression test, a force with 0.5 mm per minute speed and 
power of 25 kN was used to test the material’s compressive strength at 25 °C. A universal machine model was 
used to carry out mechanical tests, Al-7000-Taiwand. Three samples of each scaffold were prepared to perform 
the compressive strength test, and all three samples were tested. Their average compressive strength was reported 
as the compressive strength of the polymer scaffold. The error value was 0.1 MPa.

Measuring the porosity of scaffolds
Using the liquid displacement method, we could determine the porosity of scaffolds36. Scaffolds were cut into 
one cubic cm square piece. A displacement liquid was employed in this case, and it was ethanol because it does 
not dissolve the scaffolds while it is being used. To determine the porosity of the cut scaffolds, the scaffolds were 
placed in a graduated container containing ethanol with volume (V1) to measure the porosity. Using the total 
volume of ethanol and scaffold (V2), we calculated the volume difference V2-V1. After exiting the scaffold from 
the cylinder containing ethanol, the remaining volume of the ethanol in the cylinder was measured by using

Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) study
The  thermal  stability  of  the  polymer  raw  materials  and  nanocomposite  scaffolds  was  assessed  using  TGA.  A 
thermogravimetric  analyzer  (TGA-PL,  TGA  1500,  Canada)  was  employed  for  this  analysis,  conducted  in  a 
nitrogen atmosphere within the 25–600°C temperature range.

Investigation of scaffold biomineralization using simulated body fluid (SBF)
The performance of the scaffold bone graft was assessed using simulated body fluid (SBF), which was prepared 
following  established  protocols  with  chemical  reagents.  SBF  is  essential  for  examining  the  formation  of 
biomaterials on polymer scaffolds. To prepare the solution, 1000 mL of SBF was made by adding 700 mL of 
deionized water into a plastic container in a water bath. It is recommended to cover the container with either 
a glass or plastic lid while stirring; for the process to be successful, the solution should be kept at a consistent 
temperature of 36.5 °C throughout. Adding the ingredients in order is essential; once each ingredient is dissolved 
completely, the next one should be added, and so on. As soon as the ingredients were added, hydrochloric acid 
was used in the amount of 0–5 ml with an additive solution to achieve a pH of 7.4 in the resulting solution after 
adding the ingredients. A total of 1000 mL of solution was prepared by adding water to a flask and shaking it 
at 20 °C to reach the desired volume. The solution was then transferred to a polyethylene container and stored 
in a refrigerator at 5–10 °C. Scaffold samples were immersed in the SBF solution and incubated at 37 °C for 14 
days. After incubation, the samples were removed, rinsed with distilled water, and dried using the freeze-drying 
method. Finally, EDX and SEM techniques were employed to evaluate the biomineralization capability of the 
scaffold samples38.

Assessment of toxicity and cell viability
First, uniform pieces of scaffolds were cut and immersed in 70% ethanol solution for 30 min to sterilize them. 
Eventually, we must continue using PBS to remove any remaining ethanol from the system and transfer it to a 
96-well cell culture plate. Then, mesenchymal stem cells were cultured on the scaffolds with a cell density of 1 × 
104 cells per cell plate. After collecting the samples, they were cultured inside the incubator in a DMEM medium

characterization, including XRD, FT-IR, TGA, SEM, and analysis of porosity, swelling, degradation, 
and biomineralization, confirmed the formation of a porous polymer matrix with favorable properties. 
The optimal PVA/CMC/HAp/CGF scaffold demonstrated compressive strength of 12 MPa, porosity 
of 72%, swelling of 1860%, and biodegradation of 43% over 21 days, while the PVA/Alg/HAp/CGF 
scaffold exhibited a compressive strength of 8.1 MPa and porosity of 79%. Both scaffolds showed good 
biomineralization in SBF and a favorable cell viability rate (OD) in MTT toxicity tests, with an OD of 
1.483 and 1.451 for PVA/CMC/HAp/CGF and PVA/Alg/HAp/CGF scaffolds, respectively. These findings 
suggest that the PVA/CMC/HAp/CGF nanocomposite scaffold is a promising candidate for bone tissue 
engineering applications. By adding hydroxyapatite and magnetic clay modified with graphene oxide 
to the polymer scaffold, the mechanical properties of the scaffold are increased, appropriate porosity 
and swelling values are obtained, and desirable cell viability is achieved.

Keywords  Magnetic nanoclay, Hydroxyapatite, Nanocomposite scaffold, Graphene oxide, Bone tissue 
engineering

Failure  of  tissues  and  organs  due  to  damage,  congenital  disabilities,  and  aging  is  becoming  the  main  issue 
of  human  body  health  all  over  the  world.  Bones  are  one  of  the  strongest  and  primary  tissues  of  the  body, 
maintaining  the  surrounding  soft  tissues1.  Regarding  synthetic  scaffolds  that  promote  bone  tissue  repair,  the 
dual role of bone tissue engineering (BTE) scaffolds in interacting with the extracellular matrix and providing 
load-bearing capacity is a challenge. This research aims to investigate the use and processing of several materials 
and  hierarchical  architectures  to  simulate  the  structure  of  natural  bone  tissues  so  that  they  may  function  as 
bioactive artificial scaffolds2. It is widely believed that designing and preparing new tissues is one of the most
