Traditional therapies such as chemotherapy, radiation, and surgery have limitations, including systemic toxicity, drug resistance, and incomplete eradication of cancer cells. In recent years, immunotherapy has emerged as a transformative approach, harnessing the body's immune system to target and destroy cancer cells. However, the efficacy of immunotherapy is often hindered by factors within and beyond the TME, such as immunosuppressive conditions, hypoxia, and physical barriers like collagen deposition [ 1 ]. To address these challenges, innovative strategies such as nanoparticle-mediated drug delivery, combination therapies, and personalized medicine are being developed to enhance the precision and effectiveness of cancer therapy. Nanoparticle-based approaches have revolutionized cancer therapy by enabling targeted delivery of therapeutic agents, reducing systemic toxicity, and improving drug bioavailability. These nanocarriers can be engineered to respond to specific stimuli within the TME, such as acidic pH, hypoxia, or overexpressed enzymes, ensuring controlled release of drugs at the tumor site [ 2 ]. For instance, pH-responsive nanoparticles have been designed to release their payload in the acidic TME. At the same time, hypoxia-responsive systems activate under low oxygen conditions to enhance the efficacy of chemotherapy and radiotherapy [ 3 ]. Additionally, enzyme-responsive nanoparticles exploit the overexpression of enzymes like matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) to achieve site-specific drug release [ 4 ]. Combination therapies, which integrate multiple treatment modalities, have demonstrated great promise in overcoming the limitations of single-agent therapies. By combining immunotherapy with chemotherapy, photothermal therapy, or targeted drug delivery, researchers can simultaneously target multiple pathways involved in tumor growth and resistance. For example, integrating photothermal therapy and immunotherapy using iron oxide nanoplatforms has demonstrated remarkable efficacy in pancreatic cancer treatment [ 5 ]. Similarly, multifunctional nanocarriers that deliver chemotherapeutic agents and immunomodulators can enhance anti-tumor immune responses and improve therapeutic outcomes [ 6 ]. Personalized medicine represents a critical advancement in cancer therapy, leveraging patient-specific biomarkers and genetic profiles to tailor treatments. Machine learning models and quantitative histopathological analyses are being utilized to predict the efficacy of immunotherapies and identify patients who are most likely to benefit from specific treatments [ 7 ]. For instance, mitophagy-related gene signatures in rectal cancer and intestinal subtypes of gastric adenocarcinoma have been identified as predictive biomarkers for immunotherapy response [ 8 ]. These advancements improve treatment efficacy and minimize unnecessary side effects, thus enhancing the overall patients’ quality of life. Despite these advancements, challenges remain in optimizing nanoparticle-mediated therapies and overcoming biological barriers within the TME. The dense extracellular matrix (ECM), interstitial fluid pressure, and immunosuppressive conditions can impede drug delivery and limit therapeutic efficacy [ 9 ]. Therefore, to address these challenges, researchers are developing multifunctional nanoplatforms that combine TME-responsive properties with strategies to enhance drug penetration and modulate the immune response. For example, size-shrinkable nanoparticles that exploit the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect have been designed to penetrate dense tumor tissues. In contrast, iron oxide nanoparticles have been used to repolarize tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) from a pro-tumor to an anti-tumor phenotype [ 10 ]. This review focuses on the latest developments in stimuli-responsive nanocarriers (e.g., pH-, redox-, and enzyme-sensitive systems) for tumor-specific drug delivery, emphasizing strategies to overcome biological barriers, including (1) the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect—its role in passive targeting and limitations in heterogeneous tumors, (2) active targeting strategies using ligand-functionalized nanoparticles, and (3) externally triggered systems such as light-, magnetic-, and ultrasound-responsive nanocarriers.

This point emphasizes the importance of selective cell targeting for effective immune modulation. Meanwhile, natural cellular carriers present a strategy for enhanced delivery precision, particularly in challenging environments like glioblastoma [ 40 ]. Beyond natural shuttles, synthetic nanocarriers are engineered with tailored targeting capabilities to refine drug delivery. It has been suggested that dendrimers can target suppressor cells produced from monocytic myeloids systemically, providing further information on their biodistribution and possibilities for treatment [ 41 ]. Beyond the EPR effect, tumor cell-derived small extracellular vesicles can present a significant barrier to effective therapeutic nanoparticle delivery. This highlights the critical need for strategies that mitigate sEV interference to improve nanoparticle-based tumor therapies [ 78 ]. In parallel, biomimetic approaches are advancing, exemplified by cancer cell membrane-liposome hybrid nanoparticles that enhance tumor accumulation and therapeutic efficacy through tumor microenvironment-activated charge reversal and controlled drug release, demonstrating the potential of leveraging natural cell membrane properties [ 79 ]. Strategies to remodel the immunosuppressive TME are particularly promising, as evidenced by paclitaxel-loaded ginsenoside Rg3 liposomes that simultaneously target tumor cells and remodel the TME, improving antitumor efficacy through macrophage repolarization [ 80 ]. Similarly, TME-responsive nanocapsules delivering CRISPR/Cas9 effectively inhibit hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) progression and promote immunotherapy [ 81 ], while folate-modified nanocarriers co-delivering IL-12 gene and PD-L1 inhibitors enhance ovarian cancer immunotherapy [ 82 ]. In addition, targeting specific TME components, such as cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), offers another avenue, with CAF-specific nanoparticles transforming CAFs into drug-delivery reservoirs in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma [ 83 ]. Targeting strategies for enhanced nanoparticle delivery Achieving effective therapeutic outcomes with nanoparticles in cancer therapy hinges critically on their ability to preferentially accumulate at the tumor site and gain entry into target cells while minimizing exposure to healthy tissues. This challenge has spurred the development of sophisticated targeting strategies, broadly categorized into passive, active, and stimuli-responsive approaches. Each strategy leverages distinct biological or physicochemical principles to guide nanoparticles toward their intended destination, thereby enhancing therapeutic efficacy and mitigating off-target toxicity. Passive targeting The most fundamental targeting strategy, passive targeting, capitalizes on the unique pathophysiology of the tumor microenvironment. Rapidly growing tumors often exhibit aberrant angiogenesis, resulting in a chaotic and “leaky” vasculature with gaps typically ranging from tens to hundreds of nanometers [ 92 ]. Simultaneously, these tumors frequently have compromised lymphatic drainage. This combination allows nanoparticles of an appropriate size (generally 20–200 nm) to readily extravasate from the bloodstream into the tumor interstitium and become trapped, a phenomenon known as the Enhanced Permeability and Retention (EPR) effect [ 93 ]. The EPR effect provides a foundational mechanism for nanoparticle accumulation, particularly for solid tumors, and has been a cornerstone in the design of many clinically approved nanomedicines. While straightforward, the extent of the EPR effect can vary significantly between different tumor types and even within different regions of the same tumor, influenced by factors like tumor size, location, and stromal density [ 94 ]. Active targeting To overcome the limitations of passive targeting and achieve greater specificity, active targeting strategies employ ligands conjugated to the nanoparticle surface. These ligands are designed to bind specifically to receptors or antigens that are overexpressed on the surface of cancer cells, tumor vasculature, or other components of the tumor microenvironment [ 95 ]. Common ligands include antibodies or antibody fragments, peptides, aptamers, small molecules (e.g., folate, transferrin), and carbohydrates. Upon binding to their cognate receptors, actively targeted nanoparticles can exhibit enhanced cellular uptake via receptor-mediated endocytosis, leading to higher intracellular drug concentrations [ 96 ]. This approach aims to increase the tumor-to-normal tissue ratio of the therapeutic agent, potentially improving efficacy and reducing systemic side effects. The success of active targeting relies heavily on the careful selection of appropriate targets and ligands, ensuring high specificity and affinity while avoiding rapid clearance by the immune system or non-target tissues [ 97 ]. Stimuli-responsive targeting An increasingly sophisticated approach involves designing nanoparticles that respond to specific stimuli within the TME or external cues. This stimuli-responsive, or"smart,"targeting allows for controlled activation, accumulation, or drug release precisely at the disease site. TME-responsive nanoparticles can be designed to react to local changes in pH (e.g., acidic TME), enzyme activity (e.g., overexpression of matrix metalloproteinases), redox potential (e.g., higher glutathione levels), or hypoxia [ 98 ]. For example, pH-sensitive nanoparticles might undergo a conformational change or disassemble in the acidic TME, triggering drug release or enhancing cellular uptake [ 99 ]. External stimuli, such as light, heat, or magnetic fields, can also be utilized to remotely trigger nanoparticle activation or drug release at the tumor site, offering precise temporal and spatial control [ 100 ] This dynamic targeting strategy adds another layer of specificity, potentially overcoming biological barriers and ensuring that the therapeutic payload is delivered and released most effectively within the harsh and heterogeneous tumor environment [ 101 ]. Combining stimuli-responsive features with passive or active targeting strategies represents a powerful avenue for developing next-generation precision nanomedicines. Influence of nanoparticle physicochemical properties on therapeutic efficacy Designing effective nanoparticles for cancer therapy is a complex undertaking. There is a critical interplay between the physicochemical properties of these tiny carriers and their ultimate therapeutic success [ 102 ]. Factors like particle size, shape, surface charge, and overall surface chemistry (including hydrophilicity) are not merely technical specifications; these factors are fundamental determinants of how nanoparticles interact with the biological environment, where they ultimately end up (biodistribution), how effectively they accumulate in tumors, their ability to enter cancer cells, and the rate at which they release their therapeutic cargo. Ultimately, mastering these properties is key to unlock enhanced therapeutic outcomes [ 103 ]. These characteristics influence how the body processes the nanoparticles (pharmacokinetics) [ 104 ] as well as how the nanoparticles navigate the tumor's complex microenvironment to ensure that the therapeutic payload reaches its target effectively. The criticality of particle size When considering nanoparticle behavior in vivo, particle size is an important property. For strategies relying on passive accumulation in tumors via the well-known Enhanced Permeability and Retention (EPR) effect, there is generally an optimal particle size with nanoparticles typically ranging from 20 to 200 nm being favored. This specific size range facilitates extravasation through the unusually leaky blood vessels characteristic of tumors and enhances retention within the tumor interstitium due to often-impaired lymphatic drainage in these tissues [ 105 ]. Larger or overly rigid nanoparticles can have difficulty navigating and penetrating dense extracellular matrix that often surrounds tumor cells. To address this barrier, innovative strategies, such as the development of size-shrinkable nanoparticles, are being investigated to improve distribution deep within the tumor mass [ 106 ]. Beyond tumor targeting, size also impacts interactions with the immune system and the reticuloendothelial system (RES). In general, nanoparticles smaller than 10 nm tend to be cleared rapidly by the kidneys, while larger particles can be more susceptible to uptake by macrophages, unless their surfaces are modified. Of note, dynamic size changes are also being examined; size-switchable systems, such as certain PAMAM dendrimers engineered for deep tumor co-delivery, illustrate how precisely controlling size transitions can dramatically enhance therapeutic efficacy [ 107 ,  108 ]. The subtle influence of particle shape Beyond size, particle shape is another layer of complexity that dictates biodistribution and cellular interactions. While the familiar sphere remains a common form factor for many nanocarriers (e.g. liposomes), a growing body of research has begun to examine the potential of anisotropic shapes – rods, cubes, disks, and so forth. These varied geometries can influence how nanoparticles flow within blood vessels (margination), the specific mechanisms by which cells internalize them, and even their navigation through tissues. Different cell types may exhibit preferences for particles of particular shapes. The very concept of"morphological transformations of nanocarriers"being capable of boosting tumor retention [ 109 ] strongly underscores the significant impact that shape, even dynamic changes in shape in situ, can have. Moreover, biomimetic approaches that leverage the shapes of natural cells, such as platelet-mimicking nanoparticles, offer exciting possibilities to influence both targeted delivery and evasion of immune surveillance [ 110 ]. These innovative designs represent a compelling avenue to optimize therapeutic delivery while simultaneously minimizing unwanted immune recognition and clearance, thereby directly contributing to improved treatment outcomes in the landscape of cancer therapy [ 111 ]. The pivotal role of surface charge Surface charge is another critical determinant of nanoparticle behavior, impacting stability in physiological fluids, tendency to adsorb proteins (a process known as opsonization), and interactions with cell membranes [ 112 ]. Cell membranes are inherently negatively charged, meaning highly positive nanoparticle surfaces can engage in strong electrostatic interactions, potentially boosting cellular uptake [ 12 ]. This positive charge often, however, comes at a cost frequently leading to rapid adsorption of serum proteins, swift clearance by the RES, and increased non-specific toxicity. Conversely, negatively charged or neutral nanoparticles typically exhibit longer circulation half-lives due to reduced protein binding and lower RES uptake but may have lower cellular internalization efficiency. This dilemma represents a challenge, which has been addressed with promising strategies utilizing stimuli-responsive systems, such as pH-responsive charge-reversal nanoparticles [ 113 ]. These smart systems are engineered to maintain a neutral or slightly negative charge while circulating in the bloodstream – a"stealthy"state that prolongs their journey and minimizes unwanted interactions. However, upon encountering the acidic environment characteristic of the tumor microenvironment, the particles undergo a pivotal charge transition, becoming positive. This localized positive charge can enhance their uptake by tumor cells and facilitate intracellular drug delivery precisely where needed [ 114 ]. The art of hydrophilicity and surface chemistry The delicate balance of surface chemistry and the degree of hydrophilicity or hydrophobicity are can dictate nanoparticle"stealth"properties including how long the particles circulate in the bloodstream, as well as their complex interactions with biological different components [ 115 ]. Modifying the nanoparticle surface with hydrophilic polymers, most notably through the widely adopted strategy of PEGylation, is a classic technique to impart stealth. PEGylation effectively reduces the adsorption of serum proteins (opsonization) and subsequently minimizes non-specific cellular uptake by phagocytic cells, thus extending circulation time and increasing tumor accumulation via the EPR effect [ 116 ]. Surfaces designed with inherent antifouling properties, as discussed with certain dendrimer-CuS nanohybrids, are crucial to prevent unwanted non-specific binding. Furthermore, cutting-edge biomimetic surface modifications, which involve coating nanoparticles with membranes derived from natural cells like cancer cells or immune cells, offer a sophisticated approach. These coatings impart surface properties that can facilitate evasion of the immune system, promote targeted delivery through mimicking cellular interactions, and enhance beneficial interactions with the tumor microenvironment itself [ 117 ]. The intricate interplay between surface chemistry and overall hydrophilicity serves not only as a means to evade the immune system; it is also critical to achieve stable encapsulation of therapeutic cargos and control the release kinetics. By strategically engineering these critical physicochemical properties – from the subtle influence of size and shape to the dramatic impact of surface charge and chemistry – researchers may be able to overcome the biological barriers to enhance the efficacy of nanoparticles. Future design process should seek to enable tailored delivery to the tumor site, facilitate efficient cellular internalization, and ensure the controlled release of therapeutic payloads, collectively elevating both the efficacy and safety profiles of next-generation cancer immunotherapy and targeted drug delivery strategies. Moreover, cisplatin-loaded mesoporous polydopamine nanoparticles provide synergistic antitumor therapy [ 124 ], and enzyme-responsive nano-drug delivery systems enhance tumor targeting [ 125 ]. Current status and challenges in clinical translation Nanomedicine represents a novel approach in cancer treatment; in turn, an up-to-date review of the current status and inherent clinical translation challenges associated with nanomedicine is important. Nanoparticle-based drug delivery systems, with their capacity for precise targeting and controlled release, offer the potential to enhance therapeutic efficacy while mitigating systemic toxicity [ 142 ]. Indeed, several nanomedicine formulations, such as liposomal doxorubicin and albumin nanoparticles have already had clinical success, demonstrating improved outcomes across various cancer types and underscoring the promise of nanomedicine to enhance cancer treatment effectiveness [ 143 ]. Moreover, the breadth of ongoing clinical trials including nanomedicine, spanning from lung cancer to advanced theranostics [ 144 – 146 ], signals an emerging field that has the potential to be realized in a clinical setting to improve patient outcomes. Nevertheless, the path from preclinical promise to widespread clinical application is often complex. One significant hurdle lies in scaling nanomedicine production to meet clinical demands while ensuring consistent quality and batch-to-batch reproducibility [ 147 ] – a critical factor. Furthermore, the regulatory landscape related to nanomedicines can be complicated, requiring careful consideration of their unique properties and potential long-term effects. Long-term safety and immunogenicity are critical concerns, demanding rigorous and extensive clinical investigations. The cost-effectiveness of nanomedicine formulations is also important to guarantee accessibility to a broad spectrum of patients [ 148 ], a factor that influences both development and adoption. Beyond these manufacturing and regulatory considerations, the TME itself presents formidable biological barriers. The TME's inherent heterogeneity, often characterized by a dense extracellular matrix and immunosuppressive conditions, can impede nanomedicine delivery and, consequently, limit therapeutic efficacy [ 149 ]. To navigate these challenges, researchers have developed strategies including TME-responsive nanocarriers, biomimetic platforms that mimic biological systems, and personalized approaches tailored to individual patient profiles [ 150 ]. For example, there has been emerging interest in the ability of nanomedicine to modulate the immune response, repolarize tumor-associated macrophages, and deliver immunotherapeutic agents directly to the tumor site [ 151 ]. Despite the challenges, nanomedicine research and development holds hope for a compelling future of cancer therapy. Continued innovations in material science, nanotechnology, and molecular biology are steadily paving the way for more effective, safer, and highly personalized nanomedicine interventions. There is an increasing recognition that integrating nanomedicine with immunotherapy may be key to address the complexities of the tumor microenvironment and maximize therapeutic effectiveness [ 152 ].

Influence of nanoparticle physicochemical properties on therapeutic efficacy Designing effective nanoparticles for cancer therapy is a complex undertaking. There is a critical interplay between the physicochemical properties of these tiny carriers and their ultimate therapeutic success [ 102 ]. Factors like particle size, shape, surface charge, and overall surface chemistry (including hydrophilicity) are not merely technical specifications; these factors are fundamental determinants of how nanoparticles interact with the biological environment, where they ultimately end up (biodistribution), how effectively they accumulate in tumors, their ability to enter cancer cells, and the rate at which they release their therapeutic cargo. Ultimately, mastering these properties is key to unlock enhanced therapeutic outcomes [ 103 ]. These characteristics influence how the body processes the nanoparticles (pharmacokinetics) [ 104 ] as well as how the nanoparticles navigate the tumor's complex microenvironment to ensure that the therapeutic payload reaches its target effectively. The criticality of particle size When considering nanoparticle behavior in vivo, particle size is an important property. For strategies relying on passive accumulation in tumors via the well-known Enhanced Permeability and Retention (EPR) effect, there is generally an optimal particle size with nanoparticles typically ranging from 20 to 200 nm being favored. This specific size range facilitates extravasation through the unusually leaky blood vessels characteristic of tumors and enhances retention within the tumor interstitium due to often-impaired lymphatic drainage in these tissues [ 105 ]. Larger or overly rigid nanoparticles can have difficulty navigating and penetrating dense extracellular matrix that often surrounds tumor cells. To address this barrier, innovative strategies, such as the development of size-shrinkable nanoparticles, are being investigated to improve distribution deep within the tumor mass [ 106 ]. Beyond tumor targeting, size also impacts interactions with the immune system and the reticuloendothelial system (RES). In general, nanoparticles smaller than 10 nm tend to be cleared rapidly by the kidneys, while larger particles can be more susceptible to uptake by macrophages, unless their surfaces are modified. Of note, dynamic size changes are also being examined; size-switchable systems, such as certain PAMAM dendrimers engineered for deep tumor co-delivery, illustrate how precisely controlling size transitions can dramatically enhance therapeutic efficacy [ 107 ,  108 ]. The subtle influence of particle shape Beyond size, particle shape is another layer of complexity that dictates biodistribution and cellular interactions. While the familiar sphere remains a common form factor for many nanocarriers (e.g. liposomes), a growing body of research has begun to examine the potential of anisotropic shapes – rods, cubes, disks, and so forth. These varied geometries can influence how nanoparticles flow within blood vessels (margination), the specific mechanisms by which cells internalize them, and even their navigation through tissues. Different cell types may exhibit preferences for particles of particular shapes. The very concept of"morphological transformations of nanocarriers"being capable of boosting tumor retention [ 109 ] strongly underscores the significant impact that shape, even dynamic changes in shape in situ, can have. Moreover, biomimetic approaches that leverage the shapes of natural cells, such as platelet-mimicking nanoparticles, offer exciting possibilities to influence both targeted delivery and evasion of immune surveillance [ 110 ]. These innovative designs represent a compelling avenue to optimize therapeutic delivery while simultaneously minimizing unwanted immune recognition and clearance, thereby directly contributing to improved treatment outcomes in the landscape of cancer therapy [ 111 ]. The pivotal role of surface charge Surface charge is another critical determinant of nanoparticle behavior, impacting stability in physiological fluids, tendency to adsorb proteins (a process known as opsonization), and interactions with cell membranes [ 112 ]. Cell membranes are inherently negatively charged, meaning highly positive nanoparticle surfaces can engage in strong electrostatic interactions, potentially boosting cellular uptake [ 12 ]. This positive charge often, however, comes at a cost frequently leading to rapid adsorption of serum proteins, swift clearance by the RES, and increased non-specific toxicity. Conversely, negatively charged or neutral nanoparticles typically exhibit longer circulation half-lives due to reduced protein binding and lower RES uptake but may have lower cellular internalization efficiency. This dilemma represents a challenge, which has been addressed with promising strategies utilizing stimuli-responsive systems, such as pH-responsive charge-reversal nanoparticles [ 113 ]. These smart systems are engineered to maintain a neutral or slightly negative charge while circulating in the bloodstream – a"stealthy"state that prolongs their journey and minimizes unwanted interactions. However, upon encountering the acidic environment characteristic of the tumor microenvironment, the particles undergo a pivotal charge transition, becoming positive. This localized positive charge can enhance their uptake by tumor cells and facilitate intracellular drug delivery precisely where needed [ 114 ]. The art of hydrophilicity and surface chemistry The delicate balance of surface chemistry and the degree of hydrophilicity or hydrophobicity are can dictate nanoparticle"stealth"properties including how long the particles circulate in the bloodstream, as well as their complex interactions with biological different components [ 115 ]. Modifying the nanoparticle surface with hydrophilic polymers, most notably through the widely adopted strategy of PEGylation, is a classic technique to impart stealth. PEGylation effectively reduces the adsorption of serum proteins (opsonization) and subsequently minimizes non-specific cellular uptake by phagocytic cells, thus extending circulation time and increasing tumor accumulation via the EPR effect [ 116 ]. Surfaces designed with inherent antifouling properties, as discussed with certain dendrimer-CuS nanohybrids, are crucial to prevent unwanted non-specific binding. Furthermore, cutting-edge biomimetic surface modifications, which involve coating nanoparticles with membranes derived from natural cells like cancer cells or immune cells, offer a sophisticated approach. These coatings impart surface properties that can facilitate evasion of the immune system, promote targeted delivery through mimicking cellular interactions, and enhance beneficial interactions with the tumor microenvironment itself [ 117 ]. The intricate interplay between surface chemistry and overall hydrophilicity serves not only as a means to evade the immune system; it is also critical to achieve stable encapsulation of therapeutic cargos and control the release kinetics. By strategically engineering these critical physicochemical properties – from the subtle influence of size and shape to the dramatic impact of surface charge and chemistry – researchers may be able to overcome the biological barriers to enhance the efficacy of nanoparticles. Future design process should seek to enable tailored delivery to the tumor site, facilitate efficient cellular internalization, and ensure the controlled release of therapeutic payloads, collectively elevating both the efficacy and safety profiles of next-generation cancer immunotherapy and targeted drug delivery strategies.

Advancements in nanotherapeutic strategies Nanotherapeutic strategies are evolving rapidly, with significant advancements in nano-immunotherapy and vaccine development. Intrapleural nano-immunotherapy with liposomal nanoparticles enhances anti-PD-L1 therapy for malignant pleural effusion [ 118 ], while nanoparticle vaccines co-deliver peptide neoantigens and adjuvants, enhancing T cell responses and improving immune checkpoint blockade efficacy [ 119 ] (Fig.  3 ). Additionally, sono-immunotherapy-mediated controllable composite nanofluorescent probes reprogram the immune microenvironment [ 120 ] and ultrasound-responsive nanocarriers reprogram macrophages for enhanced NSCLC immunotherapy [ 121 ]. Combination therapies and enhanced drug delivery are also key areas of progress. For example, dual-targeted, multi-responsive nanoplatforms overcome drug resistance in glioblastoma [ 122 ], while the combination of GRP78-targeted and non-targeted nanoparticles enhances ovarian cancer treatment [ 123 ]. Moreover, cisplatin-loaded mesoporous polydopamine nanoparticles provide synergistic antitumor therapy [ 124 ], and enzyme-responsive nano-drug delivery systems enhance tumor targeting [ 125 ]. These approaches highlight the potential of biomimetic nanotechnology to leverage natural cell membrane properties for improved drug delivery and immune modulation.

Current status and challenges in clinical translation Nanomedicine represents a novel approach in cancer treatment; in turn, an up-to-date review of the current status and inherent clinical translation challenges associated with nanomedicine is important. Nanoparticle-based drug delivery systems, with their capacity for precise targeting and controlled release, offer the potential to enhance therapeutic efficacy while mitigating systemic toxicity [ 142 ]. Indeed, several nanomedicine formulations, such as liposomal doxorubicin and albumin nanoparticles have already had clinical success, demonstrating improved outcomes across various cancer types and underscoring the promise of nanomedicine to enhance cancer treatment effectiveness [ 143 ]. Moreover, the breadth of ongoing clinical trials including nanomedicine, spanning from lung cancer to advanced theranostics [ 144 – 146 ], signals an emerging field that has the potential to be realized in a clinical setting to improve patient outcomes. Nevertheless, the path from preclinical promise to widespread clinical application is often complex. One significant hurdle lies in scaling nanomedicine production to meet clinical demands while ensuring consistent quality and batch-to-batch reproducibility [ 147 ] – a critical factor. Furthermore, the regulatory landscape related to nanomedicines can be complicated, requiring careful consideration of their unique properties and potential long-term effects. Long-term safety and immunogenicity are critical concerns, demanding rigorous and extensive clinical investigations. The cost-effectiveness of nanomedicine formulations is also important to guarantee accessibility to a broad spectrum of patients [ 148 ], a factor that influences both development and adoption. Beyond these manufacturing and regulatory considerations, the TME itself presents formidable biological barriers. The TME's inherent heterogeneity, often characterized by a dense extracellular matrix and immunosuppressive conditions, can impede nanomedicine delivery and, consequently, limit therapeutic efficacy [ 149 ]. To navigate these challenges, researchers have developed strategies including TME-responsive nanocarriers, biomimetic platforms that mimic biological systems, and personalized approaches tailored to individual patient profiles [ 150 ]. For example, there has been emerging interest in the ability of nanomedicine to modulate the immune response, repolarize tumor-associated macrophages, and deliver immunotherapeutic agents directly to the tumor site [ 151 ]. Despite the challenges, nanomedicine research and development holds hope for a compelling future of cancer therapy. Continued innovations in material science, nanotechnology, and molecular biology are steadily paving the way for more effective, safer, and highly personalized nanomedicine interventions. There is an increasing recognition that integrating nanomedicine with immunotherapy may be key to address the complexities of the tumor microenvironment and maximize therapeutic effectiveness [ 152 ].

Synergistic modalities and combination therapies Combining diverse therapeutic modalities is a cornerstone of enhanced cancer treatment, offering synergistic effects by merging physical and immunological strategies. For example, integrating photothermal therapy and immunotherapy, facilitated by an iron oxide nanoplatform, has shown remarkable promise in pancreatic cancer treatment, underscoring the power of such combined approaches [ 153 ]. This section explores various synergistic approaches, including multifunctional nanocarriers, stimuli-responsive systems, TME-targeted therapies, and novel combination strategies. Multifunctional nanocarriers for combination therapy Multifunctional nanocarriers amplify therapeutic impact by simultaneously delivering multiple agents. Notable examples include self-assembled drug-loaded glycosyl-protein metal nanoconstructs for solid tumors [ 154 ] and artemisinin-manganese oxide co-delivery systems for precise breast cancer diagnosis and treatment [ 155 ]. The synergy between nanocarriers and biological agents enhances chemotherapy efficacy, as demonstrated by oral bioactive chitosan-decorated doxorubicin nanoparticles/bacteria bioconjugates in an in-situ breast cancer model [ 156 ]. Polymeric PLGA nanoparticles targeting these cells have been developed to overcome cancer stem cell resistance, demonstrating significant therapeutic potential [ 157 ]. Additionally, magnetic nanoparticles have been employed for targeted drug delivery, with mesoporous silica nanocarriers improving colorectal cancer therapy [ 158 ]. Biomimicry enhances therapeutic delivery, as evidenced by virus-mimicking nucleic acid nanogels for glioblastoma therapy [ 159 ] and non-lipid nucleic acid delivery vectors with dendritic cell tropism for improved nucleic acid delivery [ 160 ]. Furthermore, gene therapy has been integrated with chemotherapy using nanomicelles to co-deliver siAEG-1 and doxorubicin, showcasing a promising approach for gene-drug combinations [ 130 ]. Targeting tumor microenvironment (TME) factors, nanosized carbonic anhydrase inhibitors have been developed to counteract hypoxia in solid tumors [ 161 ]. LyP-1-modified dendrimers have also been utilized for antitumor and antimetastatic therapy, demonstrating receptor-mediated delivery potential [ 162 ]. Additionally, metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) and cell membrane coating have been combined in ligand-modified erythrocyte membrane-cloaked MOF nanoparticles, expanding the potential of nanocarrier design [ 128 ]. Stimuli-responsive and controlled-release systems Nanocarrier design for enhanced cancer therapy has focused on stimuli-responsive systems that allow controlled drug release. pH-responsive nanocarriers, such as amphiphilic dendrimers and charge-reversal polymeric nanoparticles, enable precise drug release in the TME, enhancing chemo-photothermal therapy [ 163 ,  164 ]. Additionally, dual pH/redox-responsive systems provide enhanced selectivity, exemplified by ultra pH-sensitive polymeric nanovesicles for endometrial carcinoma therapy [ 165 ,  166 ]. Redox-sensitive nanoparticles, such as diatomite carriers, allow for intracellular drug release, while ROS-responsive self-assembly nanoplatforms address hypoxia-driven tumor resistance [ 167 ,  168 ]. Novel combination therapies Nanoplatforms incorporating multiple therapeutic modalities have been explored, such as dual-prodrug-based hyaluronic acid nanoplatforms that enhance oxidative stress-induced chemotherapy [ 169 ]. Similarly, dual-targeting SERS-encoded graphene oxide nanocarriers for doxorubicin and 9-aminoacridine co-delivery demonstrate enhanced therapeutic potential [ 170 ]. Light-switchable transgene systems combined with losartan have been utilized for triple-negative breast cancer [ 171 ] while sequential-targeting nanocarriers with pH-controlled charge reversal have improved mitochondria-directed photodynamic immunotherapy [ 172 ]. Magnetosome-based DOX release systems enable tumor synergistic theranostics [ 173 ], and ATP-burning theranostic nanoplatforms sensitize tumors for synergistic therapy [ 174 ]. Nanocarrier-based combination strategies have improved antitumor immunity. Stimulus-responsive mesoporous silicon nanocarriers combined with chemotherapy and photothermal therapy demonstrate significant immune activation potential [ 175 ]. Additionally, enzyme-responsive nanocarriers targeting PD-1 and TGF-β pathways help reverse immunotherapeutic resistance [ 176 ]. Targeted delivery and tumor microenvironment (TME) modulation Nanocarriers designed to enhance drug delivery and penetration include biodegradable imprinted polymers based on ZIF-8/DOX-HA synergistically targeting prostate cancer cells [ 177 ] and pH-sensitive biomimetic nanosystems for tumor deep penetration [ 178 ]. Hybrid nanoassemblies involving natural products, carbon dots, and Cu 2 ⁺ facilitate synergistic hepatocellular carcinoma therapy [ 179 ]. Sialic acid derivatives enhance liposome performance for modulating the immunosuppressive TME [ 180 ], while vitamin-H-channeled nanomicelles target tumors via pH- and enzyme-triggered disassembly [ 181 ]. Other strategies include exosome-based sinomenine delivery for hepatic carcinoma therapy [ 182 ] and Tie2-mediated vascular remodeling using ferritin-based protein C nanoparticles for antitumor and anti-metastatic activities [ 183 ]. Next-generation nanocarriers for precision medicine The development of sophisticated nanocarriers continues to expand the horizons of targeted cancer therapy. Biomimetic approaches enhance therapeutic delivery, as demonstrated by biomimetic nanoplatelets for co-delivery of therapeutic agents [ 184 ] and smart CA IX-targeting nano-mixed micelles for breast cancer therapy [ 185 ]. Additionally, exosome-based glucocorticoid nanoparticles target decidual immune cells for miscarriage treatment [ 186 ]. Advances in tumor imaging and precision therapy include acid-triggered controlled-release phthalocyanine nanoassemblies for photodynamic therapy [ 187 ] and tumor microenvironment-activatable chemotherapy using supramolecular nanodrugs [ 188 ]. Furthermore, biomineralized extracellular vesicles encapsulated in hydrogels provide mitochondrial-targeted tumor therapy [ 189 ]. Programmable hierarchical-responsive nanoCRISPR systems showcase the potential of gene-based therapies [ 190 ], while tumor microenvironment-mimicking macrophage nanovesicles have been developed for colorectal cancer therapy [ 191 ]. Additionally, inhalable CRISPR/Cas9 nanotherapeutics have been designed to immunometabolically reprogram macrophages for acute lung injury intervention [ 192 ]. Integrating multifunctional nanocarriers, stimuli-responsive systems, and TME-modulating strategies has significantly enhanced cancer therapy. Advances in biomimetic nanoparticles, gene-editing nanoplatforms, and CRISPR-based therapies pave the way for personalized, targeted, and highly effective cancer treatments. Future research should focus on optimizing the design of multi-modal nanocarriers, further refining immunotherapy-based nanoparticle strategies, and exploring their translation into clinical applications. Nanoparticle-mediated immunotherapy enhancement Immunotherapy mediated by nanoparticles is a novel method of treating cancer. It uses the unique qualities of nanoparticles to boost immunological responses and increase the effectiveness of treatments. These nanoparticles can be engineered to deliver specific antigens or immune-modulating agents directly to targeted cells, thereby increasing the precision and effectiveness of the treatment while minimizing side effects. [ 211 ,  212 ]. Immunotherapy is an emerging field that leverages nanoparticles'unique properties to improve immunotherapy treatments'efficacy while also exploring synergistic combinations with other therapeutic modalities [ 212 ,  213 ]. This novel strategy aims to enhance cancer treatment by integrating standard therapies such as radiation and chemotherapy to bolster the body's defenses against the disease. This multifaceted approach has the potential to significantly improve patient outcomes by tailoring treatments to individual tumor characteristics and enhancing overall therapeutic effectiveness. Research in this direction is rapidly advancing, with many ongoing clinical trials paving the way for personalized medicine that could transform cancer care. As researchers continue to uncover how nanoparticles interact with immune cells, there is hope for developing targeted delivery systems that maximize treatment efficacy while minimizing side effects. TME-responsive targeted drug delivery The TME is a complex and dynamic ecosystem that plays a pivotal role in cancer progression, metastasis, and therapeutic resistance [ 254 ]. It comprises a heterogeneous mix of stromal cells, immune cells, extracellular matrix (ECM) components, and signaling molecules, all interacting to create a unique pathological environment [ 255 ]. This environment is characterized by hypoxia, acidic pH, elevated levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and overexpressed enzymes, which pose significant challenges to effective drug delivery. However, these same features also provide opportunities for developing TME-responsive targeted drug delivery systems [ 256 ]. In this context, researchers have developed new nanoplatforms that utilize the distinct biochemical and physiological characteristics of the TME to surmount biological barriers and improve therapeutic efficacy. These advancements can potentially revolutionize cancer treatment, allowing for more precise targeting of tumor cells while minimizing damage to surrounding healthy tissues. TME-responsive design: exploiting the tumor microenvironment TME-responsive drug delivery systems are designed to exploit the distinct features of the TME to achieve targeted and controlled release of therapeutic agents. For instance, the acidic pH of the TME (pH 6.0–7.0) compared with normal tissues (pH 7.4) has been utilized to develop pH-sensitive nanoparticles. These nanoparticles undergo structural changes or release their payload in response to the acidic conditions, ensuring site-specific drug delivery. Examples include pH-sensitive polymeric micelles and nanoparticles with acid-labile linkages, such as hydrazone or imine bonds, which hydrolyze in the acidic TME to release drugs like doxorubicin [ 257 ,  258 ]. While TME-responsive targeted drug delivery systems present innovative approaches to enhance cancer treatment, there are significant concerns regarding their efficacy and safety. The TME, while unique, is also highly variable between different tumors and even within the same tumor over time. This heterogeneity can lead to inconsistent responses to TME-responsive therapies, making it challenging to predict their effectiveness across diverse patient populations [ 255 ]. Moreover, the reliance on specific features of the TME, such as acidic pH or hypoxia, raises questions about the potential for unintended consequences. For instance, the acidic conditions targeted by pH-sensitive nanoparticles may not be uniformly present throughout the tumor, resulting in suboptimal drug release in some areas while potentially causing toxicity in others [ 259 ,  260 ]. Similarly, hypoxia-responsive systems may not adequately address the complexities of tumor biology, where regions of varying oxygenation exist, potentially leading to ineffective treatment in well-oxygenated areas [ 261 ]. Furthermore, there is a risk that focusing on TME-responsive designs may distract from more traditional and proven therapeutic strategies. Although innovation is vital, it is imperative to ensure that novel methodologies do not eclipse established therapies that have proven efficacy and safety over time. Whereas TME-responsive drug delivery systems present promising opportunities, their practical implementation may encounter considerable hurdles that require thorough evaluation [ 257 ]. Hypoxia, another hallmark of the TME, has been targeted using hypoxia-responsive nanoparticles. These systems often incorporate nitroimidazole derivatives or hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF)–responsive elements, which activate under low oxygen conditions to release therapeutic agents. For example, hypoxia-activated prodrugs and nanoparticles can enhance the efficacy of chemotherapy and radiotherapy by targeting hypoxic regions within tumors [ 262 – 264 ]. Enzyme-responsive nanoparticles represent another innovative approach. The TME is rich in overexpressed enzymes such as matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) and phospholipase A2, which can be exploited to trigger drug release. Nanoparticles designed with enzyme-cleavable linkers or coatings can selectively release their cargo in the presence of these enzymes, improving tumor specificity and reducing off-target effects [ 265 ]. This tailored administration improves the therapeutic index of anticancer drugs and reduces systemic toxicity, increasing therapy tolerability for patients while optimizing efficacy against malignant cells. Integrating such advanced delivery systems into clinical practice could significantly improve patient outcomes, paving the way for more personalized and effective cancer therapies [ 258 ]. As research progresses, integrating targeted delivery systems with other therapeutic modalities, such as immunotherapy and gene therapy, may yield innovative treatment strategies that enhance antitumor efficacy and surmount resistance mechanisms in cancer cells. Moreover, this multifaceted approach holds promise for revolutionizing cancer treatment, as it allows for a more precise attack on tumors while preserving healthy tissues, ultimately leading to improved quality of life for patients undergoing therapy. Overcoming biological barriers in the TME Despite the promise of TME-responsive designs, several biological barriers hinder effective drug delivery, including anomalous vasculature, dense ECM, interstitial fluid pressure, and immunosuppressive conditions [ 266 ]. To address these challenges, researchers have developed multifunctional nanoplatforms that combine TME-responsive properties with strategies to overcome these barriers. One significant barrier is the dense ECM that limits nanoparticle penetration and diffusion within the tumor. To enhance penetration, size-shrinkable nanoparticles have been developed. These nanoparticles are initially large enough to exploit the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect but shrink in response to TME stimuli (e.g., pH or enzymes) to facilitate deeper tumor penetration [ 267 ,  268 ]. This novel methodology enhances drug delivery efficacy while reducing systemic side effects, resulting in improved patient treatment outcomes. Another difficulty is the immunosuppressive TME, which impedes immune cell function and restricts the effectiveness of immunotherapies. Nanoparticles have been designed to reprogram the TME by targeting TAMs or cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs). For example, iron oxide nanoparticles have been shown to repolarize TAMs from the pro-tumor M2 phenotype to the anti-tumor M1 phenotype, enhancing immune responses and sensitizing tumors to immunotherapy [ 269 ]. This strategy boosts the efficacy of existing treatments and paves the way for novel combination therapies that can overcome resistance mechanisms inherent in tumor biology. By integrating these innovative approaches, researchers hope they can create more effective treatment regimens that attack the tumor directly and empower the immune system to recognize and eliminate cancer cells more efficiently. Interstitial fluid pressure (IFP) and abnormal vasculature also impede drug delivery. To address this, vascular normalization strategies have been employed using nanoparticles that deliver anti-angiogenic agents, including VEGF inhibitors, to restore normal blood flow and reduce IFP. This method optimizes medication delivery and augments the effectiveness of combination therapies, including chemotherapy and immunotherapy [ 270 ], ultimately leading to better patient outcomes and increased survival rates. Researchers seek to enhance the TME to surmount obstacles that have traditionally constrained the efficacy of cancer therapies, hence facilitating more personalized and focused treatment approaches [ 271 ,  272 ]. The creation of TME-responsive targeted drug delivery systems signifies a revolutionary method in cancer treatment, tackling the specific obstacles presented by the TME while utilizing its unique biochemical and physiological traits. Researchers are making significant strides in enhancing the specificity and efficacy of drug delivery to tumor sites by employing innovative strategies such as pH-sensitive nanoparticles, hypoxia-responsive systems, and enzyme-cleavable linkers. However, the inherent heterogeneity of the TME presents considerable challenges that necessitate a cautious and comprehensive understanding of these systems'efficacy and safety. Incorporating TME-responsive designs with conventional therapeutic approaches and methods to surmount biological obstacles, such as dense extracellular matrix and immunosuppressive environments, shows potential for enhancing patient outcomes. As research advances, integrating these sophisticated delivery methods with immunotherapy and gene therapy may result in innovative treatment options that boost therapeutic efficacy and improve the quality of life for cancer patients. Overall, while the prospects of TME-responsive drug delivery systems are promising, ongoing research and clinical validation are essential to fully realize their potential in revolutionizing cancer treatment. Targeted delivery and TME exploitation Targeting specific receptors and exploiting the TME's unique characteristics are crucial for effective nanomedicine. Xiao, Liu [ 273 ] reported luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone (LHRH)-targeted redox-responsive crosslinked micelles for selective drug delivery and effective chemotherapy in triple-negative breast cancer, demonstrating superior tumor distribution and therapeutic outcomes. Likewise, [ 120 ] designed a pH-responsive nano-drug delivery system based on dynamic boronic acid/ester transformation, which exhibited high anticancer activity with low systemic toxicity by targeting the acidic tumor microenvironment. This should be cited as Li et al. [ 274 ] prepared poly(aspartic acid)-based pH-responsive targeting co-delivery nanoparticles, achieving enhanced cellular uptake and cytotoxicity through hyaluronic acid ligand-mediated active targeting and pH-triggered drug release. Helmi, Elshishiny [ 275 ] synthesized PEGylated chitosan nanoparticles labeled with monoclonal antibodies, enabling targeted doxorubicin delivery and release within the breast cancer environment, thus reducing systemic toxicity. Stimuli-responsive nanocarriers, as demonstrated by Shi, Chen [ 276 ] with their ROS-responsive dextran nanosystem, are gaining prominence for their ability to achieve controlled drug release and enhance therapeutic efficacy. Zhang, Wang [ 277 ] and Feng, Xu [ 278 ] further underscored the potential of pH and ROS dual-responsive nanocarriers and pH-responsive micelles, respectively, to improve drug delivery and therapeutic outcomes. Moreover, this multifaceted approach holds promise for revolutionizing cancer treatment, as it allows for a more precise attack on tumors while preserving healthy tissues, ultimately leading to improved quality of life for patients undergoing therapy.

Overcoming biological barriers in the TME Despite the promise of TME-responsive designs, several biological barriers hinder effective drug delivery, including anomalous vasculature, dense ECM, interstitial fluid pressure, and immunosuppressive conditions [ 266 ]. To address these challenges, researchers have developed multifunctional nanoplatforms that combine TME-responsive properties with strategies to overcome these barriers. One significant barrier is the dense ECM that limits nanoparticle penetration and diffusion within the tumor. To enhance penetration, size-shrinkable nanoparticles have been developed. These nanoparticles are initially large enough to exploit the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect but shrink in response to TME stimuli (e.g., pH or enzymes) to facilitate deeper tumor penetration [ 267 ,  268 ]. This novel methodology enhances drug delivery efficacy while reducing systemic side effects, resulting in improved patient treatment outcomes. Another difficulty is the immunosuppressive TME, which impedes immune cell function and restricts the effectiveness of immunotherapies. Nanoparticles have been designed to reprogram the TME by targeting TAMs or cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs). For example, iron oxide nanoparticles have been shown to repolarize TAMs from the pro-tumor M2 phenotype to the anti-tumor M1 phenotype, enhancing immune responses and sensitizing tumors to immunotherapy [ 269 ]. This strategy boosts the efficacy of existing treatments and paves the way for novel combination therapies that can overcome resistance mechanisms inherent in tumor biology. By integrating these innovative approaches, researchers hope they can create more effective treatment regimens that attack the tumor directly and empower the immune system to recognize and eliminate cancer cells more efficiently. Interstitial fluid pressure (IFP) and abnormal vasculature also impede drug delivery. To address this, vascular normalization strategies have been employed using nanoparticles that deliver anti-angiogenic agents, including VEGF inhibitors, to restore normal blood flow and reduce IFP. This method optimizes medication delivery and augments the effectiveness of combination therapies, including chemotherapy and immunotherapy [ 270 ], ultimately leading to better patient outcomes and increased survival rates. Researchers seek to enhance the TME to surmount obstacles that have traditionally constrained the efficacy of cancer therapies, hence facilitating more personalized and focused treatment approaches [ 271 ,  272 ]. The creation of TME-responsive targeted drug delivery systems signifies a revolutionary method in cancer treatment, tackling the specific obstacles presented by the TME while utilizing its unique biochemical and physiological traits. Researchers are making significant strides in enhancing the specificity and efficacy of drug delivery to tumor sites by employing innovative strategies such as pH-sensitive nanoparticles, hypoxia-responsive systems, and enzyme-cleavable linkers. However, the inherent heterogeneity of the TME presents considerable challenges that necessitate a cautious and comprehensive understanding of these systems'efficacy and safety. Incorporating TME-responsive designs with conventional therapeutic approaches and methods to surmount biological obstacles, such as dense extracellular matrix and immunosuppressive environments, shows potential for enhancing patient outcomes. As research advances, integrating these sophisticated delivery methods with immunotherapy and gene therapy may result in innovative treatment options that boost therapeutic efficacy and improve the quality of life for cancer patients. Overall, while the prospects of TME-responsive drug delivery systems are promising, ongoing research and clinical validation are essential to fully realize their potential in revolutionizing cancer treatment.

Targeted delivery and TME exploitation Targeting specific receptors and exploiting the TME's unique characteristics are crucial for effective nanomedicine. Xiao, Liu [ 273 ] reported luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone (LHRH)-targeted redox-responsive crosslinked micelles for selective drug delivery and effective chemotherapy in triple-negative breast cancer, demonstrating superior tumor distribution and therapeutic outcomes. Likewise, [ 120 ] designed a pH-responsive nano-drug delivery system based on dynamic boronic acid/ester transformation, which exhibited high anticancer activity with low systemic toxicity by targeting the acidic tumor microenvironment. This should be cited as Li et al. [ 274 ] prepared poly(aspartic acid)-based pH-responsive targeting co-delivery nanoparticles, achieving enhanced cellular uptake and cytotoxicity through hyaluronic acid ligand-mediated active targeting and pH-triggered drug release. Helmi, Elshishiny [ 275 ] synthesized PEGylated chitosan nanoparticles labeled with monoclonal antibodies, enabling targeted doxorubicin delivery and release within the breast cancer environment, thus reducing systemic toxicity. Stimuli-responsive nanocarriers, as demonstrated by Shi, Chen [ 276 ] with their ROS-responsive dextran nanosystem, are gaining prominence for their ability to achieve controlled drug release and enhance therapeutic efficacy. Zhang, Wang [ 277 ] and Feng, Xu [ 278 ] further underscored the potential of pH and ROS dual-responsive nanocarriers and pH-responsive micelles, respectively, to improve drug delivery and therapeutic outcomes.

Personalized nanomedicine and targeting cancer stem cells Cancer stem cells (CSCs) play a pivotal role in therapeutic resistance and metastasis across multiple malignancies, necessitating innovative strategies for their effective targeting (Fig.  5 ). Recent research has provided insights into CSC vulnerabilities, highlighting distinct mechanisms such as metabolic reprogramming, immune evasion, and niche adaptation that sustain their survival and tumorigenic potential. Fig. 5 A schematic representation of nanoparticles targeting cancer stem cells. On the left, differentiated tumor cells and cancer stem cells are depicted within a tumor mass. The nanoparticle conjugated with a chemotherapeutic agent specifically designed to target the CSC marker is shown on the right. The nanoparticle structure consists of a linker chain connecting the chemotherapeutic agent to the targeting antibody, which binds to the cancer stem cell's CSC marker, ensuring targeted treatment delivery. The figure is created with BioRender Single-cell transcriptomic analysis in colorectal cancer identified a stem-like cell cluster with organ-specific metastatic preferences mediated through DLL4-NOTCH signaling and metabolic shifts [ 289 ]. In lung cancer, targeting carnitine palmitoyl transferase 1 A (CPT1 A) induced ferroptosis in CSCs enhances immunotherapy efficacy by disrupting a CPT1 A/c-Myc positive feedback loop that protects against oxidative stress [ 290 ]. Similarly, acute myeloid leukemia (AML) stem cells rely on ferritinophagy, mediated by NCOA4, to sustain quiescence, making iron metabolism an exploitable vulnerability [ 291 ]. In glioblastoma, CSCs exhibit unique metabolic dependencies, such as threonine metabolism fueling tumor growth through YRDC-mediated translational reprogramming, suggesting a potential avenue for dietary interventions [ 292 ]. Additionally, glioblastoma stem cells integrate into neural circuits, where cholinergic neurons drive tumor invasion, and radiotherapy further enhances neuron-tumor connectivity, implicating neuronal activity inhibition as a therapeutic strategy [ 293 ]. Long non-coding RNA (LINC00115) promotes chemoresistant breast CSC stemness and metastasis via SETDB1/PLK3/HIF1α signaling, presenting a novel target for intervention [ 294 ]. In pancreatic cancer, cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF) autophagy upregulates CD274/PDL1 expression, impairing antitumor immunity and suggesting that CAF autophagy inhibition with immunotherapy could improve treatment responses [ 295 ]. Finally, WNT5B has been identified as a driver of osteosarcoma stemness, chemoresistance, and metastasis, emphasizing the need for novel CSC-targeting therapies [ 296 ]. Nanomedicine strategies for targeting CSCs Nanoparticle-mediated drug delivery and combination therapies are emerging as effective approaches for eliminating CSCs and modulating the tumor microenvironment (TME). Engineered microparticles co-loaded with tumor antigen and resiquimod (imidazoquinoline) have successfully reprogrammed tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), fostering the expansion of stem-like CD8 + T cells and enhancing anti-PD-1 therapy in hepatocellular carcinoma and melanoma models [ 297 ]. Nanomedicine has enabled novel strategies to eradicate CSCs by modulating their metabolism and immune evasion mechanisms. Cuproptosis-based nanomedicine, leveraging copper ionophores in combination with photothermal therapy, has demonstrated efficacy in suppressing triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) by eliminating CSCs and enhancing antitumor immune responses [ 209 ]. Similarly, exosome-sheathed porous silica nanoparticles co-delivering 3,3'-diindolylmethane and doxorubicin have shown promise in attenuating epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in TNBC, reducing CSC-driven malignancies [ 298 ]. The use of hydrogel-based dual-drug nanocarriers encapsulating anti-CSC agents such as salinomycin or curcumin with lauroyl-gemcitabine offers a promising approach for residual glioblastoma treatment, preventing tumor recurrence [ 299 ]. Glutaminolysis inhibition has emerged as a viable method to enhance photodynamic therapy (PDT) efficacy against CSCs by disrupting reactive oxygen species (ROS) defense, as demonstrated by nanoparticle-assisted combination therapies [ 300 ]. Furthermore, HYL001, a novel lonidamine derivative, selectively targets CSC mitochondria by blocking glutamine metabolism, exhibiting substantial antitumor activity [ 301 ]. Several natural compounds and biomimetic approaches have been explored for CSC-targeted therapies. Viridiflorol, a bioactive terpenoid, has demonstrated potent anti-neoplastic effects by inducing apoptosis in breast, lung, and brain cancer cells [ 302 ]. Additionally, nano-immuno-conjugates combining photosensitizers, gold nanoparticles, and anti-CD271 antibodies have been developed to enhance PDT against esophageal cancer stem cells, offering a promising avenue for precision medicine [ 303 ]. Advances in nanomaterial design for CSC therapy Recent nanomaterial design and characterization innovations have refined CSC-targeted therapy, enabling improved drug delivery, enhanced biocompatibility, and precision targeting [ 304 ]. Stimuli-responsive biocompatible nanoparticles tailored for the TME have been developed, emphasizing the need for thorough characterization using 3D tumor spheroid models to optimize in vitro evaluation [ 305 ]. A functionalized PAMAM-based nanoformulation has been designed for targeted 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) delivery in hepatocellular carcinoma, demonstrating enhanced tumor accumulation and improved therapeutic efficiency. Similarly, metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) have been explored as multifunctional nanocarriers for drug delivery and catalytic therapy, with promising results in CSC-targeting applications [ 306 ,  307 ]. Overcoming intracellular barriers and enhancing drug penetration Overcoming intracellular drug delivery challenges and TME-imposed barriers remains a critical area of research. A significant limitation in CSC-targeted therapy is lysosomal sequestration of therapeutic agents, which prevents drugs from reaching intracellular targets effectively [351. To address this, TME-responsive protein nanogel-platelet hybrid systems have been developed to facilitate cytosolic drug release, bypassing endosomal entrapment and ensuring efficient intracellular drug delivery [ 308 ]. Future directions and clinical implications Integrating personalized nanomedicine, CSC-targeted therapies, and stimuli-responsive drug delivery systems holds immense potential for revolutionizing cancer treatment. Future research should optimize nanocarrier designs to enhance CSC targeting, improving specificity and drug payload capacity while minimizing off-target effects. Developing combination therapies that exploit CSC vulnerabilities and integrate immune modulation strategies will be crucial in overcoming resistance mechanisms. Additionally, advancing biomimetic nanomedicine to harness natural carrier systems can improve drug stability, bioavailability, and targeted delivery. Enhancing in vivo validation through clinical studies will be essential to evaluate the efficacy of nanomedicine-based CSC-targeting approaches, ensuring their translation into clinical practice. Addressing these key challenges could significantly improve cancer prognosis, reduce relapse rates, and pave the way for more effective and durable treatment strategies.

Advanced nanomedicine techniques Advanced nanomedicine technologies are revolutionizing healthcare by enabling precise drug delivery, enhancing imaging techniques, and facilitating personalized treatment strategies that optimize patient outcomes. These innovations are driving the development of more effective therapies that reduce side effects while maximizing therapeutic efficacy, ushering in a new era of precision medicine (Fig.  6 ). Fig. 6 Nanotechnology approaches for cancer diagnosis and treatment use nanostructures like liposomes, polymers, micelles, and dendrimers to deliver drugs with active or passive targeting mechanisms. Cancer can be diagnosed using nanotechnology through microfluidic chips, biomarker detection, nanoscale probes, and quantum dots. Treatment options include light-activated gene silencing, RNA-based nanotherapies, strategies to overcome drug resistance, and nanoparticle-delivered CRISPR/Cas9 systems. The figure is created with BioRender Gene therapy based on nanoparticles (siRNA, miRNA, CRISPR) Gene therapy has enormous promise for treating cancer because it precisely modifies cellular functions using nucleic acids. However, efficiently delivering gene-editing tools like CRISPR/Cas to solid tumors remains a significant challenge. Researchers have looked into novel approaches to get around this, such as altering the TME and creating non-viral nanoparticle delivery systems. Targeting the mechanics of tumor tissue to increase the effectiveness of gene editing is one promising strategy. A multiplexed dendrimer lipid nanoparticle (LNP) system that co-delivers focal adhesion kinase (FAK) siRNA, Cas9 mRNA, and sgRNA (siFAK + CRISPR-LNPs) [ 309 ]. This system significantly improved gene editing in tumor spheroids by reducing extracellular matrix (ECM) stiffness, which enhanced nanoparticle uptake and penetration. The knockdown of FAK led to a more than tenfold increase in gene editing efficiency. Additionally, using siFAK + CRISPR-PD-L1-LNPs disrupted PD-L1 expression, significantly inhibiting tumor growth and metastasis in mouse models. These findings highlight the potential of modulating tumor mechanics to improve gene editing and offer a synergistic approach for nanoparticle-based therapies [ 309 ]. Another critical strategy involves the development of stimuli-responsive non-viral nanoparticles for gene delivery. Reichel and Traeger (2023) emphasized the challenges of delivering nucleic acids, such as their high molar mass and negative charge. The success of mRNA-based vaccines has spurred the development of advanced gene transporters capable of providing various nucleic acids, including DNA (pDNA) and RNA (mRNA, siRNA, miRNA, gRNA, or ASOs). These stimuli-responsive nanoparticles enable precise gene release and expression control, enhancing therapeutic outcomes [ 310 ]. In sum, by combining mechanical modulation of the TME with advanced non-viral nanoparticle delivery systems, researchers are making significant progress in enhancing gene therapy for cancer. These approaches provide new opportunities for precise gene editing and targeted delivery, ultimately improving the potential of gene therapy as a transformative tool in cancer treatment. Nanomaterial-based photodynamic and photothermal therapy Photodynamic therapy (PDT) and photothermal therapy (PTT), two promising non-invasive cancer treatment modalities, are frequently combined to increase therapeutic efficacy. However, issues like hypoxia, drug resistance, and limited tumor targeting make the creation of advanced nanomedicines necessary. Recent research has concentrated on creating multifunctional nanoparticles that can synergistically deliver PDT and PTT to improve diagnosis and treatment monitoring. These nanoparticles frequently incorporate imaging capabilities. (Please cite references in this paragraph). One strategy involves utilizing biomimetic nanoparticles, such as platelet membrane-camouflaged magnetic nanoparticles (Fe3O4-SAS@PLT), which trigger ferroptosis and generate mild immunogenicity, enhancing immunotherapy response in non-inflamed tumors [ 311 ]. These nanoparticles repolarize macrophages and improve the efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade therapy (Fig.  7 ).
